title: Marketing as Infrastructure: On the Substitutability of Marketing Investment and Logistics Infrastructure in Service Networks

detail.title: Marketing as Infrastructure: On the Substitutability of Marketing Investment and Logistics Infrastructure in Service Networks
detail.abstract: Service networks that operate both physical access points and home delivery face a dual optimization problem: where to place infrastructure, and how to price channel alternatives. These decisions are conventionally treated as separate. This paper demonstrates that they interact through consumer spatial behavior: a marketing-funded price subsidy shifts the consumer indifference distance d*, expanding each station's geographic catchment, and can-above a quantifiable threshold-render a planned facility redundant. We formalize this substitution relationship and derive the conditions under which it is economically rational. Numerical analysis using a calibrated urban demand model reveals that the relationship is non-monotonic: optimal network size does not decrease uniformly as marketing investment grows. We show that structural network change requires both sufficient marketing budget and a minimum intrinsic station utility-neither alone is sufficient. We discuss implications for joint optimization of network design and channel pricing, and outline directions for empirical validation.

detail.abstract: We study the evolution of digital and artificial intelligence (AI) skill demand across six economies in Asia and the Pacific between 2019 and 2024 using millions of online job postings from Indeed and a large language model to classify them by their required level of digital and AI proficiency. Digital skill requirements are widespread across the occupational distribution and have expanded most rapidly in traditionally low and mid digital jobs, pointing to broad technological diffusion. Jobs requiring higher digital proficiency command substantially higher pay, even when comparing job postings within the same job title and controlling for cognitive, interpersonal, organizational, and technical skill requirements. We estimate wage premia of approximately 4%, 11%, and 26% for basic, intermediate, and advanced digital skills, respectively, with intermediate and advanced digital skills commanding larger premia than many other highly rewarded skills. We also document a sharp increase in demand for AI-related competencies, particularly those related to the use of AI tools.

title: When Suffering Hurts More: Suffering for Material Products Reduces Intrinsic Motivation, Well-Being, and Repurchase Intention Compared to Experiences

detail.title: When Suffering Hurts More: Suffering for Material Products Reduces Intrinsic Motivation, Well-Being, and Repurchase Intention Compared to Experiences
detail.abstract: Suffering (significant effort with negative valence) is increasingly present in consumption, yet little is known about when it undermines motivation or well-being. This paper examines how suffering affects intrinsic motivation, well-being, and repurchase intention, moderated by material and experiential product types. Across four studies, we test whether suffering (vs. control) has differential effects on consumer outcomes. Study 1 (N = 300) shows that suffering reduces well-being in material but not experiential purchases. Studies 2a (N = 429) and 2b (N = 394) replicate this across scenarios, showing that suffering in material contexts lowers well-being and repurchase intention, effects not observed for experiential purchases. Study 3 (N = 487) shows that in material contexts, suffering reduces intrinsic motivation and well-being, thereby decreasing repurchase intention. These findings demonstrate that suffering undermines outcomes in material consumption, while experiential consumption appears insulated. We extend self-determination theory by showing how suffering impacts motivation across consumption types. The full paper is available at  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusres.2025.115506

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Auckland Business School Research Paper

detail.abstract: Purpose-This study aims to examine the comparative effect that two widespread technologies, text-based chatbots and voicebots, have on perceived relief and subsequent customer outcomes in service failure settings. The moderating effect of service failure severity on this mediation relationship is also evaluated. Design/methodology/approach-This research adopts an experiential design, consisting of an initial exploratory field study (Study 1), to examine how AI bot modality influences real-world customer evaluations in a naturalistic service failure setting. This was followed by two between-subjects experimental studies (Studies 2 and 3), which sought to validate the underlying mechanism (i.e. perceived relief) and test the moderating role of service failure severity under controlled conditions. Findings-Study 1 provided initial empirical evidence that, in a real-world service failure context, customers who interacted with a chatbot (vs a voicebot) gave significantly higher satisfaction ratings. Study 2 provided evidence of the positive indirect effect of chatbots on customer reviews via perceived relief. Study 3 supported this mediation relationship while also demonstrating that such a relationship is moderated by the severity of the service failure. Research limitations/implications-Based on the findings of this study, it would be a stretch to conclude that chatbots are invariably better. The dynamic nature of customer preferences and technological advancements necessitates continuous evaluation and adaptation of customer service strategies. Managers should regularly review the performance of both chatbots and voicebots, incorporating customer feedback and technological improvements to optimize their service delivery approaches. By understanding and applying these insights, managers can better navigate service failures, ultimately leading to improved customer outcomes. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1108/EJM-08-2024-0693

detail.title: The Moderating Role of Intrinsic and Quest Religiosity on the Effectiveness of Religious Appeals in Promoting Cultured Meat
detail.abstract: In response to the environmental impacts of agricultural food production, alternative food sources have been developed over the past few decades. One of the latest innovations is 'cultured meat.' Despite offering an alternative to raising animals for meat, the idea of lab-grown meat has received a mixed response from religious consumers. Thus, the present research investigates the effect of using religious appeals in advertising on consumers' intention to purchase cultured meat. The authors propose that consumers' religiosity (intrinsic and quest religiosity) moderates their green identity, which subsequently affects their intentions to purchase cultured meat. The results of two experimental studies show that at low levels of quest religiosity, a religious (vs. non-religious) appeal led to higher intentions to purchase cultured meat among participants with high (but not low) levels of intrinsic religiosity. The findings of this research have implications for religious leaders, ethicists, and policymakers when dealing with the commercialization of cultured meat. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10551-025-05954-6

detail.abstract: In an era where corporate social responsibility (CSR) dominates organizational agendas, the dimension of team diversity remains largely overshadowed. Despite its transformative potential, the interplay between team diversity and consumer product acceptance has been underrepresented in the literature. This study illuminates the potency of team diversity as a critical CSR dimension, revealing its impact on bolstering product acceptance. In the context of clean meat, two experimental studies demonstrate that consumers are more willing to try a product developed by a company with a more diverse team (e.g. race and gender), as such firms are likely to account for a diversity of perspectives, thus enhancing consumer trust. Additionally, perceived authenticity moderates this effect, in that consumers of more authentic brands will be more trusting, regardless of the level of team diversity. The study provides critical insights into how consumers' perception of team diversity within the firm influences product adoption, and how both team diversity and perceived authenticity drive trustworthiness. The findings offer practical implications for marketers of clean meat and other novel products to accelerate market acceptance and consequently, address broader societal challenges, whilst emphasizing the importance of fostering diversity and promoting brand authenticity. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1177/14413582241235414

detail.abstract: While veganism has been growing and receiving increasing attention, there is a gap on how factors such as health and environmental beliefs and anti-speciesism values, that create attitude towards their diets, influence their vegan behaviour. Furthermore, the role of social stigma experienced by vegans has not been examined within this context. Building on the value-attitude-behaviour model, the present study addresses this gap by conceptualizing these different streams of variables to build a testable conceptual framework for understanding how these factors contribute to maintaining a vegan lifestyle. The study uses structural equation modelling to analyse the data on 315 vegan consumers, testing the framework and its variables. The study shows that the valueattitude-behaviour model can successfully be applied to vegan behaviour. The findings show that anti-speciesism values are strong predictors of a positive attitude toward a vegan diet. Furthermore, social stigma does not inhibit consumers from maintaining a vegan lifestyle. Ultimately, the study contributes to a novel multifaceted model for understanding veganism in broader terms, allowing for the examination of other influencing factors on a complex outcome. The findings are useful for policymakers and marketing practitioners to engage in understanding behavioural segments.  The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2021.104479

detail.abstract: Robots are increasingly deployed in frontline service roles to interact directly with customers. However, little is known about how robots should communicate in emotionally charged situations, such as service failures that elicit customer anger. Across three experimental studies, we show that when service robots acknowledge customer anger using the emotion specific term "angry" rather than the more generic term "bad," customers perceive the robot as more emotionally competent and report higher satisfaction. We further show that this effect is specific to service robots and does not extend to humans in the same roles. These findings highlight how subtle design choices in robots' emotional communication shape customer responses in anger driven service interactions and suggest that careful attention to emotional context is critical when deploying robots in service recovery settings. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusres.2026.115971

detail.abstract: Content created by employing artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms, also known as synthetic content, promises to radically change the advertising and marketing landscape in the coming decades, presumably for the better. It is fundamental for advertising and marketing scholars and practitioners to have solid knowledge of how synthetic content is perceived by consumers before widespread adoption is promoted. Across three experimental studies we tested how consumers in charitable giving contexts reacted to advertising messages featuring content generated by an AI neural network. We show that potential donors responded differently to children's faces when they knew they had been generated by AI. Study 1 established that awareness of the falsity of a face or its status as an AI-generated image has a negative impact on donation intentions. This negative impact is serially mediated by empathy and anticipatory guilt and empathy and emotion perception. Study 2 investigated several motives for employing AI-generated images and indicated that charities employing those images can benefit by making their ethical motives salient. Finally, Study 3 revealed that under extraordinary circumstances the use of AI images by charities is considered acceptable by consumers and is likely to lead to similar outcomes as the use of real images. Therefore, we recommend a cautious approach to the adoption of synthetic content. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1080/00913367.2023.2183285

title: AI Adoption and Systemic Risk: A Multi-Loop Causal Analysis

detail.title: AI Adoption and Systemic Risk: A Multi-Loop Causal Analysis
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the structural risks arising from large‑scale AI adoption, not as isolated disruptions, but as a network of interconnected feedback loops. Each locally rational decision to automate, cut costs, or integrate AI, when scaled across firms, sectors and institutions, can generate reinforcing causal loops that reshape economic stability in ways that are difficult to interrupt once underway.

The analysis constructs a nine‑loop causal architecture, distinguishing primary economic loops (corporate automation, financial cascade, institutional erosion), structural constraints (global dependency, rote conditioning, cognitive stratification), amplifying loops (energy, distraction), and a meta‑loop (recovery tool destruction). A central innovation is tracking not only what each loop produces, but which corrective resource it depletes – wage income, credit markets, state capacity, cognitive adaptability, political coalition, and public understanding.

A Cognitive Tier Framework (Tiers 1–5) explains why displacement is concentrated in procedural (Tier 2) work and why retraining cannot close the gap: Tier 3+ thinking is a conditioning pattern, not a knowledge level that can be taught in short courses. The paper identifies six vulnerability thresholds (demand floor breach, institutional capacity loss, cognitive workforce sufficiency, sovereignty transfer, algorithmic financial synchronisation, fiscal‑redistribution paradox lock) and maps risk pathways across six observable stages of systemic stress.

The framework is purely theoretical – a causal problem‑space analysis. It makes no claim that the described outcomes are inevitable. Instead, it maps the conditions under which systemic erosion becomes plausible, identifies boundary conditions that would weaken each loop, and provides a falsifiable structure for empirical testing. The paper closes with a discussion of structural interventions (pre‑funding, education reform, energy decoupling) and their implementation sequencing, alongside an appendix formalising the model as a system of proportionality relations.

title: Why We Like To Touch: Consumers' Tactile Esthetic Appreciation Explained By A Balanced Combination Of Unity And Variety In Product Designs

detail.title: Why We Like To Touch: Consumers' Tactile Esthetic Appreciation Explained By A Balanced Combination Of Unity And Variety In Product Designs
detail.abstract: Tactile experiences are a pivotal part of consumer behavior and choice. However, very little is known about why consumers esthetically appreciate touching products. The principle of Unity-in-Variety, stating that consumers like to perceive variety but only when this variety is presented as a coherent whole, has been shown to partly explain consumers' esthetic appreciation in the visual domain. We theorize that the psychological mechanisms underlying the esthetic principle of Unity-in-Variety are modality-independent, and therefore that this principle also applies to consumers' tactile esthetic appreciation. Across three studies, using existing products and novel 3D printed product designs systematically manipulated along the perceptual dimensions of unity and variety, we show that both unity and variety independently contribute to tactile esthetic appreciation. Furthermore, because unity and variety are inherently partial opposites, esthetic appreciation of products is highest when both unity and variety are simultaneously maximized. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1002/mar.21798

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can often assist writers more effectively when the tools have access to the writers’ goals, preferences, habits, subject-matter interests, and writing style.  This article describes a process for developing a personalized writing system that can be used to improve AI-assisted writing.

The process involves assembling representative writing samples, using AI to analyze recurring stylistic and substantive patterns, identifying strengths and opportunities for improvement, examining scholarly interests and themes, reflecting on changes in one's writing over time, and creating a personalized writing profile that can be uploaded into future AI chats.  The article also describes how writers can combine the profile with a personalized AI assistant document to create a writing system for future projects.

In addition to improving the quality and consistency of AI assistance, the process can help writers better understand their own writing practices, scholarly interests, and professional development.  The resulting writing system can be revised periodically as writing habits, interests, and goals evolve.  The process is particularly well suited for scholars and other professionals who engage in sustained writing projects over time.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) can assist scholars at many stages of the writing process, including brainstorming, research, organization, drafting, revision, and editing.  However, AI often produces generic responses unless it is provided with information about the writer’s preferences and clear instructions about how to assist.

This article provides a practical template for using AI as a personalized assistant throughout the scholarly writing process.  The template includes guidance for using AI before, during, and after drafting to help develop ideas, analyze arguments, consider audience reactions, improve organization and language, conduct substantive reviews, and perform copy editing.  The template is intended as a starting point that writers may use as provided or modify to create a document reflecting their own preferences, goals, disciplines, audiences, and writing practices.

The writing assistant document is designed to be used together with a personalized writing profile document, described in a companion article, Using AI to Understand Your Scholarly Writing and Development.  That article describes a process for developing the profile based on a writer's prior work, interests, goals, and stylistic patterns.  The profile document helps AI understand the writer's interests, goals, preferences, and writing style.  The assistant document helps AI understand how to assist the writer throughout the writing process.  Together, the writing profile and assistant documents can be combined into a personalized AI writing system document that provides tailored assistance while helping writers preserve their voice, exercise independent judgment, and retain intellectual control of their work.

detail.title: The Role of Demand-Based Scarcity Appeals in Promoting Cultured Meat

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Auckland Business School Research Paper

detail.abstract: A significant barrier to the adoption of cultured meat is perceptions of the product as risky. Across three experimental studies, we show that scarcity appeals that are demand-based constitute an effective strategy for promoting cultured meat because of their negative influence on perceptions of risk. In study 1, we show that a demand-based scarcity appeal is more effective than a supply-based scarcity appeal (or no scarcity appeal) for promoting cultured meat and that this effect is mediated by consumer perceptions of risk. In study 2, we show that the effect of the type of scarcity appeals on perceptions of risk is moderated by perceived naturalness. In particular, we show that demand-based scarcity appeals are especially effective when targeted at consumers who consider cultured meat unnatural. In study 3, we retest our moderated mediation model and show that it is corroborated by employing new stimuli and measures. We contribute to the literature on factors that have a nuanced impact on the acceptance of cultured meat as well as to the academic literature on advertising appeals and social norms. Our findings also offer insights for managers on crafting marketing communications that reduce perceptions of risk associated with cultured meat. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1002/mar.21821

detail.abstract: The entertainment world is at a turning point in its history. Over the past few decades, it's been a gradual digital revolution, and now it's an era of fast consolidation, with legacy media giants and tech-fueled streaming services competing against each other to reach the critical mass needed to make the business viable. Warner Bros. Discovery, Inc. (WBD) is a major U.S. media group known for its film production, television broadcasting, and television streaming services, while Paramount Skydance Corporation is a subsidiary of Warner Bros. Entertainment, Inc. (DISN). On February 27, 2026, Warner Bros. Discovery, Inc. (WBD) announced an acquisition of its television streaming rival, Paramount Skydance Corporation, for approximately $110 billion. Two of the biggest Hollywood studios, two OTT streaming services (Paramount+ and Max) and a massive library of well-known IP are coming together in the deal, which replaces a bid from Netflix. This paper adopts a qualitative approach, using a case-study primary research approach with secondary research, to explore the strategic rationale, financial implications, regulatory context and market implications of the Paramount-WBD merger. The study is based on financial disclosures, media industry reports and published research on media consolidation, as well as original data analysis of box office trends around the world, examining the impact this mega merger will have on the competitive landscape of the streaming industry, and the potential long term consequences of theatrical cinema. Key findings include that the merger presents considerable synergy potential of more than USD 6 billion, but also induces a high level of debt load, is subject to antitrust scrutiny and poses the risk of content homogenization. The paper finds that the Paramount-WBD merger is a symptom and catalyst of a much wider structural change in global entertainment, and will have far-reaching implications for studios, cinema chains, creative communities and audiences around the world.

detail.title: Non-User Externalities

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2026-76
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We review an emerging literature on how non-user externalities-the benefits or harms that product adoption imposes differentially on non-users versus users-shape market outcomes. We first present a unified framework that distinguishes non-user externalities from network effects and classic externalities, such as pollution. A key distinction is that those harmed by classic externalities cannot mitigate harm by joining the externality-producing activity, whereas those harmed by negative non-user externalities can-simply by becoming users. This can expand the harm borne by remaining non-users, generating cascade dynamics that can culminate in product market traps: situations in which individuals would prefer the product not to exist, yet nonetheless choose to adopt it rather than remaining non-users. Using new survey evidence covering 25 product markets, we document that negative non-user externalities are pervasive, that the mechanisms behind them differ systematically across products, and that they generate adoption pressure on non-users. We then discuss how non-user externalities affect welfare analysis, firms' strategic incentives, and market structure. We conclude by discussing policy responses, including design regulation and collective coordination mechanisms.

detail.abstract: Private-equity (PE) consolidation activity in fragmented industries follows recognisable stage patterns, but the empirical literature has primarily documented these patterns ex post, after consolidation cycles complete. This paper proposes an ex ante cycle-stage classification framework and applies it to fifteen U.S. service and trade industries currently exhibiting heterogeneous consolidation activity. The framework draws on three observable signals: the count of named PE-backed platforms operating in a vertical (zero to one indicating a pre-cycle stage, one to three early-cycle, four to eight mid-cycle, and above eight late-cycle), trade-press coverage frequency, and the trajectory of observed transaction multiples. The framework is calibrated against two completed reference cycles, the U.S. HVAC consolidation wave of 2018–2022 and the roofing wave of 2024–2026, and applied to fifteen candidate industries including funeral services, electrical contracting, IT managed services, accounting, marketing services, eldercare subsegments, masonry, paint contracting, and residential cleaning. The analysis finds that funeral services remains durably pre-cycle despite four decades of activity by Service Corporation International, that IT managed services and accounting are in mid-cycle expansion with active named platforms (Citrin Cooperman, Aprio, ConvergeOne, Evergreen Services Group, Logically), and that electrical contracting, masonry, paint contracting, and residential cleaning are at pre-cycle or early-cycle stages with platform formation expected over a twenty-four to forty-eight month horizon. The paper situates these findings within the industry-life-cycle literature originating with Gort and Klepper and within the buy-and-build empirical literature, and discusses implications for owners considering sale timing, capital allocators evaluating sector entry, and intermediaries advising on process design. Limitations of forward-looking classification and self-selection of the analyst's data window are acknowledged.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Communication, and Strategic Pricing: Evidence from Large Language Models
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School - Department of Economics, The Rockwool Foundation Research Unit and University of Düsseldorf - Düsseldorf Institute for Competition Economics (DICE)

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Communication, and Strategic Pricing: Evidence from Large Language Models
detail.abstract: We analyze the behavior of large language model (LLM) agents as strategic actors in a price-setting environment. In an experimental market based on a repeated Bertrand pricing game, we find that LLM agents generate coordinated pricing outcomes. Allowing agents to communicate increases prices and profits while reducing variation in both outcomes. Moreover, communication increases the likelihood that agents coordinate on identical prices. Analyzing communication patterns shows that more frequent, longer, and more explicit exchanges reinforce these outcomes. A detailed analysis of agents' decision rationales suggests that communication affects pricing less through explicit game-theoretic reasoning than through reinforcement by cooperative language and pattern completion. Further tests involving different LLM temperature settings, varying the number of interacting agents, and various LLM architectures show that the results hold across these conditions. This consistency can be attributed mainly to language adjustments across different conditions. Overall, these findings highlight how language-based artificial intelligence systems can generate coordinated market outcomes even without specialized training in pricing or strategic interaction.

The framework underpins commercial programmes offered by Vantaris Consulting. No third party funded, commissioned, or had any role in the design, execution, or reporting of this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual paper presenting a theoretical framework; it does not involve human participants, patient data, or empirical fieldwork requiring ethics review.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently and self-funded.

detail.abstract: Competency frameworks describe observable managerial behaviour but offer limited insight into how senior leaders integrate capacities they already possess in uneven measure, on why leaders effective at mid-level stall at enterprise scope, or on why senior derailment follows elementspecific patterns. This paper proposes the Alchemy of Leadership model as a complementary conceptual framework for individual executive development whose primary contribution is the generation of testable directional predictions about plateau and derailment that competency frameworks and adjacent developmental theories do not independently generate. The model comprises Five Elements (Fire, Water, Earth, Air, Aether), with Aether as the meta-level integrative capacity, and Four Archetypes (Sovereign, Magician, Coach, Oracle), each carrying functional and shadow expressions. The framework draws on Jungian analytical psychology, Adlerian individual psychology, complexity science, and affective neuroscience, and is positioned alongside vertical development, behavioural complexity, paradox leadership, and identity-based approaches. Seven propositions, each paired with a specific disconfirming condition, are made operationally testable through a measurement and operationalisation roadmap. Two practical implications for talent-system design are developed: leadership assessment architecture and executive-development architecture. Team-level implications and other HR domains are flagged for future theoretical work.

title: The Value of Non-Value-Maximizing Managers
affiliations: Queen's University, Institute of Finance and Accounting and HEC Montreal - Institute of Applied Economics

detail.title: The Value of Non-Value-Maximizing Managers
detail.abstract: Companies pursue multiple goals, such as financial returns and societal impact. Conventional wisdom suggests they should appoint managers who share investors' preferences across these goals. We show that, when performance measurement is asymmetric, appointing a manager who is biased towards the worse-measured activity ("impact") may instead be optimal. Doing so allows for stronger incentives on the better-measured activity ("profits") without distorting resource allocation. Strong financial incentives need not indicate that the manager lacks intrinsic motivation; instead, they counteract his intrinsic motivation for impact. Similarly, strong financial incentives need not imply that a mission-focused firm is greenwashing; it pursues its mission through a biased manager rather than impact incentives. In a market equilibrium with a continuum of managers, we characterize the optimal level of bias and how it affects the level and structure of pay. The framework offers new insights into executive incentives, corporate purpose, and organizational culture.

title: Government Borrowing from Unclaimed Dividends and Dormant Accounts in Nigeria: A Doctrinal and Comparative Analysis of Legality
affiliations: and Usmanu Danfodiyo University, Sokoto

detail.title: Government Borrowing from Unclaimed Dividends and Dormant Accounts in Nigeria: A Doctrinal and Comparative Analysis of Legality
detail.abstract: The increasing incorporation of unclaimed dividends and dormant bank account balances into Nigeria's public debt framework raises fundamental legal and normative concerns. Pursuant to the Finance Act 2020, such funds are transferred into the Unclaimed Funds Trust Fund (UFTF) and may be invested in Federal Government securities, effectively transforming private dormant assets into instruments of sovereign borrowing. This paper interrogates the legality of this practice through a doctrinal analysis grounded in contract law, trust law, and property law principles, complemented by a comparative evaluation of analogous frameworks in the United States, the United Kingdom, and France. It argues that the Nigerian approach constitutes a mischaracterisation of the legal nature of unclaimed funds, which are more appropriately classified as custodial or trust property rather than loanable capital. Applying the IRAC methodology, the paper demonstrates that the absence of consent, consideration, and mutual intention undermines the validity of any purported borrowerlender relationship between the government and the rightful owners of such funds. Furthermore, the use of these assets for public financing purposes potentially violates fiduciary obligations, particularly the prohibition against self-dealing by custodians of trust property. Comparative analysis reveals that, unlike Nigeria, other jurisdictions maintain a strict custodial framework, ensuring that unclaimed assets are preserved for eventual reclamation without being converted into sovereign debt instruments. The paper concludes that, notwithstanding statutory authorization, the practice is doctrinally unsound, constitutionally questionable, and normatively problematic. It recommends a reorientation toward a purely custodial regime that prioritizes owner reunification and safeguards property rights.

title: Bursting the Retail Shareholder Bubble: Re-Evaluating Retail Shareholders' Role in Corporate Voting
affiliations: and Bar-Ilan University

detail.title: Bursting the Retail Shareholder Bubble: Re-Evaluating Retail Shareholders' Role in Corporate Voting

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Israel Science Foundation (Grant No. 1621/23)

detail.abstract:
A fundamental element in corporate governance research is the agency problem: in dispersed ownership markets, conflicts arise between shareholders and managers; in concentrated ownership markets, it more commonly arises between controlling and minority shareholders. Although institutional investors can monitor management and potentially protect minority shareholders, their size, market centrality, and role as agents managing others’ capital generate their own agency concerns.

In response, scholars and regulators have increasingly envisioned retail investors as an additional counterweight governance mechanism vis-à-vis institutional investors. While majority-of-the-minority rules were not enacted specifically for their benefit, they have enhanced the formal weight of minority votes and thus indirectly strengthened retail investors’ potential role. Participation costs have likewise been reduced, including through the adoption of online voting, to incentivize and facilitate retail investor participation and enhance its impact on corporate governance.

This Article challenges the expectations that regulators and scholars have placed on retail investors. First, it identifies the conditions necessary for meaningful retail monitoring and demonstrates that they are not realized in practice: the participation rate of retail investors is low; it remains largely homogeneous (and low) across different subjects, contrary to expectations that it would increase for more important matters or in cases where retail voting becomes pivotal; and it appears to be driven more by the number of items on the agenda than by their substantive importance.

Second, when examined in relation to institutional investors, a concerning picture emerges. Rather than constituting a counterweight governance mechanism vis-à-vis institutional investors, retail shareholders reduce their participation as institutional investors increase their holdings and influence. Thus, instead of constituting a counter mechanism to the institutional agency problem, retail investors effectively “clear the stage” for the growing dominance of the institutional voice.

All in all, this Article suggests that reforms aimed at empowering minority shareholders do not necessarily yield a more prominent retail voice; rather, they may predominantly benefit institutional investors.

detail.abstract: We study how artificial intelligence is being adopted in three industrial sectors that recruit the largest proportion of MBA graduates-banking and financial services, management consulting, and technology, media and e-commerce-and examine the resulting implications for MBA hiring and skills requirements from MBA graduates. To conduct the study, we interviewed 34 executives at 30 companies across these sectors and in senior-, mid-, and early-career levels and supplemented the interviews with desktop research. Through this study, we develop guidelines for how the MBA curriculum needs to evolve to meet the evolving requirements of the industry. While the study is focused on MBA programs, its insights are broadly applicable to graduate and undergraduate business programs at universities.

title: Corporate Social Responsibility, Organizational Structure, and Process of Sensegiving

detail.title: Corporate Social Responsibility, Organizational Structure, and Process of Sensegiving
detail.abstract: Firms seeking to balance profitability and prosocial responsibility often face a dilemma when institutional expectations around corporate social responsibility (CSR) shift. Structural efforts to demonstrate commitment to CSR may enhance legitimacy and stakeholder trust, yet the substantive impact of such efforts remains debated. This study theorizes that organizational structuring-through the creation of formal roles, routines, and governance bodies-enables firms to engage in credible sensegiving that aligns prosocial intent with financial outcomes. Drawing on a longitudinal case study of Panasonic's supply chain CSR initiatives, we trace how the firm evolved from a compliance-oriented stance to a strategic narrative of innovation and resilience. We further argue that the performance benefits of CSR depend not on the volume of initiatives but on how these initiatives are structurally embedded within the organization. We test this proposition with a large-scale panel analysis of Japanese firms and find that CSR structuring, rather than activity count, is positively associated with subsequent financial performance. Our findings contribute to research on CSR, sensegiving, and organizational design by showing how firms navigate institutional complexity through structured meaning-making. We also extend theory by highlighting how culturally embedded norms shape the form and function of CSR in practice.

title: Offline Learning and Optimization for Multi-product Inventory Management with Stockout-based Substitution
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, City Univ. of Hong Kong - College of Business, Dept of Management Sciences, University of Liverpool and Rutgers University, Business School, Department of Management Science and Information Systems

detail.title: Offline Learning and Optimization for Multi-product Inventory Management with Stockout-based Substitution
detail.abstract: We deal with a retailer's multi-product inventory system where customers randomly seek acceptable substitutes if their initial requests are not satisfied. Unsuccessful quests for substitutes would result in lost sales. Motivated by a consulting project as well as other real practices, we also choose to deal with further challenges posed by initially unknown base demand distributions and substitution probabilities; moreover, we aim to develop an offline learning method that (i) takes advantage of given data derived from bygone decisions rather than of any learning-while-doing opportunity, (ii) makes inferences about base-demand distributions and pairwise substitution probabilities without knowing whether there have been demand arrivals after inventory depletions, and (iii) is unhindered by the lack of knowledge about the assortments faced by customers and their purchase-or-no-purchase decisions at their individual arrivals. To address these challenges, we propose an innovative approach based on the Kaplan-Meier estimator that circumvents unrealistic data requirements. Our substitution probability estimates employ carefully designed weighting schemes to facilitate rigorous theoretical analysis through tools such as the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality. Both one-time substitution scenarios and more complex Markov-chain substitution patterns would be accommodated. Using large deviation tools, we establish provably optimal convergence rates of our estimates on top of consistency. The precision in parameter estimates would translate into accuracy in replenishment decisions. For inventory management, we take advantage of a submodularity property to obtain an exact algorithm for the two-product case and a good heuristic for the general multi-product problem. Computational studies based on simulated and actual data confirm the merits of our approach.

title: Emergence via Phase Transitions: Mechanism Landscapes and Universal Convergence Across Complex Systems
affiliations: Clevix AI Research

detail.title: Emergence via Phase Transitions: Mechanism Landscapes and Universal Convergence Across Complex Systems
detail.abstract: Why do independently trained neural networks converge to the same internal representations [37, 23]? Why does grokking-sudden generalisation after memorisation-follow universal statistics across architectures and tasks [42]? Why do independent evolutionary lineages repeatedly arrive at the same metabolic solutions across 993 yeast species [38]? We propose a candidate explanation for a structural motif common to these phenomena: when a system's energy budget crosses a critical threshold Ec, competing mechanisms undergo a phase transition that drives convergence toward a unique fixed point determined by the system's physical constraint set P. We do not claim to explain all emergence, but to identify a recurring phase-transition structure across convergence phenomena in learning, biology, and physics. Concisely: many emergence phenomena can be understood as phase transitions in mechanism landscapes under physical and informational constraints. We formalise this structural motif as the Hierarchical Emergence Framework (HEF), specified by a six-tuple (R (1) , L, A0, G, mode, E) together with P = (P thermo , P info , Φ), where the translation map Φ is an order-isomorphism of constraint lattices grounded in Landauer's Principle and the Jarzynski Equality. Three theorems follow. The Physical Feasibility Theorem guarantees that all generated entities satisfy thermodynamic and information-theoretic constraints simultaneously. The Energy-Diversity Theorem establishes a phase transition at Ec between an exploration regime and a convergence regime. Universal Feature Convergence then follows via the Banach Fixed-Point Theorem: any two HEF instances sharing P and operating below Ec converge to the same fixed-point representations, independent of initial conditions. A Causal Emergence Theorem additionally shows that the fixed point R∞ has strictly higher Effective Information [21] than the micro-level R (1) , with the gain bounded by a measurable training-dynamics quantity. We validate HEF empirically through 111 grokking experiments (p ∈ {23, 31, 41, 53, 67, 83, 97}, λ ∈ {1, 2}, multiple seeds). Universal Convergence is confirmed : all grokked models converge to 0.9745±0.014 regardless of p, λ, or training fraction (ANOVA p > 0.13; CV= 1.47%). A novel Ec fingerprint is identified: the weight norm ∥w∥ 2 peaks ∼1,050 steps before grokking in 92% of runs, tracing the threephase HEF trajectory. Accuracy curves collapse onto a tanh kink (R 2 = 0.93), placing grokking in the Landau-Ginzburg mean-field universality class. G2 scaling ∆t ∝ 1/(frac • p • λ) is supported across seven primes (β =-1.39 ± 0.20, R 2 = 0.91). HEF makes three falsifiable cross-domain predictions: (P1) anaerobic yeast lineages have higher genomic convergence than aerobic lineages at the same phylogenetic distance; (P2) LLMs trained with higher weight decay produce representations with higher causal potency; (P3) a critical weight-decay threshold λc(p) ∈ (2, 4) exists beyond which grokking fails via mechanism starvation. Code, data, and a diagnostic toolkit (hef-tools) are provided to enable independent replication and application to new systems.

title: From Intent to Exit: Linking Employee Engagement Responses to Voluntary Turnover in Child Welfare
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Intent to Exit: Linking Employee Engagement Responses to Voluntary Turnover in Child Welfare
detail.abstract: This study examined whether employees’ self-reported intent to leave predicts verified voluntary turnover in a public child welfare agency and assessed whether employee engagement factors contribute to turnover risk. Data came from the 2024 Survey of Employee Engagement and administrative exit records for 125 employees across three child welfare service divisions. A retrospective comparison group design was used, and multivariable analyses were conducted using binary logistic regression.Results indicated that intent to leave was a strong and statistically significant predictor of voluntary turnover. Employees who reported that they did not plan to remain with the organization had more than nearly ten times the odds of leaving, even after considering demographic characteristics and employee engagement factors. Greater years of experience were associated with a reduced likelihood of turnover, while older age was associated with increased likelihood. In contrast, employee engagement factors (supervision, workplace environment, and job satisfaction) were not significantly associated with turnover.These findings suggest that a single-item measure of intent to leave can serve as a meaningful and practical indicator of turnover risk in child welfare settings. While workplace perceptions are frequently emphasized in turnover research, they did not predict the turnover observed in this sample. By linking attitudinal survey data with verified administrative outcomes, this study advances understanding of turnover processes and suggests the value of low-burden, real-time indicators for workforce monitoring. Child welfare agencies may use intent to leave as early warning signals to inform targeted retention strategies and strengthen workforce stability.

title: Behind the Scenes of Law School Administration & Leadership: What Does an Associate Dean Actually Do & Why Would I Want to Do That?
affiliations: Loyola University New Orleans College of Law

detail.title: Behind the Scenes of Law School Administration & Leadership: What Does an Associate Dean Actually Do & Why Would I Want to Do That?
detail.abstract:
This article is unique in its comprehensive approach to what it means to serve as an associate dean in a law school.  It will provide both sitting associate deans and professors considering taking on the role with valuable information they can use in the job. 

This article discusses the associate dean role, leadership, and lessons learned from ten years of serving as an associate dean for faculty development and academic affairs. My experience also includes lessons learned as an active member of the associate dean national community, having presented on issues relevant to associate deans on several occasions and having served on the AALS Associate Deans’ section executive committee and as chair of that committee, during which we were selected as Section of the Year.  During my time as associate dean, my law school experienced many things common to serving in a law school and many extraordinary things that have challenged us at every step: the wrap-up of one ABA accreditation cycle and a second full one, budgeting issues, the pandemic, national and global political unrest, racial tensions, societal polarization, the hiring of faculty and a dean, university leadership changes, and the usual running of a law school, including creating new courses, concentrations, and programs.  Through the article I define the role of associate dean, identifying the tasks most frequently handled.  I then identify attributes and characteristics that are helpful to be successful in the associate dean role and many similar roles.  I discuss the benefits of taking on the leadership role, both professionally and personally.  Further, I address the downsides of the role and ways to minimize them.     

When I was first approached about becoming an associate dean, I asked the question in the article’s title of one of the sitting associate deans—"What does an associate dean actually do, and why would I want to do that?”  I accepted the position to serve my school despite the response I received, which focused on the long hours and the constant juggling.  Now, with considerable time in the job, I believe my response to that question will resonate with a subset of law professors who are drawn to leadership and team work.  The person who wants to do this work wants to be a part of guiding faculty, students, and staff to maximize their potential.  The person wants to lift others up.  The person wants to support, inspire, facilitate, create opportunities, encourage, and work to make things happen for their law school, for everyone associated with their law school, for the legal community, and for the larger community of people who need lawyers to represent them well, create laws, interpret laws, and enforce laws.

title: Taking One for the Team: How Salient Individual Performance Metrics Discourage Team-Benefiting Actions
affiliations: and University of South Carolina

detail.title: Taking One for the Team: How Salient Individual Performance Metrics Discourage Team-Benefiting Actions
detail.abstract: Organizations use performance evaluation systems to motivate desired behaviors, yet the structure of these systems can suppress collectively beneficial actions. When individuals face concrete evaluative costs for failed attempts, they may avoid uncertain actions that improve team outcomes but expose them to personal risk-even when incentives are aligned and the expected value of the attempt is positive. We study this dynamic using a natural experiment in the National Basketball Association (NBA). Beginning in the 2025-2026 season, late-quarter, long-distance shots ("heaves") were excluded from individual shooting percentages. Notably, the reform applied only to heaves attempted in the first three quarters, while fourth-quarter heaves remained subject to the prior recording convention. We use a within-player differencein-differences design that compares the post-reform change in Q1-Q3 heaves to the post-reform change in Q4 heaves, finding that the recording reform led to a doubling in heave attempts. This effect was largest among players with higher three-point shooting percentages-those for whom a missed heave imposed the greatest evaluative cost under the prior system. We further document that players attempt fewer heaves in contract years and that teams attempt more heaves when trailing or facing elimination. Together, these findings demonstrate that performance evaluation systems can suppress team-benefiting actions by concentrating the costs of failure in salient individual metrics. Redesigning evaluation rules, rather than increasing rewards for success, may be more effective for encouraging cooperation and experimentation in organizations.

title: Economic Opportunity and the Rule of Law on Tribal Lands
affiliations: Albany Law School and Loyola University Chicago School of Law

detail.title: Economic Opportunity and the Rule of Law on Tribal Lands
detail.abstract:
Beginning in 2021, electric automaker Tesla began operating retail showrooms and repair shops on tribal lands in the United States. It appears Tesla’s primary motivation in locating facilities on tribal lands was to avoid state prohibitions on selling cars directly to consumers. In partnering with Native American tribes, Tesla was able to take advantage of economic opportunities tribal lands afford to corporate America. 

And yet, there is reason for companies to be skeptical of such partnerships as Indian country is rife with legal uncertainty. On tribal land—both land held in trust by the federal government and land help by tribes in fee simple—it is often unclear whether tribes or states have jurisdiction over contracts, taxation, and other business matters. In addition to jurisdictional uncertainty, tribal lands lack key infra-structure, including affordable housing, that make recruiting and training skilled workers difficult. Further, tax-sharing agreements be-tween states and tribal governments reduce the potential tax savings, with respect to sales and property tax liability, for locating on tribal lands.

In framing the issue of economic development on tribal lands as a rule of law issue, this Article explores difficulties lawmakers encounter when encouraging development on native lands. It focuses on the Opportunity Zone incentive, adopted in 2017 by Congress, to explore how a well-intentioned law can lead to specious outcomes with respect to tribal economic development. In so doing, this Articles eeks to improve law and policymaking with respect to unique rule of law issues impacting tribal economic development.

title: Infrastructure and Productivity: A Country-Sector Panel Analysis
affiliations: University of Roma, Tor Vergata, LUISS Guido Carli - Department of Economics and Roma Tre University

detail.title: Infrastructure and Productivity: A Country-Sector Panel Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of physical infrastructure on sectoral total factor productivity (TFP). In the first part, a neoclassical growth model with multiple productive sectors and public capital (in the form of infrastructure) uncovers a long-run relationship between infrastructure and sectoral TFP.  In the second part, a panel-cointegration analysis evaluates the long-run impact of 4 distinct types of infrastructure –transport, energy, ICT, health– on the TFPs of 22 manufacturing sectors in a sample of 65 (developed and emerging) countries between 1995 and 2018.  We find that infrastructure is a positive and significant determinant of sectoral TFPs. A panel error-correction model also confirms that causality runs from infrastructure to TFPs. These results are robust to further empirical analysis conducted on sub-samples segmented by several dimensions. Our findings can inform policy in designing targeted interventions and prioritizing investment.

title: Smart Vehicle Disposal: Balancing Mobility Needs with Asset Costs and Environmental Impact
affiliations: Institut Mines-Télécom Business School, INSEAD and INSEAD

detail.title: Smart Vehicle Disposal: Balancing Mobility Needs with Asset Costs and Environmental Impact

publicationDetails.journalName: INSEAD Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This report reassesses the widely used humanitarian vehicle disposal rule recommending replacement after 5 years or 150,000 km. Drawing on interviews with multiple organizations, cost simulations, and pilot projects with Sightsavers and the World Health Organization, we find little evidence to validate this benchmark, which is rarely followed in practice. The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO), which is the basis of the standard disposal rule, varies significantly depending on vehicle usage, operating conditions, resale constraints, and local contexts. These differences make it inappropriate to apply a single replacement threshold to all cases. Current disposal practices are often ad hoc, driven by conflicting incentives between headquarters and country offices, and are impeded by limited data transparency. As an alternative to managing only total asset costs, our research highlights the need to balance three core objectives: minimizing asset costs, ensuring operational mobility, and reducing environmental impact. To address these shortcomings, we design an evidence-based disposal framework incorporating three decision checks: supply (mobility needs), cost (TCO trends), and replacement feasibility (business continuity). Pilot studies show that organizations can implement this framework using existing data, improving transparency and strengthening decision-making.

title: Cross-Country Heterogeneity in Potential-GDP and NAIRU Hysteresis: A Bayesian Approach
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Cross-Country Heterogeneity in Potential-GDP and NAIRU Hysteresis: A Bayesian Approach
detail.abstract: This paper extends the class of semi-structural New Keynesian models to jointly estimate the potential GDP hysteresis elasticity ([[EQUATION]]) and the NAIRU hysteresis elasticity ([[EQUATION]]) across 30 economies via Bayesian methods. Prior distributions for both parameters are elicited through a meta-analysis of existing literature. The cross-country posterior averages are 0.45 for [[EQUATION]] and 0.43 for [[EQUATION]]), implying that, on average, roughly 45% of the prevailing output gap is absorbed into potential output each period; cumulatively, the estimated dynamics imply that about two-thirds of a temporary demand shock remains in GDP at the ten-year horizon. Substantial heterogeneity exists across economies: [[EQUATION]] ranges from 0.25 in Korea to 0.71 in Spain, with European economies displaying systematically higher hysteresis than non-European ones. Cross-country variation in both elasticities is partially explained by labour market institutions, supporting insider-outsider theories. Using the identified demand shocks, local projections reveal that hysteresis operates primarily through persistent employment and capital accumulation effects, consistent with AK-type endogenous growth mechanisms rather than TFP or human capital channels. These findings imply that the costs of recessions and aggressive disinflation are substantially higher than conventional frameworks suggest.

title: The Returned Effect: Quantifying Reconciliation in Models of Domestic Violence
affiliations: Universidade Federal do Ceará and CAEN - UFC

detail.title: The Returned Effect: Quantifying Reconciliation in Models of Domestic Violence
detail.abstract: Standard economic models of intimate partner violence (IPV) treat separation as an absorbing state, ignoring the empirical reality that many victims return to abusive partners. This paper develops a dynamic equilibrium model with a specific "returned" state to quantify how reconciliation dynamics shape aggregate violence and policy effectiveness. We decompose the impact of reconciliation into an extensive margin (increased exposure to risk) and an intensive margin (reduced violence severity due to behavioral adjustments). Calibrating the model to administrative records of 2.1 million cases, we find that the economy operates in a "tolerant-majority" regime, where policies reducing separation costs primarily increase reconciliation rather than permanent exit. Counterfactual analyses reveal a strong complementarity: empowerment policies facilitate temporary exit, while batterer treatment programs ensure safety upon return. We show that ignoring these dynamics leads to biased assessments of welfare and policy design.

title: Child Advocacy Studies (CAST) Implementation and Trainee Response: Associations with Perceived Competence Across College Disciplines
affiliations: Mississippi State University, Mississippi State University, Mississippi State University, Mississippi State University and Mississippi State University

detail.title: Child Advocacy Studies (CAST) Implementation and Trainee Response: Associations with Perceived Competence Across College Disciplines
detail.abstract: More than 70 percent of the over 3 million child maltreatment reports made in 2023 were submitted by professionals who work with children as part of their job in education, medicine, law enforcement, or other fields. Those professionals are likely to have had little to no training in child protection, given that 60% of colleges/universities offer no maltreatment-related courses. The Child Advocacy Studies (CAST) curriculum was developed to address the training gap, so that child-serving professionals across disciplines gain competencies in identifying, and responding to, signs of potential child maltreatment. This study evaluates CAST implementation in university setting, examining the extent to which incremental exposure to CAST courses results in knowledge uptake among undergraduate college studentsUsing an observational, longitudinal cohort design, the study assessed program feasibility, fidelity, and preliminary outcomes. Results indicated significant improvements in attitudes toward trauma-sensitive response and increased utilization of consultation services.Findings underscore the importance of training relevance and program adaptability in fostering on-going professional development community. While the program enhanced students’ responses to case vignettes, barriers such as systemic barriers to data sharing and inconsistent follow-up limited broader impact. Future research should explore strategies for strengthening continued trainee engagement, and sustaining trauma-sensitive initiatives in professional development.

title:
Private Equity Selection 
An Empirical Analysis on Selecting Distressed Companies
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
Private Equity Selection 
An Empirical Analysis on Selecting Distressed Companies
detail.abstract:
Turbulent times, punctuated by a Credit Crisis, have persisted into the year 2013, causing 
a strong emergence of distressed firm investment opportunities. Through this rising 
opportunity, one is inclined to question the sourcing and selection process of these 
investments. Successful private equity exits have been researched to show criticality in 
ensuring striking returns in private equity. The importance of the exit of investment has 
been researched extensively by private equity researchers. However, the beginning, 
which consists of selecting the investment, has overlooked in on the wave of research 
into private equity. This study aims to provide a stepping stone into the starting stage of 
investing into distressed investments, through both theoretical and practical development, 
using the analysis of the selection criteria that private equity investors use to select 
distressed portfolio companies. 

Fundamentally, this study develops the selection in two fold. Firstly a ranking of the 
criteria that have been identified to affect the selection of investments, using both 
interviews with experts in the field, and a questionnaire to survey industry practitioners. 
Through responses from over 40 private equity houses, the study finds nine main criteria 
that private equity practitioners find important in the selection of distressed portfolio 
companies. The analysis done in this study suggests that experience leads a private equity 
company to incur less write-offs and that suggests superiority in selecting investments. 
Secondly, a framework incorporating value creation attributors is created and tested using 
an exploratory research methodology. This enables an understanding of the essential 
criteria that affect the selection, as well as provide a uniform method in the selection 
process to allow the practitioner to to capitalize on this study, and incorporate the 
methods and framework into future distressed investment selection. 

Through this study, there is an expansion on the work from early stage private equity, 
extended to late stage distressed investments. This work represents a starting step towards 
the consolidation of theory, and the development of a selection tool for private equity 
professionals.

title: Financial Bubbles and Market Regime Transitions: A Historical Recurrence Framework

detail.title: Financial Bubbles and Market Regime Transitions: A Historical Recurrence Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available financial and macroeconomic data and does not involve human participants, personal data, or animal subjects. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a Historical Regime Recurrence Framework (HRRF) for studying financial bubbles and market regime transitions. The central argument is that major financial booms and crashes exhibit recurring structural characteristics driven by four interacting forces: liquidity expansion, investor sentiment amplification, valuation pressure, and political-economic shocks. Unlike canonical Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) approaches that treat large price movements as largely unpredictable, the HRRF models financial markets as dynamic regime-transition systems cycling through speculative expansion, fragility accumulation, crisis triggering, and recovery.

We formalise this idea in three components. First, a Bubble Pressure Index (BPI) aggregates liquidity, valuation, sentiment, momentum, and shock-exposure signals into a scalar fragility measure. Second, a Historical Similarity Index (HSI) quantifies the distance between current market conditions and the standardised feature vectors of canonical historical crises. Third, a Time-Varying Transition Probability Markov-Switching (TVTP-MS) model allows regime-change probabilities to depend on BPI and HSI, delivering an econometrically identified framework with testable predictions.

Four historical episodes—the 1929 Great Crash, the 2000 Dot-com Bubble, the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, and the 2020–2022 COVID-era market cycle—are examined as case studies of the recurring regime-transition dynamic. Empirical analysis using monthly U.S. financial data from 1925 to 2024 is broadly consistent with the Historical Regime Recurrence Hypothesis: (i) BPI peaks systematically precede major corrections; (ii) HSI elevations identify structural similarity between separated episodes; and (iii) a rolling-window logit model combining BPI and HSI achieves an out-of-sample AUROC = 0.76 at the 12-month horizon (correction defined as cumulative log return below -15%), substantially outperforming the constant-probability benchmark. The two-state TVTP-MS specification yields statistically inconclusive evidence regarding time-varying transition dynamics (LR = 3.41, p = 0.49), pointing to the need for a richer specification in future work. The COVID cycle, in particular, exhibits a rapid three-phase regime sequence—panic, liquidity-driven speculation, and tightening-driven deleveraging—structurally consistent with earlier bubble episodes.

title: Impact of Climate Change on South Africa: Evidence from a DSGE Model
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Pretoria

detail.title: Impact of Climate Change on South Africa: Evidence from a DSGE Model
detail.abstract: We analyze the impacts of climate change and carbon taxation on South Africa using a calibrated small open economy New Keynesian Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) model featuring sticky- and flexible-price specifications. A permanent productivity shock reducing GDP by 5% by 2050 lowers the natural interest rate by 7.5 basis points, appreciates the real exchange rate by 4%, and generates 4 basis points of inflation, requiring 0.5 basis point policy rate increases above the natural rate. A tenfold carbon tax increase (R236 to R2,360/ton CO2) produces modest long-run output losses (0.22%) with 0.2% immediate inflation, necessitating 6 basis point policy tightening. Compressed adjustment horizons (2033 versus 2050) amplify short-run effects fivefold, with the natural interest rate declining by 40 basis points under accelerated climate impacts. Results suggest the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) must incorporate climate-adjusted potential output and natural rate estimates into its monetary policy framework, with particular attention to the timing of climate-induced productivity decline materialization which fundamentally determines the magnitude of required policy responses.

title: American Manufacturing and the Architecture of Capital: Why Capital Markets Disadvantage Production and What It Means for American Industrial Renewal

detail.title: American Manufacturing and the Architecture of Capital: Why Capital Markets Disadvantage Production and What It Means for American Industrial Renewal
