detail.abstract:
From 2016 through 2025, the median U.S.-listed manufacturer gained 13.5 percent in market capitalization against roughly 33 percent CPI inflation. The typical manufacturer lost real wealth even as aggregate manufacturing market capitalization quadrupled and more than 90 percent of the gain accrued to the top decile. The firms inside this wealth signature anchor regional economies, supply components on which American defense systems and critical infrastructure depend, and constitute the principal channel through which American households participate in the productive economy through pensions and retirement accounts. We examine U.S. public equity markets because they are large, liquid, broadly owned, and measurable, and because they are the clearest window into the broader manufacturing-finance architecture. The divergence reflects not simply capital scarcity but a recognition problem: capital is abundant in aggregate, while recognition of manufacturing capability is selective.

Two concepts organize the analysis. Appropriable value is what a firm can collect through productive capability; capitalization value is what public markets are willing to price. Where capability fits recognized templates, the two tend to track; where it does not, they diverge. We use SaaS and manufacturing as diagnostic opposites. SaaS concentrates historically recognized signals of scalable platform value: growth, gross margins, recurring revenue, and the possibility of superlinear returns. Manufacturing concentrates capability that compounds through operating learning, capacity, reliability, and process control.

Using a ten-year panel of 949 U.S.-listed manufacturers and SaaS firms, we document the appropriability–capitalization gap from four angles: a SaaS valuation premium that survives matched fundamentals; a “capital-light” signal dependent on stock-based compensation conventions; weak market distinction between operating profitability and equity-financed profitability; and manufacturers sorted into stable sovereignty classes with limited mobility. Recognition is not only a pricing question. A recognized premium becomes a financing platform: equity compensation, acquisition currency, secondary markets, and lower-cost equity. For American industrial renewal, the implication is that manufacturing capability must become financeable on its own terms. We develop a capital-market architecture for industrial renewal built around recognition infrastructure, demand commitment, first-of-a-kind certification and adoption finance, capacity insurance, and patient capital, while identifying private-channel migration and ownership distribution as future research priorities.

title: Possible Economic Impacts from aMPV and HPAI in the Iowa Turkey Industry
affiliations: and

detail.title: Possible Economic Impacts from aMPV and HPAI in the Iowa Turkey Industry
detail.abstract: We assess the potential economic impacts to the state of Iowa from outbreaks of Avian Metapneumovirus (aMPV) and Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) in the Iowa turkey industry. We use an input-output model assessing the direct impact at the processing level for a 5% and a 30% decline in processing activity from the diseases and the indirect and induced impacts at the turkey production level, as well as other sectors of the Iowa economy. The results show a statewide loss in employment of 182 jobs, $72 million in revenue, and $4 million in tax revenues in the 5% scenario, and over 1,000 lost jobs, $434 million in lost revenue, and $24 million in lost tax revenues in the 30% scenario. Aside from the losses directly attributable to the turkey processing industry, approximately 24% of total sales losses would be to the turkey farming industry in Iowa, or, from about $17 million in the 5% scenario to $105 million in the 30% scenario. The impacts would be especially felt in the counties of Buena Vista and Muscatine where the state’s two turkey processors are located, but the effects are statewide.

title: One Great Pool or Many? A Dynamic Time Warping Hierarchical Cluster Approach to Global Oil Market Integration
affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University (XJTLU) - International Business School Suzhou and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: One Great Pool or Many? A Dynamic Time Warping Hierarchical Cluster Approach to Global Oil Market Integration
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to assessing global crude oil market integration using hierarchical cluster analysis combined with dynamic time warping. Unlike pairwise tests, our method captures system-wide patterns of comovement without restrictive assumptions. Applying this framework to ten global crude oil prices (2000-2026), we find that markets cluster primarily by geography: West African, Middle Eastern, and U.S. markets each form distinct regional clusters, with Brent occupying an intermediate position. Rolling window analysis reveals increasing integration over time but a remarkably stable regional structure. Subsample analysis shows that during turbulent periods (2020-2024), integration increases but the clear geographical pattern weakens. Validation metrics (silhouette width, cophenetic correlation) confirm robust clustering across all periods. The evidence suggests several regional pools rather than a single fully integrated market.

title: Restricting Rivals Through Geography: A Game-Theoretic Analysis of Spatial Input Foreclosure in India’s Bioenergy Feedstock Markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Restricting Rivals Through Geography: A Game-Theoretic Analysis of Spatial Input Foreclosure in India’s Bioenergy Feedstock Markets
detail.abstract: In India, around 92 million tonnes of agricultural waste is burned annually, creating high concentrations of PM2.5 pollution that have adverse health impacts. India’s SATAT programme aimed to convert this residue into compressed biogas (CBG) yet 69.9% of the 1,681 approved CBG plants have not commenced construction despite guaranteed offtake pricing and contracted feedstock procurement. This paper identifies the structural mechanism driving this investment failure as Spatial Input Foreclosure (SIF): Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) exploit the physical transport ceiling of biomass procurement — straw cannot be profitably sourced beyond 87.5 km from a plant — to pre-contract feedstock within a 20 km radius, rendering private entry economically non-viable without any exclusive contract, predatory pricing, or vertical integration. We model SIF as a two-stage extensive-form game and establish the Subgame-Perfect Nash Equilibrium. About 668 Indian districts are categorised into three types of market: 429 Blockaded markets, where private CBG developers’ entry is non-viable; 100 Deterred markets, where incumbent procurement deters private firm investment; and 139 Accommodated markets, where Cournot duopoly emerges. Counter-intuitively, the incentive to foreclose is maximised at medium biomass density, not in the highest-residue districts. Aggregate annual deadweight loss totals Rs 1766 Crore, with 65% concentrated in 100 medium-density Deterred districts. We test the validity of the model's structure using Generalised Method of Moments structural estimation and a regression discontinuity. We consider five forms of regulation, including price caps. Results show that geographic procurement zoning reduces deadweight loss by 55% to 100% at zero fiscal cost.

title: Modeling Decision Making Under Uncertainty Across Obsessive Compulsive Symptom Dimensions Using the Free Energy Principle and Stochastic Optimal Control
affiliations: Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Advanced Telecommunications Research Institute International (ATR), Nara Institute of Science and Technology and Nara Institute of Science and Technology

detail.title: Modeling Decision Making Under Uncertainty Across Obsessive Compulsive Symptom Dimensions Using the Free Energy Principle and Stochastic Optimal Control
detail.abstract: Decision making under uncertainty is a central feature of obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) and is associated with persistent doubt, repetitive behavior, and impaired adaptation to changing environments. In this study, we propose a computational framework that integrates the Free Energy Principle with the Stochastic Maximum Principle to model how disruptions in belief updating and action selection contribute to maladaptive decision-making under uncertainty.The proposed framework formalizes the interaction between probabilistic belief formation and stochastic control policies through precision-related parameters governing sensitivity to uncertainty. Within this model, belief updating represents the agent’s internal inference about latent environmental contingencies, while action selection is described as a stochastic control process operating over time. Decision uncertainty evolves according to a stochastic differential equation that captures the interplay between free energy minimization and stochastic perturbations.Model validation was performed using behavioral data from a probabilistic reversal learning task involving 266 participants. The framework reproduced key behavioral patterns associated with elevated obsessive–compulsive symptom dimensions, including persistent uncertainty, reduced learning from feedback, and impaired adaptation following environmental reversals. Model performance was evaluated using the root mean square error and coefficient of determination, demonstrating meaningful agreement between predicted and observed behavioral dynamics.These findings provide a formal computational account of how altered belief precision and stochastic control dynamics may contribute to maladaptive decision-making under uncertainty. More broadly, the framework offers a computational psychiatry perspective linking probabilistic inference, behavioral adaptation, and uncertainty-related cognitive dysfunction.

title: Collinear by Construction: Why Battery Cannibalization Cannot Be Identied from Price Spreads

detail.title: Collinear by Construction: Why Battery Cannibalization Cannot Be Identied from Price Spreads
detail.abstract: Battery arbitrage revenue in the two largest United States storage markets has fallen by about two-thirds in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) and half in the California Independent System Operator (CAISO) from its peak, widely blamed on cannibalization. We ask whether a per-gigawatt cannibalization gure for batteries can be read from market prices. It cannot, and neither can a clean compression of any kind. Battery and solar capacity are collinear at 0.98 and each nearly a function of time, so a spread regression splits their combined eect arbitrarily, the battery coecient running minus 10.9 with solar controlled, minus 0.4 without it, and turning positive under a time trend. The combined eect, which needs no such split, is in ERCOT a precise zero, so the per-gigawatt gures the literature reports are one arbitrary side of a split whose aggregate does not compress the spread. In CAISO a combined compression survives inference, but capacity two quarters ahead explains it as well as capacity today, the mark of a secular trend, and the solar coecient that carries it lowers the overnight price solar cannot reach. A cross-zone design recovers solar's local midday dip in ERCOT but cannot see the system-wide compression, which lives in the common price the trend moves. The credible per-technology estimate must come from the discrete timing of entry rather than a levels regression.

title: Set-Aside Procurement and Small Business Growth: Evidence from Russia
affiliations: University of Padua - Department of Economics and Management, University of Padua - Department of Economics and Management, DSEA and University of Padua

detail.title: Set-Aside Procurement and Small Business Growth: Evidence from Russia
detail.abstract: To support small business enterprises (SBEs), governments implement set-aside (SA) auctions to procure goods and services. Only SBEs can participate in such auctions. This paper empirically studies the effect of winning an SA auction on SBE growth by matching firm-level financial data with participation and winning records in public procurement contracts for the supply of sugar in Russia in 2011-2013. We find that winning an SA auction is positively associated with SBEs' revenue and employment growth, conditional on participation in public procurement. Furthermore, we find that older firms are more likely to win public procurement contracts in other markets after winning an SA auction.

title: Fat Tails in Solar Renewable Energy Certificates and the Impact of Price Jumps on Investment
affiliations: University of Wyoming - College of Business - Department of Economics and Finance and University of Minnesota - Duluth - Department of Economics

detail.title: Fat Tails in Solar Renewable Energy Certificates and the Impact of Price Jumps on Investment
detail.abstract: Economies are increasingly adopting renewable energy certificates as a policy mechanism to support the transition away from reliance on fossil fuels. We investigate the price of solar renewable energy certificates (SRECs) in New Jersey, allowing for the potential presence of jumps and time-varying volatility.  We find that both features play an important role in the stochastic process describing SREC price returns.  We also simulate the implied probability that at least one jump would occur in any given week.  These implied probabilities indicate that jumps played a consistently important role in both SRECs and electricity prices.  Jumps in SRECs appear to have been particularly noteworthy between late 2011 and early 2013, a period when electricity prices in New Jersey were relatively high.  Using an investment under uncertainty framework, we describe analytically the impact of jumps upon investment.

title: School Entry Policies, Maternal Education, and Pregnancy Outcomes: New Causal Evidence
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Charlotte and

detail.title: School Entry Policies, Maternal Education, and Pregnancy Outcomes: New Causal Evidence
detail.abstract: Despite growing research interest in school entry policies, their effects on newborn well-being remain underexplored. This study provides new causal evidence using restricted birth data from three states, based on the 2003 revision of birth certificate instruments. Our normalized-and-pooled regression discontinuity analysis shows that young mothers born just after the school entry cutoff have significantly lower levels of education than those born just before. These women also tend to experience poorer birth outcomes, including a modest reduction in birth weight and higher risks of adverse pregnancy outcomes, though the strength and precision of these estimated effects vary across states. Maternal health behaviors, insurance coverage, and paternal age emerge as important channels for these intergenerational health effects.

title: Digital Transformation Resilience Model (DTRM): Integrating Framework, Instrument Specification, and Multi-Programme Empirical Support

detail.title: Digital Transformation Resilience Model (DTRM): Integrating Framework, Instrument Specification, and Multi-Programme Empirical Support
detail.abstract:
The Digital Transformation Resilience Model (DTRM) is an integrative precondition assessment framework identifying the structural conditions that durable digital transformation requires. Operating across three independently necessary layers — a governance precondition (Leadership Selection Effects, LSE), an infrastructure precondition (Infrastructure Trust Index, ITI), and an ecosystem precondition (Exit Feasibility Index, EFI) — DTRM assesses whether the structural foundations for benefit realisation are present before spend is committed, during programme execution, and at reset decision points.

This paper integrates three companion theoretical contributions into a single coherent framework. It formalises the Leadership Selection Effects construct and the Performance Visibility Incentive Regime (PVIR) as the governance precondition mechanism; the Infrastructure Trust Precondition Model (ITPM), including Application Design Debt (ADD), Design Debt Cascade (DDC), and Data-by-Design Principles (DBDP), as the infrastructure precondition mechanism; and Structural Optionality (SO) and the Exit Feasibility Matrix (EFM) as the ecosystem precondition mechanism. It specifies the Infrastructure-Conditioned Return on Investment model — conditioning the plausibility of programme benefit claims on precondition status using four structural variables: f(ITI), A(t), δ (DDC compounding rate), and PV(SO) — and introduces the Tier 1 / Tier 2 benefit distinction as a structurally determined governance instrument.

The framework is applied across three major national digital transformation programmes: the Universal Credit digital programme (two windows: Q4 2012 and Q1 2016), the NHS Federated Data Platform (two windows: Q4 2023 and April 2026), and the NHS Single Patient Record (prospective inception window: June 2026). All three programmes exhibit Critical Red precondition profiles and EFI triple-gate conditions at their earliest assessment windows. The three-programme comparison yields three structurally distinct ROI gap movement patterns: a narrowing gap where governance preconditions are restored without infrastructure precondition recovery (Universal Credit); a widening gap where operational deployment proceeds without precondition restoration (NHS FDP); and a pre-widening condition where legislative commitment precedes structural readiness (NHS SPR). These patterns together constitute preliminary empirical support for the precondition hierarchy thesis across three independent assessment windows. Seven falsifiable propositions are derived. The conditions under which the framework’s central claims would be weakened are explicitly stated. Denmark’s MitID national identity transition is introduced as a positive structural contrast demonstrating that exit feasibility is achievable in practice when treated as a design requirement rather than a procurement option.

The paper concludes with governance instrumentation implications for programme initiation, procurement gateway design, reset decision-making, and annual precondition cadence. An illustrative scoring rubric and a falsifiability conditions table are provided.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a novel model comparison to examine the challenges for monetary policy posed by changes in carbon intensive energy prices. The environmental monetary models employed have a detailed multi-sector structure. The comparison assesses the effects of both a temporary and a permanent energy price increase, with a particular focus on the euro area and the United States. The temporary and permanent price shocks are both inflationary. However, the inflationary impact of the permanent shock depends on the underlying model assumptions and monetary policy response. In addition, the analysis establishes that these models share significant commonalities in their quantitative and qualitative results, while also revealing cross-country differences.

detail.title: Investment Irreversibility in a Granular World

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banco de Espana Working Paper No. 2546
publicationDetails.journalName: Banco de Espana Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Does micro-level investment irreversibility amplify or dampen business cycles? We show this depends on the source of aggregate risk. Investment irreversibility reduces fluctuations in both aggregate output and investment when firm-level idiosyncratic shocks aggregate up to economy-wide effects. This contrasts with models driven by aggregate productivity shocks, where irreversibility has little effect on volatility. The key is whether idiosyncratic shocks are sufficiently volatile to cause the irreversibility constraint to bind cyclically for a significant mass of firms. If so, investment irreversibility hampers productivity enhancing capital reallocation and reduces business cycle volatility. Moreover, household consumption smoothing is impeded when firms cannot adjust capital optimally, increasing real wage volatility. This labor market effect, combined with capital misallocation, reduces aggregate output volatility by 22 percent and investment volatility by 60 percent. These results highlight the importance of considering the source of economic volatility when assessing investment frictions. We provide empirical support for these predictions using firm-level investment data from Compustat.

detail.abstract:
The Quarterly Model of the Banco de España (MTBE, by its Spanish acronym) is a largescale macroeconometric model used for medium-term macroeconomic forecasting of the
Spanish economy, as well as for performing scenario and policy simulations. The model is
for a small, open economy within a monetary union. It is specified as a large set of error
correction equations. This document presents an update of the model, which includes some
specification changes and a re-estimation using data up to 2022. The main change in this
version is the explicit inclusion of expectations in the main equations. This makes the model
suitable for performing simulations under different assumptions about the way agents form
their expectations. The update also enhances the financial channels included in the model
and introduces additional detail in aspects that have gained importance in recent years,
such as energy shocks.

detail.title: The Transmission of Foreign Shocks in a Networked Economy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banco de Espana Working Paper No. 2607
publicationDetails.journalName: Banco de Espana Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We analyze how production networks transmit foreign price shocks and reshape monetary policy trade-offs in an open-economy New Keynesian model with domestic and international input–output linkages. Analytically, we show that closing the output gap does not generally stabilize domestic inflation, as sector-level terms-of-trade movements and trade imbalances become additional drivers of inflation dynamics. Quantitatively, we study an international energy price shock in a model calibrated to major euro area countries and their trade partners. We find that production networks significantly amplify the cumulative headline inflation response and substantially worsen monetary policy trade-offs, as measured by the sacrifice ratio.

title: Linking Blood Demand Forecasts with Emergency Distribution Planning: A TabTransformer and Stochastic MILP Approach
affiliations: Iran University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Linking Blood Demand Forecasts with Emergency Distribution Planning: A TabTransformer and Stochastic MILP Approach
detail.abstract: Blood services work with a narrow safety margin. Too little compatible blood creates a direct service risk, while excessive stock may expire before use. The problem becomes harder during emergencies, when hospital demand may change before the distribution system has fully adjusted. This study links structured blood-demand estimation with a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer linear programming model for one-day emergency blood logistics. The forecasting layer estimates facility-level and blood-group-level demand using a TabTransformer model. The optimization layer then chooses planned truck redistribution before scenario realization and mobile emergency recourse after the demand scenario is observed. The model includes ABO-Rh compatibility, storage capacity, vehicle capacity, route limits, mobile-unit stopping limits, shortage caps, and an end-of-period inventory-loss penalty. A computational case study with five hospitals, four donation or supply centers, eight blood groups, and two mobile emergency units is used for evaluation. In the final validation run, TabTransformer achieved an RMSE of 2.354 and an R² of 0.8387, which was competitive but not better than the historical-mean baseline. The stronger result appears in the optimization layer. The proposed prediction-based stochastic model reduced expected shortage from 11.53 units under average deterministic planning and 13.71 units under prediction-deterministic planning to 2.23 units. Compatibility-based substitution also reduced expected shortage compared with exact-match-only allocation. The results show that the main value of the approach is not forecasting alone, but the conversion of demand estimates into feasible, auditable, compatibility-aware logistics decisions.

detail.abstract: Contemporary supply chains operate under conditions of systemic volatility, geopolitical fragmentation, and accelerating algorithmic dependency. Dominant paradigms anchored in cost minimization prove structurally inadequate when confronted with tail-risk events and the financialization of operational decisions. This paper presents Supply Chain as a Leverage (SCaL), a modular framework developed through Design Science Research (DSR) that repositions the supply chain from a reactive cost center to an active strategic lever for differentiation, financial value creation, and systemic resilience. SCaL is organized around ten interdependent archetypes—each governed by a formally specified master key performance indicator (KPI)—grounded in antifragility theory (Taleb, 2012), real options valuation (Trigeorgis, 1996), information entropy (Shannon, 1948), and network resilience principles (Sheffi, 2005; Ivanov, 2018). The framework's primary theoretical contribution is the formalization of algorithmic sovereignty—a supply-chain-specific extension of the resource-based view (Barney, 1991) that identifies proprietary optimization logic as a defensible strategic intangible. A three-tier maturity model (Stabilization → Synchrony → Leverage), aligned with the supply chain process-maturity literature (Lockamy & McCormack, 2004), provides a structured implementation pathway. The paper concludes by delineating a research agenda for empirical validation through panel econometrics and field-based case studies.

detail.abstract: The objective of this study is to examine the impact of total reserves on Nigerian economic growth using time-series data from 1998 to 2022. The data used for the analysis were sourced from the CBN statistical bulletin and World Development Indicator. The total reserve served as the independent variable and was proxied into external reserve and monetary gold and special drawing rights. The economic gross domestic product served as the dependent variable and the exchange rate served as the control variable. The study employed the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) estimation technique in other to determine the long and short-run run relationship between Total reserve and economic growth. The study found that there is a negative and insignificant relationship between total reserve and economic growth in the long run. This finding shows that the accumulation of total reserves has no impact on economic growth. This is a result of the governmental excessive borrowing, low production of goods and services including excessive importation of goods and services thereby reducing the level of foreign reserve to trade. Therefore, based on these findings, it is recommended that the government should reduce borrowing and provide policies that will support the growth of local producers in the country including granting subsidies to promote production in the country thereby boosting exports which attracts foreign direct investment leading to increase in the foreign reserve and the total reserve in general.

title:
Failure Cost as an Ordering Mechanism: 
Why Systems Stop Optimizing and Start Protecting Viability

detail.title:
Failure Cost as an Ordering Mechanism: 
Why Systems Stop Optimizing and Start Protecting Viability
detail.abstract:
Why do systems abandon apparently superior options and begin selecting slower, safer, or less efficient paths? Profitable projects are delayed. Costly redundancies remain. Efficient reforms stall. High-performing technologies are restricted. These choices are often described as irrationality, bureaucracy, risk aversion, or political obstruction. This paper argues that such explanations often stop at the visible interface. Beneath the surface, a deeper ordering mechanism may be operating: failure cost. 

Failure cost refers to the cost imposed on a system when an error, breakdown, reversal, or exposure cannot remain local, reversible, or procedurally containable. When failure cost is low, systems can prioritize optimization: speed, efficiency, gain, expansion, and performance improvement. When failure cost rises, optimization is structurally downgraded and viability protection becomes dominant. The system begins to rank actions not only by expected benefit, but by whether it can still carry the consequence if the action fails. 

This paper develops failure cost as an ordering mechanism rather than a conventional risk variable. Its central claim is that systems under pressure do not merely calculate higher risk; they reorder what counts as acceptable action. As local error becomes system-level exposure, formally attractive options may lose priority even when they remain technically feasible, legally compliant, or economically beneficial. The system begins to favor pathways that preserve continuity, reversibility, containment, legitimacy, and institutional survivability. 

Drawing from the Ordering framework, the paper traces a causal sequence: failure cost rises; optimization logic loses authority; viability logic gains priority; behavioral ranking changes; and the system selects a different set of feasible paths. By treating failure cost as an ordering mechanism rather than a conventional risk variable, the paper offers a framework for explaining how high-pressure systems shift from optimization to viability protection before failure becomes visible at the interface. This framework enables ex-ante diagnosis of systemic behavioral shifts before visible failure occurs.

title: Microeconomic Analysis of Petroleum Development Oman (PDO)
affiliations: and Sultan Qaboos University

detail.title: Microeconomic Analysis of Petroleum Development Oman (PDO)
detail.abstract: This paper applies microeconomic theory to analyze the behavior and performance of Petroleum Development Oman (PDO) within Oman's oil sector, drawing on secondary data from official industry reports and international energy sources. With a production share of approximately 62% and an industry HHI of 4,346, PDO operates within a highly concentrated oligopoly where high capital requirements, regulatory barriers, and significant government ownership collectively limit competitive entry. The US–Iran conflict of 2026 serves as the central case study, representing a negative supply shock that reduced global oil supply from around 107 million to 97 million barrels per day and pushed average prices from roughly $65 to $140 per barrel. Given the highly inelastic nature of short-run oil demand, with elasticity estimates ranging between −0.05 and −0.10, this supply contraction translated into sharply higher prices rather than meaningful reductions in consumption. PDO, largely insulated from the disruption geographically, responded with a controlled 5% output increase and saw estimated profit per barrel rise from $38 to $113, with daily revenues more than doubling from $44.2 million to $99.9 million. The paper concludes with recommendations focused on maintaining cost efficiency, managing production within the OPEC+ framework, and supporting economic diversification to reduce Oman's long-run exposure to oil market volatility.

detail.title: Australian Monetary Sovereignty: Origins, Evolution and Implications for Federal Spending

contentType.other: Peer reviewed accepted manuscript, yet to be copy-edited

detail.abstract: This article examines how Australia obtained a high degree of monetary sovereignty which increased the federal government's freedom to spend. It examines key episodes in Australia's history, culminating in the float of the Australian dollar in 1983, to demonstrate that the Australian government need not tax before it spends, because its powers to create and spend Australian currency are limited by political choices-not any need to first acquire the currency. While the Commonwealth nonetheless aims to match its spending with tax receipts, with any shortfall met by selling government bonds, these are self-imposed conventions intended to restrain government spending to protect the currency's purchasing power. Although historically, political actors assumed there were constitutional limits on the Commonwealth's power to more directly manage inflation, these debates were ideologically informed and constitutional interpretations have since critically changed, creating possibilities for more innovative economic solutions. Curbing such innovation, however, political restraints on government spending have yet to appropriately adapt to Australia's achievement of monetary sovereignty. The article argues that better understanding the implications of Australia's monetary sovereignty can enhance policy debate by revealing the breadth of the nation's economic policy choices.

title: Neuroleadership Research in HRM: A Systematic Review
affiliations: Southern Cross University - Gold Coast Campus, Southern Cross University and Southern Cross University

detail.title: Neuroleadership Research in HRM: A Systematic Review
detail.abstract: Neurocognitive patterns in leadership shape employee behavior and organizational outcomes, offering important insights for advancing human resource management (HRM) theory and practice. Using a focused, theory-driven journal-based content analysis of ten high-ranked HRM and organizational journals, this review synthesizes neuroleadership research published between 2005 and 2025. The analysis is guided by six integrated neuroleadership themes (decision-making, emotional regulation, motivation and reward processing, social cognition, stress resilience, and attentional control) across six core HRM domains and interpreted through performance-oriented and sustainability-oriented HRM perspectives. The findings suggest that neuroleadership research predominantly emphasizes sustainability-oriented HRM, with decision-making and emotional-cognitive themes most frequently examined within learning and development, followed by employee engagement and well-being and organizational development. In contrast, performance-oriented HRM emphases, such as performance control and transactional management, receive comparatively less attention. The review highlights the need to expand research on motivation, stress resilience, and attentional control to address the demands of an increasingly digitalized workforce.

title: Equilibrium in Endogenous Coalition Sizes
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Kyoto University - Institute of Economic Research

detail.title: Equilibrium in Endogenous Coalition Sizes
detail.abstract: When strategies are chosen by coalitions, equilibrium behavior depends on the distribution of coalition sizes. We introduce a model in which coalition sizes themselves are endogenously determined. Coalitions that obtain higher average payoffs per member are selected at the expense of coalitions that obtain lower payoffs. Thus, coalition sizes co-evolve with behavior. Applying the model to threshold and linear public goods games, we find that typically only coalitions of size one (i.e. individuals) and grand coalitions (i.e. all players in a game) survive. Individuals free ride on contributions by others in the population. Grand coalitions contribute efficiently.

title: Public Policy Evaluation in Malawi: Substantive Governance or Procedural Theatre?
affiliations: Stellenbosch University

detail.title: Public Policy Evaluation in Malawi: Substantive Governance or Procedural Theatre?

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Malawi's national development blueprint, the Malawi Vision 2063, articulates an ambitious trajectory toward middle-income status premised on a transformed, high-performing public service. Central to this ambition is the effective institutionalisation of public policy evaluation mechanisms that can ensure accountability, transparency, and evidence-based governance. This article critically interrogates the effectiveness of Malawi's public policy evaluation framework, with particular attention to the Performance Management System (PMS) introduced in 2008. Drawing on empirical literature, institutional reports, and theoretical frameworks in public administration, the article demonstrates that while the formal architecture of policy evaluation has been progressively elaborated through legislative and procedural instruments, its substantive operationalisation remains profoundly deficient. The PMS has been undermined by supervisory incapacity, limited stakeholder consultation, systemic corruption, and a culture of procedural compliance over results-oriented governance. The article argues that Malawi's evaluation landscape is characterised by a paradox of institutional richness and operational poverty, a phenomenon described herein as 'procedural theatre.' It recommends sector-differentiated evaluation approaches anchored in professional competency mapping, decentralised accountability structures, and sustained investment in evaluative capacity building.

title: Platform Asymmetry and the Two Gates of Cooperation: Feasibility, Self-Enforcement, and Two-Lever Governance in Autonomous Mobility Ecosystems

detail.title: Platform Asymmetry and the Two Gates of Cooperation: Feasibility, Self-Enforcement, and Two-Lever Governance in Autonomous Mobility Ecosystems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this study does not involve human subjects, patient data, personally identifiable information, or proprietary firm-level data. The numerical experiments use synthetic, theory-driven toy instances for analytical illustration.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Cooperation between rival mobility platforms-such as a vertically integrated autonomous-fleet entrant and a demand-aggregating ride-hailing platform-has become a central strategic problem in emerging robotaxi ecosystems. Such partnerships can create value by improving coverage, matching quality, and asset utilization, yet they may collapse even when cooperation appears mutually beneficial. We develop a tractable theoretical model of cooperation under platform asymmetry, where one firm controls critical upstream assets and autonomous-fleet technology while the other controls demand access and intermediation. The model yields a two-gate logic. Gate 1, feasibility, asks whether any cooperative arrangement can make both parties better off than noncooperation. Gate 2, sustainability, asks whether such an arrangement can be self-enforced over time when each party has an incentive to deviate after cooperation expands the market. We show that forces often viewed as pro-cooperation-stronger crossside feedback and policy support-can open Gate 1 while tightening Gate 2, because market expansion can amplify deviation gains and accelerate tipping. This logic generates a governance insight: surplus sharing is not merely a fairness choice; it is stability engineering. A well-chosen sharing rule can balance continuation values and reduce the patience required for self-enforcement. Building on this mechanism, we characterize two-lever policy design, where an incentive lever expands total surplus and a distribution lever selects a stable and defensible split. The model produces empirically testable predictions about where cooperation emerges, where it fails, and when stronger incentives can reduce welfare net of policy costs.

title: Statistical distributions of 3D surface deviations in marching cube-based 3D reconstructed surface tessellations of regular smooth geometries
affiliations: and Indian Institute of Technology Dharwad

detail.title: Statistical distributions of 3D surface deviations in marching cube-based 3D reconstructed surface tessellations of regular smooth geometries
detail.abstract: 3D surfaces generated from tomographic imaging carry geometric errors due to the finite voxel size. Those errors are typically quantified using scalar metrics, such as the root-mean-square, which do not capture their statistical and spatial distributions. This exploratory study focuses on a systematic statistical analysis of geometric errors across geometries of varying curvature anisotropy. Geometric primitives such as spheres, ellipsoids, tori, hyperboloids, and cylinders with hemispherical end caps, with dimensions commensurate with the consistent bounding box, were voxelised at varying resolutions. Surfaces reconstructed from voxelisations using marching cubes were compared with reference surface tessellations by point cloud registration, and nearest-neighbour computation was used to compute local surface deviation. Multiple candidate probability distribution functions (PDFs), including Gamma, Generalised Gamma, Weibull, Folded Normal and others, were fitted using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and evaluated using Akaike and Bayesian Information Criteria (AIC and BIC), Cramer von Mises (CvM) goodness-of-fit (GoF) test. Mean surface deviation increased almost linearly with voxel sizes. Error distributions were consistently non-Gaussian. Bulkier geometries resulted in higher mean and RMS errors than slender ones. For most of the geometry-voxel combinations, the generalised gamma distribution was found to be best amongst all explored distributions. AIC and BIC agreed with each other in almost all scenarios, while CvM differed in the case of ellipsoids. No single PDF provided a consistently adequate fit across all geometries and voxel sizes, indicating that the distributional patterns depend on geometry topology and voxel sizes. The generalised gamma distribution could be the first preferred choice for modelling the statistical distribution of surface errors.

title: From Classical Optimization to Bayesian Integration: A Comprehensive Analysis of Systematic Portfolio Management
affiliations: and

detail.title: From Classical Optimization to Bayesian Integration: A Comprehensive Analysis of Systematic Portfolio Management
detail.abstract: This paper compares a series of contemporary portfolio construction approaches by employing ten U.S. stocks (TSLA, WMT, BAC, GS, LLY, MRK, GOOG, META, AAPL and XOM) in a time frame from September 2023 to December 2025. The paper explores both basic mean-variance optimization, constrained optimization, Fama French five factor regression modeling, Monte Carlo simulation, and the Black-Litterman model to determine how constraints to a solution, risk factors to a strategy, simulated approximations, and specific market views may all impact the outcome of portfolio allocation, performance and stability. Overall, the results show that standard optimization may result in highly concentrated portfolios, while constrained optimization leads to changes in portfolio allocations by altering the efficient frontier, five factor regression models suggest that a basic investment style of defensive large value and profitability exposure, Monte Carlo approximation is a viable technique to arrive at mean-variance optimal portfolios provided the simulations are high enough especially under a box constraint, the Black Litterman portfolio approach produces more economically intuitive allocations and greater stability compared to standard mean-variance optimization as the approach balances equilibrium returns with investor views.

title: Strategic Governance of Integrated Nuclear Medicine, Diagnostic Radiology, and Radiation Therapy in Comprehensive Cancer Centres: A Balanced Scorecard Framework
affiliations: International Atomic Energy Agency, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Kenyatta National Hospital, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Hospital Sirio-Libanes - Department of Radiation Oncology and International Atomic Energy Agency

detail.title: Strategic Governance of Integrated Nuclear Medicine, Diagnostic Radiology, and Radiation Therapy in Comprehensive Cancer Centres: A Balanced Scorecard Framework
detail.abstract: ​Comprehensive cancer centres depend on nuclear medicine, diagnostic radiology and radiation therapy for diagnosis, staging, treatment planning, image guidance, treatment delivery, response assessment and follow-up. Although these services are clinically interdependent, they are often governed through separate departmental structures, budgets, information systems, quality routines and performance reports. This fragmentation can limit the ability of cancer-centre leaders to balance access, clinical quality, patient safety, workforce capacity, equipment sustainability, innovation and data stewardship. This policy analysis proposes a Balanced Scorecard and Strategy Map for integrated radiation medicine governance in comprehensive cancer centres. The framework adapts the classical Balanced Scorecard by making six domains explicit: patient access and experience, clinical quality and safety, integrated care pathways, resources and sustainability, workforce learning and innovation, and data, digital infrastructure and decision support. It also proposes a two-tier governance dashboard, with a concise strategic scorecard for executive and cancer-centre leadership and more detailed operational scorecards for nuclear medicine, diagnostic radiology and radiation therapy teams. The framework is intended to complement, not replace, discipline-specific audit, accreditation, quality assurance and incident-learning systems. Its purpose is to align these systems within a shared governance architecture that supports transparent investment prioritisation, workforce planning, access improvement, technology adoption and quality improvement. The scorecard should not be used as a punitive performance system. Its value depends on co-design, precise indicator definitions, trusted data sources, contextual interpretation and recurring non-punitive review. Future work should pilot the framework and evaluate feasibility, acceptability, data burden and influence on leadership decisions.

title: ITAGREEN Mrio: Towards a Multiscale Ecological Macroeconomic Model
affiliations: University of Florence, University of Florence and University of Florence

detail.title: ITAGREEN Mrio: Towards a Multiscale Ecological Macroeconomic Model

declarations.funderStatement: This work was funded by the Next Generation EU - Italian National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), Mission 4, Component C2, Investment 1.1, “Fondo per il Programma Nazionale di Ricerca e Progetti di Rilevante Interesse Nazionale (PRIN)” (Directorial Decree n. 2022/1409) — under the project “MUlti-scale modelization toward Socio-ecological Transition for Water Management (MUST4Water)”, n. P2022R8ZTW. This work reflects only the authors’ views and opinions, neither the Ministry for University and Research nor the European Commission. This work is also carried out in the context of the project “Modelli Regionali per lo Sviluppo Umano e Sostenibile in Toscana” (Regional Models for Human and Sustainable Development in Tuscany.

detail.abstract:
This study presents ITAGREEN-MRIO, a novel Multi-Spatial Integrated Assessment Model
(MS-IAM) developed to explore the socio-economic impacts of climate change in Italy within the
context of sustainability transitions. Rooted in Ecological Macroeconomics, the model is built on
a modular system dynamics framework and extended to capture spatial heterogeneity across five
macro-regions. Its design enables the analysis of complex socio-economic and ecological dynamics
under alternative techno-climatic scenarios, with particular attention to the propagation of regional
shocks and their aggregation at the national scale. The main methodological contribution lies in
the explicit incorporation of a multi-regional input–output structure, region-specific household
consumption, and spatially heterogeneous climate damage impacts. This configuration provides a
detailed representation of how climate-induced productivity shocks affect intermediate goods flows,
household demand, and value added across regions and sectors. The results show that neglecting
regional heterogeneity leads to a systematic underestimation of long-run aggregate losses, as climate
shocks propagate unevenly through interregional production networks and are amplified by
regions with strong manufacturing centrality. The analysis further highlights the interaction between
endogenous technological change and climate damages. While innovation supports output
growth, it does not fully offset productivity losses and may amplify resource pressures through increased
intermediate input requirements. Overall, ITAGREEN-MRIO provides a spatially explicit
framework capable of capturing the intertwined economic, technological, and ecological dimensions
of climate impacts, offering a robust tool for regionally informed policy design.

title: NULL at Scale: The Burgess Principle Applied to an Institutional Accountability Failure

detail.title: NULL at Scale: The Burgess Principle Applied to an Institutional Accountability Failure
detail.abstract: This paper presents a documented case study of the Burgess Principle SOVEREIGN/NULL binary test applied at institutional scale to a named public authority-Durham Constabulary-across five accountability dimensions: responsiveness to the binary question, evidence of individual human review, timeliness relative to statutory obligations, remedy offered, and systemic change. The case study is distinguished from hypothetical or modelled assessments by a methodological constraint: every finding in this paper is corroborated exclusively by documents produced by independent statutory bodies-the Information Commissioner's Office, His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services, and the Independent Office for Police Conductor by the institution's own formal correspondence. No finding depends on the author's characterisation of events alone. The case study produces an aggregate NULL finding across all five dimensions, scored 2/20 under the Burgess Principle Institution Audit Taxonomy v1.0. The result is corroborated by: an ICO data protection audit (July 2024) finding more than half of assessed controls below reasonable assurance; an HMICFRS integrity inspection (February 2026) grading the force inadequate in vetting and counter-corruption and requiring improvement in professional standards; and the force's own SAR response containing a substantive date error corrected only after formal challenge. The case study demonstrates the framework's core proposition: that institutional accountability failure is not a single event but a systemic condition, detectable through independent corroboration at multiple dimensions simultaneously, and documentable before any adverse outcome is adjudicated. Implications are drawn for: police accountability under the Police Reform Act 2002; data subject rights enforcement under UK GDPR and the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; AI governance under EU AI Act Article 14; and the use of empirical case study evidence in institutional accountability research. The paper is the third in a series: the first (SSRN abstract 6759778) operationalised the binary test against statutory frameworks; the second (abstract 6864621) grounded the framework in political philosophy from Locke to Manin. This paper supplies the empirical proof of concept.

title: Contraction without Convergence: Intersectional Occupational Inequality among Women in India, 1992-2021
affiliations: and Azim Premji University

detail.title: Contraction without Convergence: Intersectional Occupational Inequality among Women in India, 1992-2021
detail.abstract: This paper examines the structure and evolution of occupational inequality among women in India over the last thirty years using National Family Health Survey (1992-2021). Employing the Index of Representation, entropy-based segregation measures, and regression models, we show that the decline in female labour force participation since the mid-2000s has coincided with a contraction of the occupational structure rather than a broad-based shift toward higherquality employment. Disadvantaged groups remain concentrated in low-skilled and informal work, while access to skilled occupations is increasingly selective and shaped by education, wealth, and intra-household autonomy. Importantly, rural and urban labour markets operate through distinct mechanisms: rural women's participation is largely driven by economic compulsion and scarcity of jobs, whereas in urban areas participation, exclusion, and access to skilled employment are more strongly shaped by social norms, household constraints, and labour market segmentation. The findings suggest that declining participation and declining segregation have coexisted with persistent and, in some dimensions, intensifying occupational inequality among women in India over the last three decades.

title: Goodwill Accounting and Bank Supervision
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Sustainable & Green Finance Institute (SGFIN), Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU), Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Singapore Management University - School of Accountancy

detail.title: Goodwill Accounting and Bank Supervision
detail.abstract: We examine whether accounting-based signals shape bank supervision. SFAS 142 mandated a shift from goodwill amortization to annual impairment testing. We exploit this adoption as a quasi-natural experiment and find that bank regulators are 3.1 percentage points more likely to issue Enforcement Decisions and Orders (EDOs) to banks with goodwill after the adoption. The effect is stronger when regulators face tighter resource constraints and when banks attract greater public scrutiny. We further document a reallocation of regulatory attention: post-adoption, regulators appear to shift attention to goodwill by issuing more EDOs to highgoodwill banks with strong capital positions. Machine learning analysis of EDO texts confirms that regulators place greater emphasis on asset quality, management, and earnings after the adoption. These are the dimensions most informationally tied to goodwill impairment. Despite this reallocation, regulatory actions become less pro-cyclical, and treated banks exhibit lower risk and failure rates during the 2007-2009 financial crisis. These findings demonstrate that impairment accounting measuring bank goodwill generates actionable forward-looking signals that enhance the efficacy of prudential bank supervision.

title: Keeping up with Caitlin Clark: Evolving Coverage of Women's Basketball
affiliations: University of South Carolina

detail.title: Keeping up with Caitlin Clark: Evolving Coverage of Women's Basketball
detail.abstract: Bias in product markets is a longstanding concern, but distinguishing whether it reflects seller preferences or a lack of information about consumer demand is empirically difficult. Women's athletics have historically received less attention than men's athletics, raising concern about gender bias. I explore this possible bias by studying ESPN's coverage decisions between 2023 and 2025, during which women's basketball rose in popularity. Using high-frequency data on ESPN's rank ordering of headlines and article engagement, I find that ESPN initially underestimated the popularity of women's basketball. The apparent bias was short-lived, suggesting ESPN adjusted its ranking behavior to reflect reader preferences.

title: Regional Economic Impacts and Emission Responses under Solar Radiation Modification
affiliations: University of Oslo, University of Oslo, Yale University, Yale University - Cowles Foundation and University of Oslo

detail.title: Regional Economic Impacts and Emission Responses under Solar Radiation Modification

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Solar Radiation Modification (SRM) has been proposed as a potential tool to limit increases in global or regional temperatures caused by anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions. While previous research has extensively examined the climate system’s response to various SRM strategies, as well as their aggregate economic consequences, the regional distribution of economic impacts has received less attention. In this study, we use NorESM2–DIAM—an Earth System Model coupled to a high-resolution integrated assessment model—to assess the economic impacts, measured in GDP per capita, in an idealised SRM scenario where incoming solar radiation is reduced by 1%. Our results suggest that, relative to a baseline without SRM, most countries experience economic gains under SRM, with only a few countries facing negative impacts. Low-income countries tend to see the largest benefits, reducing global economic inequality relative to the baseline. However, reduced damages and lower inequality are accompanied by higher emissions under SRM, potentially leading to additional adverse effects not captured here. These findings highlight potential trade-offs between economic benefits, reduced inequality, and increased emissions relevant for SRM governance.

title: Falling Dominoes? The Impact of the US Exit from Free Trade on the Sustainability of Trade Cooperation
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University, Abu Dhabi, University of Michigan - Department of Economics and University of Texas at Austin - Department of Economics

detail.title: Falling Dominoes? The Impact of the US Exit from Free Trade on the Sustainability of Trade Cooperation

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper quantitatively evaluates other countries' optimal tariffs and the prospects of sustaining international trade cooperation when a large player—the United States—exits the cooperative trade regime. To guide the analysis, we rely on an analytical characterization of the optimal tariff in a simplified multi-country trade model with endogenous labor supply. A country's optimal import tariffs are a function of its trade partners' expenditure shares on its goods, and the trade and labor supply elasticities. In both the simplified model and the full quantitative multi-country, multi-sector global network model, the impact of the US withdrawal from free trade on other countries' optimal tariffs and the sustainability of the cooperative trade regime is minimal. This is because quantitatively, the key determinants of these objects—domestic and international trade shares of other countries—change little from the US withdrawal. This main finding is not sensitive to the trade or labor supply elasticities. Thus, the fall of the US free trade domino is unlikely to cause further dominoes to fall.

title: Do Female Leaders Reduce Corruption? New Evidence from Brazil

detail.title: Do Female Leaders Reduce Corruption? New Evidence from Brazil

detail.abstract:
Does female leadership reduce corruption? We study this question using close mixed-gender elections in Brazilian municipalities over two decades and multiple measures of corruption: budget-based predicted corruption scores, audit irregularities, and legal sanctions. We find no evidence that electing a woman mayor affects corruption. This null result holds across time periods, mayor characteristics, and the electoral cycle. We only detect a negative effect in the small subsample of municipalities randomly audited in early terms, which coincides with a sharp imbalance in incumbency. Because incumbency directly impacts corruption, these previously documented effects likely reflect the impact of incumbency rather than gender.

title: Wagering the Bread Money: Sports Betting Legalization and Food Sufficiency
affiliations: Capital University of Economics and Business, University of West Georgia and Lehigh University

detail.title: Wagering the Bread Money: Sports Betting Legalization and Food Sufficiency

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This is the first study to estimate the impact of sports gambling legalization on food sufficiency using the staggered implementation of state laws between 2021-2023. By analyzing Google searches for online sportsbooks and legal wagers, we show that interest in sports gambling increases sharply following legalization. Applying an imputation-based difference-in-differences design to biweekly Household Pulse Survey (HPS) data, we find that legalized sports gambling reduces household food sufficiency by 2.1 percent among working-age adults without a college degree, which translates to a 10.5 percent decline among active bettors. This effect is cyclical, persisting for three-to-five months during NFL seasons. Additionally, the declines in food sufficiency are larger among households with adults aged 25-44 and racial/ethnic minorities. Using additional data from the HPS, Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System and Current Population Survey, our exploration of mechanisms suggests that the negative effects on food sufficiency operate through financial distress rather than changes in mental health or labor supply. A back-of-the-envelope calculation indicates that legalization of sports gambling in nine states resulted in an additional 284,000 food-insufficient households and $130.2 million in excess healthcare expenditures annually.

title: How Frontline Supervisors Shape Priorities: Evidence from Police Lieutenants

detail.title: How Frontline Supervisors Shape Priorities: Evidence from Police Lieutenants

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study how frontline supervisors shape outcomes in public organizations with competing objectives and limited monitoring. We examine lieutenants in the Chicago Police Department, exploiting its rotational operations calendar for identification. We document dispersion in lieutenant fixed effects on team arrests and find race to be a key predictor. We then compare days Black and Hispanic lieutenants are predicted on duty to days supervised by white lieutenants. Teams under Black and Hispanic lieutenants make fewer low-level arrests while improving 911 call dispatch time. Lieutenants shape effort allocation by differentially granting overtime and awards for serious rather than discretionary arrests.

title: Are carbon tariffs climate policy?
affiliations: Williams College, University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) - Donald Bren School of Environmental Science & Management and Cornell University - Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management

detail.title: Are carbon tariffs climate policy?

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Carbon import tariffs, traditionally considered a complement to domestic climate policy, are increasingly proposed as standalone policies. We build a quantitative trade model to compare U.S. carbon tariffs with and without a domestic carbon tax, each applied to a set of carbon-intensive, trade-exposed sectors. We find three main results. First, a U.S. carbon tariff increases U.S. emissions, lowers foreign emissions, and on net achieves half the global emissions reductions of the combined policy, which lowers both U.S. and foreign emissions. Second, both approaches increase U.S. GDP and welfare, but the combined policy has a larger effect due to terms of trade improvements. Third, global emissions reductions from multilateral tariff-only agreements are modest and do not increase monotonically with greater membership, whereas under combined policies they scale considerably with membership.

title: But I Like Doing This! Enjoyable Tasks, Contracting, and Automation

detail.title: But I Like Doing This! Enjoyable Tasks, Contracting, and Automation

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Workers sometimes enjoy productive tasks and voluntarily devote unpaid time to them. We study O-ring jobs in which firms can either price a complete task bundle or specify paid task floors while workers remain free to add time. For any allocation supported by both hourly contracts, the wage bill is identical: voluntary top-up is not a discount. The contracts differ because paid floors cannot cap attractive tasks below the worker's voluntary supply. This implementability constraint adds a containment motive for automation alongside replacement and scale effects. It also makes payroll measures incomplete: conditional on a common automated set and a common AI technology, jobs with the same payroll footprint can differ in worked time and task mix. Rich salaried bundle pricing removes the hourly-contract distortion.

title: Is the iPhone Birth Control? Causal Evidence from AT&T’s 2007–2011 Carrier Monopoly
affiliations: Middlebury College and Middlebury College

detail.title: Is the iPhone Birth Control? Causal Evidence from AT&T’s 2007–2011 Carrier Monopoly

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The U.S. general fertility rate has fallen by 22% since 2007, a sustained decline not readily explained by economic conditions, contraceptive use, housing or childcare costs, or other commonly cited factors. We assess the potential role of a different shock: the diffusion of the smartphone. The U.S. rollout of the iPhone, the first modern smartphone, provides a natural experiment: from June 2007 through February 2011, the device was sold only on AT&T, allowing us to identify its effect from variation in AT&T’s mobile broadband coverage. Entropy-balanced Poisson and synthetic difference-in-differences event studies imply that access to the iPhone reduced births by 4.5–8.0% at ages 15–19 and 3.2–6.6% at ages 20–24, with statistically significant but smaller declines among older cohorts. Placebo analyses applied to Verizon and Sprint’s pre-2011 coverage footprint are null. Taken together, these cohort effects imply that the diffusion of the iPhone deepened the decline in births among women under 30 while suppressing the rise in births among older women. Overall, the diffusion of the iPhone explains 33–52% of the decline in the general fertility rate among women aged 15–44. National-survey evidence on time use and sexual behavior is consistent with the iPhone reducing in-person interactions, increasing pornography use, and reducing sexual frequency.

title: How Small is Small? Non-linearities in Heterogeneous Agent Models

detail.title: How Small is Small? Non-linearities in Heterogeneous Agent Models

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In plausibly calibrated heterogeneous-agent models, marginal propensities to consume (MPCs) are highly non-linear in wealth, falling sharply away from borrowing constraints. As a result, the aggregate consumption response to a fiscal transfer is strongly concave in its size: larger transfers shift households out of high-MPC regions and thereby dampen the consumption response. Across partial- and general-equilibrium settings, linear methods substantially overstate the effects of fiscal stimulus at empirically relevant sizes. Local methods are not reliable for studying shocks and policies where a failure of Ricardian equivalence is important.

title: Preferences for Everyday Objects are Strongly Stochastically Transitive
affiliations: Uppsala University - Department of Psychology, Uppsala University and Uppsala University

detail.title: Preferences for Everyday Objects are Strongly Stochastically Transitive
detail.abstract: The APA Dictionary of Psychology states that intransitive relationships "appear to be illogical and inconsistent but are often found in matters of personal preference". This received view mainly rests on a literature that has demonstrated the existence of intransitive preferences for so-called monetary gambles. Such novel, artificial stimuli scarcely exist outside of the laboratory and are not representative of the objects people encounter in their everyday lives. To make general statements, we should instead sample representative real-world options ("representative design"). Across three large-sample experiments that address methodological limitations of previous work, we find intransitivity to be virtually inexistent across ten categories of everyday objects, with an estimated prevalence of strong stochastic transitivity close to 100%. The high rate of strongly stochastically transitive preferences holds also when we increase the discriminative difficulty between the everyday objects. For monetary gambles, the rate of intransitivity is systematically higher but only a few percentages. These results would restrict the set of viable theories of two-alternative forced choice between everyday objects to be those that predict strong stochastic transitivity. While not denying that people can be placed in situations where they \emph{have to} construct preferences, which occasionally may violate transitivity, we present a theory where subjective value forms part of one's conceptual knowledge of a category of objects. Such conceptual preferences are well-informed and transitive. The received view that preferences are "often" intransitive appears to be driven by an exaggerated focus on a particular kind of artificial stimulus for which people lack conceptual preferences.

title: Bayesian Non-Persuasion
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Bayesian Non-Persuasion

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Rules against persuasion often focus on beliefs: an institution should not manipulate the information on which a decision rests. We show that such rules can miss a distinct source of directional influence. An institution can steer an outcome without changing beliefs by selecting among authorised procedures that translate the same belief into different actions. Jury instructions provide the leading example: a judge may alter no juror’s assessment of the facts yet still affect the verdict through the permissible formulation of the law. The gap is sharpest near a decision threshold. There, the scope for belief movement that preserves the default action vanishes, while procedural steering can remain maximal whenever authorised procedures disagree near the boundary, even with genuinely informative communication. In general, exposure to procedural steering is the concavification of a local steering score. The geometry of Bayesian persuasion thus reappears in reverse: it measures not the value of manipulating beliefs, but the directional discretion left open by institutional rules.

title: Innovation Theater: Frontier Narrative Adoption, Investment Decoupling, and Cross-sectional Return Predictability
affiliations: University of London - School of Business, Economics and Informatics, , University of Surrey - Surrey Business School, University of Surrey - Surrey Business School and University of Surrey

detail.title: Innovation Theater: Frontier Narrative Adoption, Investment Decoupling, and Cross-sectional Return Predictability
detail.abstract: Firms increasingly adopt frontier technology narratives in public disclosures while simultaneously reducing investment, which is a pattern we term Innovation Theater. We introduce the Narrative-Action Gap (NAG), a continuous measure of the divergence between frontier technology discourse in 10-K filings and total investment intensity, constructed from approximately 63,000 firm-year observations spanning 2000-2022. Instrumental variable estimation reveals that discourse escalation and investment decline are co-evolutionary responses to capital market pressure rather than a sequential causal chain; operational distress plays no role. The NAG predicts lower future profitability, operating entirely through the investment channel and amplified during crisis periods when foregone investment becomes competitively binding. In asset markets, within-firm NAG deviations negatively predict next-year stock returns, concentrated among informationally opaque small firms with sparse analyst coverage and dissipating beyond a one-year horizon. We interpret this pattern as institutionalized investment forgone: firms under capital market pressure jointly produce elevated discourse and suppressed investment as co-outputs of a common institutional adaptation, with return consequences that markets incorporate with delay proportional to firm-level information opacity.

title: Innovation without Borders? The Geography of Technological Diffusion
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB), Harvard University - Business School (HBS), Goethe University Frankfurt, European Central Bank (ECB), University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Innovation without Borders? The Geography of Technological Diffusion

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
How well does innovation diffuse across geographic boundaries? To shed light on this question, we present a large-scale field experiment involving 3,300 firms across twelve European Union countries. We elicit firms' perceptions of the share of similar firms in their own country that had invested in artificial intelligence (AI), as well as the corresponding share among similar firms in Germany, France, and Italy. We randomly provide half of the sample with accurate information about both domestic and foreign AI investment. We show that firms substantially underestimate competitors' current AI investment, both domestically and abroad, and that they update their expectations about competitors' future AI investment in response to the information treatment. The treatment also causes a statistically significant increase in firms' own expected AI investment rate (p-value < 0.001). We find strong strategic complementarities within borders: a 1 pp increase in the expected share of domestic peers investing in AI raises a firm's own expected AI investment rate by 0.570 pp. These complementarities are absent across borders: the effect of an increase in the expected share of foreign peers investing in AI on a firm's own expected AI investment rate is statistically insignificant. Overall, our evidence shows that innovation diffusion and strategic complementarities in AI investment are much stronger domestically than internationally.

title: Intergenerational Mobility in Late Qing Dynasty: Evidence from Northeast China
affiliations: University of Chicago, University of Chicago - Stone Center for Research on Wealth Inequality and Mobility and New Economic School (NES)

detail.title: Intergenerational Mobility in Late Qing Dynasty: Evidence from Northeast China

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper examines intergenerational mobility across social classes during the late Qing dynasty employing a remarkable data set from Liaoning province in Northeast China. We identify two distinct epochs with markedly different mobility dynamics. Before 1850, mobility patterns exhibited stability and convergence toward a steady state. The second epoch, beginning around 1850, was characterized by unstable intergenerational class dynamics that persisted until the dynasty’s collapse. The transition between epochs coincides with the Opium Wars and Taiping Rebellion, demonstrating how the footprints of major crises in the late Qing era can be traced in mobility dynamics. Employing Markov-chain measures and two alternative mobility concepts—the persistence of class origin across generations and intergenerational class movement—we document that intergenerational mobility increased over the period. However, this aggregate increase masked a decline in upward mobility alongside a rise in downward mobility—disparate patterns that resonate with broader theories of political instability.
