title: A Geometric Interpretation of Default Correlation in CDO Tranches
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Geometric Interpretation of Default Correlation in CDO Tranches
detail.abstract: We develop a geometric framework for understanding default correlation in collateralized debt obligations (CDOs). Under the standard one-factor Gaussian copula model, the latent Gaussian dependence structure of 𝑁 obligors has ellipsoidal covariance contours defined by the correlation matrix. As the pairwise correlation 𝜌 increases from 0 toward 1, the ellipsoid deforms from a sphere to a line segment along the diagonal of ℝ 𝑁. We partition ℝ 𝑁 into 2 𝑁 default zones and illustrate how probability mass is redistributed toward extreme zones (all-default and no-default) as correlation increases. This provides geometric intuition for why, in standard homogeneous or endpoint-comparison settings, equity tranches exhibit long-correlation behavior while senior tranches exhibit short-correlation behavior, whereas total expected loss is invariant. We extend the visualization to three dimensions and derive a polynomial endpoint-balance condition characterizing when the expected loss of an elementary one-default-thick mezzanine tranche coincides at the two extreme correlation regimes. The geometric approach complements algebraic treatments and is particularly relevant for small-𝑁 portfolios where the zone structure remains computationally tractable.

title: Cognitive Sovereignty in the Age of Generative AI: Language, Culture, and Epistemic Autonomy in the Iranian Context

detail.title: Cognitive Sovereignty in the Age of Generative AI: Language, Culture, and Epistemic Autonomy in the Iranian Context
detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of large language models across non-Western societies raises a question that technical benchmarks cannot answer: whose cognitive frameworks are being normalized at scale? This paper introduces cognitive sovereignty the capacity of individuals and communities to maintain epistemic autonomy, preserve culturally-situated modes of reasoning, and critically engage with algorithmically-mediated knowledge as a conceptual lens for analyzing the cultural stakes of artificial intelligence deployment beyond the Anglophone West. Drawing on the observation that Iranian civilization has historically absorbed foreign intellectual currents while retaining its distinctive epistemic character, we argue that the central threat posed by current AI systems is not technological dependence per se, but the subtler erosion of the conditions under which genuine cultural adaptation as opposed to passive assimilation remains possible. Preliminary evidence suggests that dominant large language models encode systematic representational defaults through training data composition and value alignment procedures, producing measurable gaps when confronted with Persian linguistic structures such as the gender-neutral third-person pronoun that English-centric Parsa, R. Cognitive Sovereignty in the Age of Generative AI 2 models consistently mishandle and with collective moral reasoning frameworks that resist reduction to individualist cost-benefit logic. Through comparative analysis of sovereign AI initiatives in China, India, and the UAE, assessed against a key variable of ecosystem openness versus securitization, alongside an honest account of Iran's structurally constrained but strategically significant national AI efforts, we identify prerequisites for meaningful cognitive sovereignty: culturally-informed red teaming, epistemic diversity standards, and accountable governance mechanisms situated within realistic infrastructure conditions. Building on Floridi's philosophy of information and Joseloff's sociotechnical imaginaries, we conclude that cognitive sovereignty is not a defensive posture against modernity but a precondition for the creative cultural synthesis that has historically defined Iran's engagement with transformative intellectual forces. The capacity to shape the epistemic conditions of AI use not merely to consume its outputs may prove as consequential for cognitive democracy as the capacity to build the systems themselves.

title: Freedom of Contract at Common Law
affiliations: Yale Law School and University of Toronto - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Freedom of Contract at Common Law
detail.abstract: We defend the common law conception of freedom of contract against criticisms that unregulated contractual freedom permits strong parties to impose unjust terms on weak parties. Common law courts enforce contracts when the parties are informed, competent and free from coercion, and performance of such a contract would not impose costs on nonparties. These contracts are "preferred" in the sense that each party believes that it reflects the best deal the party could have made given its circumstances. The contractual social justice critique responds that such a contract nevertheless can be unjust in four ways: (i) it divides the expected surplus a deal could yield unequally; (ii) it does not realize substantive justice between the parties because the contract contains unjust terms; (iii) performance of the contract would degrade the weaker party or otherwise violate his dignitary interest; and (iv) systematically enforcing unjust contracts-eg, very one-sided risk allocations-would increase the economic subordination of nonparties or otherwise negatively affect them.

title: Tax Talk in Analyst Reports
affiliations: Brigham Young University, University of Iowa - Henry B. Tippie College of Business, Brigham Young University and Brigham Young University - Marriott School

detail.title: Tax Talk in Analyst Reports
detail.abstract: We study how tax discussion in analyst reports reflects specialized analyst expertise and whether that expertise is associated with more accurate forecasts and stronger market responses to forecast revisions. Using analyst reports from 2013-2017, we show that the incidence of taxrelated discussion is primarily driven by analyst-and brokerage-level expertise rather than firmspecific demand, underscoring the supply-side origins of tax discussion. Reports containing such references exhibit significantly greater accuracy in effective tax rate, tax expense, and earnings forecasts, consistent with tax analysis enhancing analysts' predictive performance. Capital markets also respond more strongly to forecast revisions when they include tax-related discussion, with no evidence of reversal, suggesting that investors efficiently incorporate these insights. Together, our findings establish tax expertise as a transferable, supply-side dimension of analyst skill that improves forecast quality and enhances price formation in capital markets.

title: Finance or Gambling? Prediction Markets After Loper Bright and the Administrative Record
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Department of Law, , Ben Gurion University and University of Haifa School of Criminology, Faculty of Law

detail.title: Finance or Gambling? Prediction Markets After Loper Bright and the Administrative Record

publicationDetails.detailsText: American Business Law Journal (forthcoming: 2027), Volume 64 Issue 1.

detail.abstract: After Loper Bright displaced Chevron deference, how an agency constructs and defends the administrative record became a central question of administrative law, and prediction markets have become one of its most contested settings. As Americans increasingly trade on outcomes ranging from sports and entertainment to elections and geopolitical events, regulators and courts struggle over whether these products should be governed as financial instruments or as gambling. Prediction markets now facilitate substantial trading volume, command significant valuations, and operate amid active litigation across multiple states and federal courts. Regulators continue to assess these products through the lenses of hedging, price discovery, and information aggregation, while critics characterize them as gambling. Reframing that classification dispute as a problem of administrative law, this Article examines how it manifests not in theory, but in the administrative record itself. Recent empirical work using large language model (LLM)–based computational text analysis demonstrates that regulatory outcomes track the structure, complexity, and informational content of public comments, and that certain forms of participation are more likely to shape the administrative record and, in turn, agency reasoning. By treating the notice-and-comment record as a legally consequential evidentiary object rather than a passive aggregation of preferences, this Article demonstrates how linguistic framing shapes the factual predicates on which agencies must now defend regulatory choices under independent judicial judgment. The empirical inquiry applies computational text and sentiment analysis to public comments submitted on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) 2024 Event Contracts Notice of Proposed Rulemaking. Although the CFTC withdrew the proposal on February 4, 2026, the resulting notice-and-comment record remains a durable evidentiary source shaping litigation and future governance. Using natural language processing, LLM classification, multi-model validation, and confidence-weighted semantic analysis, the study assesses whether commenters characterize prediction markets primarily as economic instruments or emphasize their gambling-like features and risks. The analysis reveals a pronounced asymmetry: of 812 submissions, 87.2% addressed economic, financial, or regulatory consequences rather than gambling-related characteristics, employing terminology central to financial discourse. Only 5.8% emphasized gambling risks or entertainment dynamics, with high-confidence gambling terminology, with the remaining 7% mixed or neutral. This economic-dominant framing appears across all stakeholder positions (opponents of the rule, supporters of the restriction, and neutral commenters), suggesting that regulatory disagreement reflects not competing conceptualizations of what event contracts are, but rather how a shared economic understanding should be regulated. The dataset also reveals skewed participation: while the median comment length was 147 words, the average exceeded 2,500 words, indicating that most participants submitted brief statements while a small minority provided extensive filings. One hundred eighty comments included attachments, some representing coordinated filings by elected officials or organizations. Professional industry representatives and organized stakeholders, though a numerical minority, dominate the record through the length and density of their submissions, amplifying the financial framing presented to regulators. Despite substantial scholarship documenting gambling-like mechanisms, the administrative record reflects predominantly financial framing. These findings illuminate how stakeholder framing shapes the factual record upon which classification decisions rest. Because courts now exercise independent judgment over both statutory meaning and the adequacy of agency fact-finding, In a post–Loper Bright environment, where courts apply heightened scrutiny to agency fact-finding and statutory interpretation, the administrative record's rhetorical construction can prove decisive. By demonstrating empirically how language and framing constitute the evidentiary foundation for regulatory classification, this Article reveals that the legal status of prediction markets may turn less on their inherent characteristics than on the discursive strategies through which interested parties present them to regulators and courts, a dynamic that reaches any agency defending a contested classification on the record. This dynamic raises foundational questions about whether notice-and-comment produces records courts can treat as genuinely independent evidentiary foundations.

title: Paying More and Buying Less: 2025 Tariffs and U.S. Household Spending

detail.title: Paying More and Buying Less: 2025 Tariffs and U.S. Household Spending

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2026-035, 2026[10.17016/FEDS.2026.035]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: This paper estimates the effects of the 2025 U.S. tariffs on household spending using transaction-level data linked to tariff exposure and a tariff sentiment survey. Comparing high versus low tariff-exposed categories, we find 15 to 20 percent price pass-through. At the mean increase in tariff exposure, prices rise by 1 to 2 percent while spending falls by roughly 4 percent. Survey evidence linking stated intentions to revealed behavior identifies a mechanism for the large spending response: reallocation toward essentials and trade-down within categories, concentrated among middle-income households with discretionary slack who express tariff concerns. Low-income households bear a disproportionate welfare burden through regressive pass-through.

title: Dietary Transitions Reshape the Geography of Global Food Production and Trade
affiliations: , University of Oxford - Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment, University of Oxford and Delft University of Technology

detail.title: Dietary Transitions Reshape the Geography of Global Food Production and Trade
detail.abstract: The potential for sustainable dietary transitions to benefit human health and environmental sustainability is well understood. Yet their implications for the geography of global food production and trade remain poorly quantified. We model how five dietary pathways might reshape bilateral trade networks through 2050 under different climate and trade scenarios. Dietary transitions could increase trade volumes by 50-135%, while substantially altering trade composition: under plant-rich scenarios, fruits and vegetables rise from 9% to 28% of traded crops, while grains decline from 34% to 24%, driven by reduced feed trade. These shifts are projected to reconfigure trade geography, with Sub-Saharan Africa emerging as a major exporter of legumes and nuts, while grain and soybean exports from the Americas to Asia decrease. Relaxing trade constraints increases both import dependence and supplier concentration, while dietary pathways shape import dependence in commodity-specific ways. Our findings help anticipate trade implications of dietary policies and trends.

title: Cooperative Unilateralism and the WTO [forthcoming in Elgar Handbook on Unilateral Measures in Trade, Investment and Economic Law, Luca Rubini (ed.)] ]
affiliations: Stanford University - Law School

detail.title: Cooperative Unilateralism and the WTO [forthcoming in Elgar Handbook on Unilateral Measures in Trade, Investment and Economic Law, Luca Rubini (ed.)] ]
detail.abstract: In recent years, U.S. trade policy has increasingly disregarded the legal obligations of the United States under the World Trade Organization. Commentators have decried this turn toward "unilateralism" and the damage that it has done to the stability of the world trading system. I do not defend U.S. policy but nevertheless suggest that it results from flaws in the design and operation of the WTO that left the institution unable to respond to shocks that fundamentally changed the political calculus in the United States regarding the utility of its WTO commitments. The sclerotic nature of the WTO ensured that it would eventually start to unravel in the face of changing circumstances. Reforms at the WTO could shore up its support and ongoing relevance, but its future is murky at best.

reference: University of Baltimore School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper
title: Child Support Factory: Racist History, Harm, and Unconstitutionality of the Child Support System's Contractual Operations
affiliations: University of Baltimore - School of Law

detail.title: Child Support Factory: Racist History, Harm, and Unconstitutionality of the Child Support System's Contractual Operations

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Baltimore School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Baltimore School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Within America’s justice institutions, the child support system has become a business. The intended mission of aid has been traded and abdicated through contractual deals to churn vulnerable families into factory-like revenue operations. Juvenile and family courts across the country have partnered through countless intertwined interagency contracts with human service agencies, prosecutors, attorneys general’s offices, probation departments, and policing offices—all aimed at generating revenue from impoverished children and parents rather than serving their best interests. The resulting child support factory is vast, harmful, unconstitutional, unethical, and grew from a racist history that devastated Black families, and still operates with starkly disproportionate racialized impact.

The child support system established by Title IV-D of the Social Security Act is an immense operation of the federal and state governments, processing approximately eighteen percent of all children in the United States in the fiscal year 2022. The history of the IV-D system is interlinked with slavery, Black Codes, Jim Crow laws, Poor Laws, and Bastardy Acts. This history reverberates into current practices, and the harm is monetized, as the IV-D system is increasingly viewed by state entities as a source of revenue rather than a means of providing aid.

This Article uncovers vast unconstitutional contractual mechanics in our justice systems that are not addressed by other scholars. Part I sets the stage by explaining the harm and racialized impact inflicted by the current IV-D child support system. Part II exposes how America’s justice institutions are expanding and generating revenue from the harm through a web of interagency contracts—and analyzes how those contractual operations are unethical and unconstitutional. Part III looks back to understand the racist history that still permeates the IV-D system operations, a devastating history that is now monetized. The Article concludes with a call for ending the child support factory harm, in the hopes that our institutions become more ethically true to providing justice and welfare for the people rather than using the people to serve themselves.

title: Double Inertia, Taylor Rules, and Monetary Policy Gradualism
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, , Federal Reserve Board and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Double Inertia, Taylor Rules, and Monetary Policy Gradualism

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2026-036, 2026[10.17016/FEDS.2026.036]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: In recent decades, an empirically estimated double-inertial rule fits the path of changes in the federal funds rate better than a standard inertial Taylor rule. Inertial Taylor rules aim to capture monetary policy gradualism via slow adjustments in the level of the policy rate. Double-inertial rules build on this specification by also gradually adjusting the pace of change in the policy rate. Because a double-inertial rule explains more than twice the variation of changes in the policy rate than its standard inertial counterpart, we argue that practitioners should consider a double-inertial rule when characterizing  U.S. monetary policy.

title: Financial Liberalizations, Booms, and Crashes
affiliations: , University of Bonn - Department of Economics and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Financial Liberalizations, Booms, and Crashes

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2026-034, 2026[10.17016/FEDS.2026.034]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: Financial liberalization is often seen as a way to deepen credit markets and stimulate economic growth, but it may also fuel credit booms that end in crisis. We construct a new cross-country database of banking regulation policies covering 21 regulatory indicators for 18 advanced economies since World War II. We distinguish liberalizations that directly relax constraints on credit supply from broader financial reforms. Liberalizations that directly affect credit supply lead to substantial expansions in private credit. Credit expansion is concentrated in non-tradable sectors and is not accompanied by higher interest rates or credit spreads in the short run, consistent with an outward shift in credit supply. Real GDP rises over the following 2 to 4 years, but the gains are temporary. On average, GDP returns to trend in the medium run, and there is an increase in the risk of financial crisis and worse downside growth outcomes. Only liberalizations that directly expand credit supply generate these boom-bust dynamics. Based on these estimates, financial liberalization is welfare-improving for coefficients of relative risk aversion below 7.2, a moderately high value.

reference: New Mexico Law Review, Volume 56, pp. 101-43
title: On the Securitization of Residential Real Property
affiliations: Seattle University School of Law

detail.title: On the Securitization of Residential Real Property

publicationDetails.detailsText: New Mexico Law Review, Volume 56, pp. 101-43

detail.abstract: This article aims to reframe the scholarly discussion about securitizations - transactions in which multiple passive investors use a special purpose entity to take passive fractional ownership shares in one or more assets - in the context of residential real property interests. Residential real property securitizations (including mortgage-backed securities and real estate investment trusts) are relatively modern financial instruments and so are relatively underexamined from a policy perspective, and this article seeks to evaluate whether residential real property interests are amenable to securitization at all, concluding that they are not. In so doing, this article uses the principles of property law to present a new reading of the central issues in both today's residential real estate market and in the lead-up to the 2007 financial crisis: instead of being a problem of the borrowers' inability to repay, the actual problem was lenders gambling on assets they did not want to own and could not steward. This article advances a broad normative definition of securitization, describing common aspects across a variety of securitization transactions and explaining the benefits of securitizations to investors across a variety of asset classes. This article then explains why residential real property securitizations are distinct from securitizations of other asset classes, detailing why such securitizations are bad for investors, renters, homebuyers, and community members in which securitized properties are situated, highlighting the social dimension of residential real property's value that is effaced by securitization. Finally, this article addresses the policy implications of this perspective, suggesting several paths forward to promote more equitable, community-based ownership of residential real property.

title: The Fragility of Perfectly Safe Digital Money
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, , Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: The Fragility of Perfectly Safe Digital Money

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2026-037, 2026[10.17016/FEDS.2026.037]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: Digital money differs from previous forms of money in an important way: it unbundles trust. Instead of relying on a trustworthy institution to settle payments, it relies on decentralized verification, whose cost is priced separately through congestion-sensitive gas fees. This arrangement creates a novel fragility from the interaction of two opposing forces: network externalities, which make digital money more valuable as adoption rises, and congestion fees, which make it more costly to use. We show that these forces generate strategic complementarities in redemption decisions and can create runs even when digital money is backed by perfectly safe reserves.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Architecture of Modifiable Constraints (AMC), a method for decomposing and profiling modifiable barriers in behavioral research. The motivating problem is simple: two people or populations can have the same total modifiable gap but call for different intervention logic because the relevant constraints are organized differently. AMC decomposes a response-scale benchmark gap into Shapley domain contributions, separates total modifiable burden from its simplex-valued domain composition, flags zero-burden and discordant cases, and uses a population-mean burden-weighted κ layer to describe whether domains are substitutable, multiplicative, complementary, or bottlenecklike. In known-truth simulations, AMC recovered broad simplex architecture better than raw closure in multiplicative, complementary, and bottleneck-like systems. The κ profile was usually well supported: the ΔAIC ≤ 2 support set contained the true pattern in 97.1% of known-truth replications, and single-pattern calls were highly accurate, including 94.7% for complementary systems. Applied to HINTS cancer-prevention outcomes, AMC revealed outcome-specific opportunity gaps, domain-contributed architectures, and profile supported interaction patterns across information, belief/trust, and access constraints.

title: Day Trading: Adapting to Change
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Day Trading: Adapting to Change
detail.abstract: This study explored how extreme stock market volatility influenced the effectiveness of different short-period momentum-based day trading strategies. Financial markets across the globe are becoming more unpredictable due to economic news, war, and new technological advancements, and traders everywhere are struggling to maintain profitability. Using a correlational research design, this study analyzed the performance of multiple short-term trading strategies, including the Opening Range Breakout (ORB) and common ICT concepts, through simulated trading on TradingView's Paper trading platform with a strict focus on E-mini S&P 500 futures (ES Futures). The performance of my trading was measured from October to December by measuring profitability and win percentage under volatile conditions. Results showed an overall profitable performance with a 53% win rate, while the ORB strategy achieved a statistically significantly higher success rate of 75% compared to the other momentum continuation models. A two-proportion z-test indicated that the difference in the strategies was statistically significant, as I achieved a z = 1.68 and p = 0.047. These findings indicate that structured momentum strategies can remain effective in volatile markets but only when combined with risk management and discipline. This study contributes to existing research by focusing specifically on short-term momentum trading during periods of volatile movement and shows that traders anywhere can learn to adapt to the market.

title: Noise Shocks and the Great Depression: A Structural Reassessment
affiliations: Central European University

detail.title: Noise Shocks and the Great Depression: A Structural Reassessment
detail.abstract: Earlier empirical work finds that bad news unrelated to fundamentals had a prominent role in the Great Depression, suggesting that a very important element is missing in the existing analyses of the recession. We test whether noise shocks, once embedded in a general equilibrium framework, are relevant sources of variation during the Great Depression. We estimate a medium-scale DSGE model with a signal extraction on productivity on the Great Depression period. We find that noise shocks, while significant on impact, are not important sources of variation, particularly because of their low persistence: the estimated signal-to-noise ratio implies that agents quickly learn the true state of productivity. We argue that the earlier exploratory results are mainly driven by the omission of competing sources of disturbances. Our result can be read as a lower bound on the role of noise in the Great Depression-one that advances in identification through survey expectations, richer propagation via financial frictions, and departures from full-information rational expectations may revise upward.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Collusive Algorithms: A Quantitative Analysis of Wage Discrimination in the Platform Economy

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Collusive Algorithms: A Quantitative Analysis of Wage Discrimination in the Platform Economy
detail.abstract: The advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) applied to corporate management has structurally transformed the dynamics of the contemporary labor market. While traditional economic literature on AI has primarily focused on consumer harm via algorithmic price collusion, this research empirically examines its impact on labor supply within the platform economy. We propose the concept of the "AI Monopsony" to describe how reinforcement learning models and predictive algorithms exert asymmetric market power that depresses the compensation of digital workers. Using a quantitative methodological approach, we estimate a multiple linear regression model with two-way fixed effects using a random sample of 1,000,000 observations drawn from the public transit records of the City of Chicago (2025-2026). The econometric results demonstrate that increases in AI-controlled market concentration systematically and significantly reduce the worker's effective pay per minute. Furthermore, the evidence shows that the AI autonomously optimizes rent capture by manipulating the corporate retention rate (Take Rate), operating as an automated wage discrimination mechanism that extracts the worker's economic surplus. The article concludes that current labor and antitrust regulatory frameworks are incapable of containing this new frontier of technological exploitation, urging the design of public policies based on algorithmic auditing and transparency.

title: Mode of Entry, Occupational Choice, and the Economic Impacts of US Immigration Reform
affiliations: National University of Singapore

detail.title: Mode of Entry, Occupational Choice, and the Economic Impacts of US Immigration Reform
detail.abstract: US immigration policy proposals have called for reducing the number of family-based visas. However, whether such policy changes would reduce overall US immigration depends crucially on immigrants' ability to substitute toward alternative entry modes. I assemble microdata from multiple countries to estimate a general equilibrium model of migration, entry-mode, and occupational choice. My analysis suggests that policy proposals centered on large cuts to family visas may not reduce low-skill immigration as intended and could instead increase undocumented immigration.

title: SIRC-SMLP: An Integrated Theoretical Framework for Urban Resilience Governance

detail.title: SIRC-SMLP: An Integrated Theoretical Framework for Urban Resilience Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: nil
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: nil

detail.abstract:
Why do governance systems for urban resilience repeatedly fall into the same traps-fragmented efforts, rigid inertia, fragile stability, and the domination of subjects by the tools they created? Existing paradigms-from network-based collaboration (R-CN) to technical diagnosis (CRP) to roadmap advocacy (MCR2030)-each capture important dimensions of resilience but remain incomplete. No single paradigm addresses the full cycle of how cities perceive risk, mobilize resources, adapt institutions, and learn from crisis. This fragmentation is not merely a practical inconvenience but a theoretical gap: the field lacks a common language for comparing diverse approaches, diagnosing points of failure, and translating insights from one paradigm into actionable inputs for another.
This paper proposes the SIRC-SMLP framework as a unifying theoretical lens for urban resilience governance. SIRC (Subject, Information, Resources, Capital) provides an analytical grammar — four analytical positions that recur across a wide range of governance systems. SMLP (Subject → Methods → Limitations → Purposes) provides a dynamic narrative — how subjects navigate constraints, switch methods (actively or passively), and generate new limitations through the law of unintended consequences. Together, they form a complete analytical toolkit: grammar without narrative is static; narrative without grammar is chaos.
The framework introduces six diagnostic links (S-I, I-R, R-C, C-S, I-C, S-R) to identify where governance systems succeed or fail. It distinguishes active switching (cognition-driven, less costly) from passive switching (crisis-driven, costly) along a spectrum, and develops a typology of inertia — cognitive, behavioral, institutional — to explain why switching fails. The paper further anchors the framework normatively in the capability approach (Sen, Nussbaum), establishing the RCI-flourishing isomorphism as an analytically constitutive axiom within the framework: Resources condition survival, Capital enables agency, Information safeguards dignity.
The paper demonstrates the framework's integrative power by mapping three global paradigms (R-CN, CRP, MCR2030) onto the SIRC-SMLP space, showing that each excels at specific diagnostic links and requires supplementary inputs from the others to complete the resilience governance cycle. It also engages with alternative frameworks (TOE, Seven Dimensions, SETS) to show how SIRC-SMLP can function as a voluntary analytical lens for those who adopt its categories — not as a replacement but as a translational logic.
The paper concludes that the SIRC-SMLP framework offers a path beyond fragmentation. It provides a common grammar for comparing diverse paradigms, a dynamic narrative for explaining change and inertia, a normative anchor for evaluating purposes, and a translational logic for converting work from one paradigm into inputs for another. The framework lays the theoretical groundwork for operational methodologies such as SIRC-DRP, which translate the framework into measurable indicators and strategy generation tools for city-level application. The paper also specifies scope conditions, falsifiability criteria, and operationalization previews, positioning the framework as a contribution to debate rather than a closed dogma.

detail.title: Self-Calibrating ML Directional Signals in Equity Markets: Live Evidence from 18,494 Forward-Verified Predictions
detail.abstract: We present preliminary evidence from a live machine learning directional signal system operating on 204 US equities and ETFs from January 27 to May 21, 2026. Unlike backtested systems, all 18,494 predictions were locked before outcomes were known, with the model retrained daily using only historically available data at the time of each prediction. The overall directional accuracy across all tickers and confidence levels is 45.2%. We find that the model's confidence score-termed readiness-acts as a genuine self-awareness signal: at 35-45% readiness, 62.3% of tested tickers show positive lift over their own baseline win rate, with an average positive lift of +15.2 percentage points. A filtered subset of 29 tickers (Tier 1) achieves 69.2% combined directional accuracy on 211 high-confidence signals, compared to a 48.0% baseline for the same tickers across all confidence levels. The system was live during the March-April 2026 tariff volatility shock, achieving its strongest monthly result (50.4%) in April 2026demonstrating model resilience under genuine market stress. We discuss why this dataset cannot be replicated from historical price feeds, the limitations of current sample sizes, and the implications for confidence-calibrated signal filtering in equity markets.

detail.abstract:
Micro-scale spatial data on inland fisheries are rarely available over long periods, limiting our understanding of historical resource patterns and constraining evidence for evaluating the long-term impacts of large-scale development. This study aims to establish a comparable pre-development reference point for Lake Biwa fisheries by analyzing port-level catch data from 1962 to 1972, immediately preceding major coastal modifications under the Lake Biwa Comprehensive Development Project. The dataset covers 44 fishing ports, 11 years, and 13 species. Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) was applied through three complementary analytical configurations: port-based analysis, species-based analysis, and species-specific analysis of the four species with the highest catches. Spatial proximity among fishing ports was incorporated as a covariate in the estimation. 
All three configurations consistently show that the fisheries landscape of Lake Biwa was not spatially uniform. Instead, it consisted of coexisting structures that differed in resource dependence, spatial stability, and temporal variability by port. Four major resource patterns were identified: a small endemic fish type, a large endemic fish type, a Lake prawn-dependent type, and a freshwater clam-dependent type. Port-based analysis further revealed that single-dominant systems and alternating or mixed systems coexisted across the lake. Species-specific analysis showed that structural complexity varied systematically among species, ranging from spatially stable types associated with fixed environmental conditions to temporally variable types whose components shifted between the first and second halves of the study period.
This study contributes to inland fisheries research by transforming historical catch statistics from records of volume into interpretable records of structure. The resulting port-level baseline provides a framework for evaluating how large-scale lakeshore development may reorganize resource dependence, rather than assessing impacts only through changes in total catch volume.

title: Ecosystem Diagnostics and Strategic Cost Camouflage: The Tengku Akbar-Chen Synthesis of Transnational Value Extraction

detail.title: Ecosystem Diagnostics and Strategic Cost Camouflage: The Tengku Akbar-Chen Synthesis of Transnational Value Extraction
detail.abstract:
Traditional management accounting frameworks and classical economic models heavily rely on enterprise-level metrics to evaluate transnational joint ventures, operating under the assumption that resource allocation occurs transparently via standard cost accounting compliance. This paper challenges this paradigm by introducing the Tengku Akbar-Chen (TAC) Synthesis to expose how dominant multinational partners utilise 'Strategic Cost Camouflage' within asymmetric multi-node technology networks. By blurring the operational boundaries between shared global infrastructure maintenance, centralised research and development (R&D) cost-pooling arrangements, and localised assembly expenses, dominant partners can execute cross-border value extraction prior to the determination of local corporate profitability. 
To model these dynamics, this study conceptualises the Sanctuary-Extraction-Enclosure (S.E.E.) Loop and the Axiom of Instantaneous Recoupment, illustrating how host-country resources are systematically drained to fund the global parent's regional expansion. To make this invisible structural power visible, this paper develops a non-invasive forensic methodology termed the Ecosystem Resource Audit (ERA) framework. 
Applying the ERA framework to an anonymised empirical exemplar within the ASEAN automotive sector, the research unmasks a profound capital misallocation: a structural per-unit 'Parental Tax' (tp) of RM10,981, culminating in a cumulative cross-border extraction of RM1.734 billion. This results in an extreme Resource Distortion Index (RDI) of 6.13:1 relative to the segment profits, triggering severe localised capital starvation and structural industrial dependency. Ultimately, this paper outlines concrete regulatory reforms for state planning ministries and fiscal authorities, advocating a shift from passive transaction tracking to active, substance-over-form ecosystem diagnostics.

title: False Discovery Rate Control in Panel Data via Mirror Statistics

detail.title: False Discovery Rate Control in Panel Data via Mirror Statistics
detail.abstract: Empirical asset pricing increasingly involves testing hundreds of candidate predictors in panel data, making false discovery rate (FDR) control central to credible inference. Standard p-value-based procedures, including Bonferroni, Benjamini–Hochberg (BH), and Benjamini– Yekutieli (BHY), rely on marginal p-values whose validity and dependence structure are often difficult to justify in finite-period asset-pricing panels. This paper proposes a mirrorstatistic-based FDR framework for panel data. Rather than relying on marginal p-values, the procedure ranks candidate predictors using relative importance scores constructed from mirror statistics. The framework delivers theoretical FDR control under arbitrary dependence across hypotheses and remains valid in finite period. Simulation evidence shows that the proposed approach achieves lower realized FDR and higher power than standard p-value-based procedures across empirically relevant designs, including settings with strong cross-feature, cross-firm, and time-series dependence. Applying the framework to firm-characteristic data supports the simulation evidence. An average portfolio formed from the five characteristics selected by the mirror-statistic approach earns a monthly out-of-sample return of 0.60% (t = 2.94), which is six times larger than the 0.10% (t = 1.11) return earned by the portfolio formed from the thirty characteristics selected by BH. These results indicate that mirrorstatistic methods more effectively identify characteristics with true explanatory power.

This research examines how reading competence is presented in secondary school students, from the guidelines of applied linguistics and from the indicators that define educational quality. All this goes hand in hand with the qualitative phase of interpretation, both technical and semantic, which places the results in context with the conceptual framework of the work.

After all, there is a relationship between the low performance of students and certain environmental and institutional conditions that make it necessary to restructure the curriculum.

The objective is none other than to raise the academic excellence of secondary education and align itself with quality standards, for this purpose a classroom practice coherent with the demands of critical literacy is proposed.

title: Structural Dynamics of Flow Collapse: The DTDMC Universal Pathway Law

detail.title: Structural Dynamics of Flow Collapse: The DTDMC Universal Pathway Law

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involves no human or animal subjects. The paper is a mathematical formalization of the DTDMC universal pathway law. Numerical simulations are based on the mathematical model described in the paper and are independently reproducible through the Python source code provided in Supplementary A.

detail.abstract:
The second law of thermodynamics specifies the direction in which systems progress toward disorder, but it does not describe the order in which they collapse. The theory of critical transitions in complex systems captures the timing of transition, yet it does not prescribe the pathway that follows. To fill this gap, the present paper formalizes mathematically a single universal pathway law — DTDMC (Determinants → Trigger → Dual Blockade → Manifestation → Collapse) — that the collapse of a circulatory system follows.

The core of the model is as follows. Once the cumulative determinant A(t) exceeds a threshold θ, a trigger is activated, and a nonlinear deposition R(t) = ∫η·Tᵏ dτ (k > 1) develops in proportion to the trigger intensity. Deposition is the structural flattening of the gradient; once it exceeds the blockade threshold θR, the system enters dual blockade (B* = CAM · DLT), in which supply and discharge are simultaneously blocked. Under dual blockade, the flow Φ(t) = I(t)·O(t) converges to zero, and the system progresses from manifestation to collapse.

Numerical simulations show that, regardless of the initial values of the control variables (λ, η, k), once the condition k > 1 holds, deposition accumulates with positive feedback and Φ converges to a collapse state. This indicates the universality of the pathway. Recovery is described by a suppression coefficient β and a removal rate γ; the collapse is irreversible whenever β = 0 and γ = 0. The model proposes a new evaluation paradigm — path conformity rather than numerical prediction — and secures testability by specifying explicit Popperian falsification conditions.

title:

detail.title:
Supply Chain Network Adequacy Under Dynamic Conditions 
A Systematic Literature Review Across Network Design, Resilience, and System Dynamics
detail.abstract: This systematic literature review examines three intersecting research domains-supply chain network design (SCND), supply chain resilience (SCRes), and system dynamics (SD)-to address three core research questions: (1) what dimensions do researchers and practitioners use to evaluate whether a supply chain network performs adequately under dynamic conditions; (2) what metrics are tracked; and (3) where are the structural gaps between static optimization and dynamic reality. The review draws on literature spanning operations research, simulation science, and supply chain management to establish the conceptual foundations for a proposed construct of supply chain network adequacy-a term not yet formally defined in the literature but grounded in convergent themes across the reviewed domains. Findings indicate that existing evaluation frameworks are fragmented across performance, resilience, and dynamic behaviour literatures; that no unified measurement model for dynamic network performance exists; and that system dynamics remains underutilized as a design-evaluation tool in SCND contexts. These gaps constitute the basis for a proposed research agenda.

title: The Production-Correlation Blind Spot in Grain Cooperative Mergers

detail.title: The Production-Correlation Blind Spot in Grain Cooperative Mergers
detail.abstract: This study analyzes correlations in county-level grain production in Oklahoma and Kansas from 2013 to 2023 to evaluate risk diversification potential in cooperative mergers. Using ordinary least squares, and Bayesian regression, we model how spatial distance, crop composition, adjacency, and production scale affect production correlations. Results show modest county-level heterogeneity, with east-west distance consistently reducing production correlations. Overall, findings reveal that distance alone is an insufficient guide for merger decisions: diversification potential depends on the interaction of spatial separation and crop composition, and varies substantially across counties. County-specific correlation analysis is essential for identifying partners that meaningfully reduce production risk.

detail.title: The Archaeobyte: A Foundational Thesis on the Artifacts of the Digital Past
detail.abstract: This foundational thesis defines the artifacts of the digital past, distinguishing the focused excavation of the Archaeobytologist from the broad data mining of the digital sphere. It introduces the "Archaeobyte" as the fundamental unit of the emerging discipline of Archaeobytology (also known as Digital Archaeology)-a discrete unit of information defined by its provenance from a past technological epoch. By establishing a taxonomy for these finds (Tangible versus Conceptual) and outlining a "Triage" methodology to classify their current states as Living (Vivibyte), Liminal (Umbrabyte), or Petrified (Petribyte), this essay builds the epistemological framework necessary for the specialized classification studies that follow, offering a rigorous method for excavating meaning from the noise of the digital dark age.

title: Pay Beliefs and the Amenity-pay Tradeoff

detail.title: Pay Beliefs and the Amenity-pay Tradeoff
detail.abstract: This paper studies how workers' beliefs about pay shape the tradeoffs between pay and workplace amenities. We design a multi-stage incentivized survey experiment that combines hypothetical choice experiments with elicited beliefs about starting salaries in real jobs and randomly varies the provision of explicit pay information. Although stated preferences imply sizable willingness to pay for amenities consistent with prior literature, baseline beliefs about salaries in real jobs are systematically biased along two margins: respondents under-predict starting salaries by 18% and expect higher-amenity jobs to pay more, substantially over-predicting the amenity-pay gradient. Exposure to pay information raises mean pay beliefs for similar jobs by 4% and reduces belief dispersion by 15%, but does not alter the strong positive association between perceived pay and advertised amenities, leaving the amenity-pay tradeoffs in stated choices essentially unchanged. While workers have strong preferences for workplace amenities, the tradeoffs they perceive deviate sharply from those present under full information.

title: Economic and Financial Development as Determinants of Cryptocurrency Adoption: Evidence from 26 Selected Countries, 2021–2024

detail.abstract: The rapid development of cryptocurrency as a digital financial innovation has attracted global attention both as an investment instrument and a potential tool for financial inclusion. This study analyzes the economic and financial determinants of cryptocurrency adoption in 26 selected countries during 2021-2024 using a panel data regression approach. Variables examined include digital infrastructure (mobile cellular subscriptions, internet usage, and fixed broadband subscriptions), macroeconomic conditions (GDP per capita and inflation measured via GDP deflator), the Economic Freedom Index, and electricity prices. Results from Fixed Effects and Random Effects models selected through Chow, Hausman, and Lagrange Multiplier tests indicate that mobile cellular subscriptions (MCS) represent the most significant positive driver of cryptocurrency adoption, consistent with Rogers' Diffusion of Innovation Theory. GDP per capita also shows a significant positive effect, supporting Markowitz's Portfolio Theory. The Economic Freedom Index exhibits a negative and significant relationship, suggesting that countries with weaker institutional frameworks experience greater cryptocurrency adoption as an alternative financial system. Inflation and electricity prices are not statistically significant across most models. Cryptocurrency adoption demonstrates a dual role: functioning as a portfolio diversification instrument in high-income countries and as an alternative financial system in economies with limited traditional financial access, where mobile infrastructure serves as the primary catalyst.

title: Green Investment, Fiscal Sustainability, and NDC Compliance: A Fiscal Cost Decomposition for Korea Using the CO-STIRPAT Dynamic System

detail.title: Green Investment, Fiscal Sustainability, and NDC Compliance: A Fiscal Cost Decomposition for Korea Using the CO-STIRPAT Dynamic System
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether fiscally neutral green investment can simultaneously improve NDC compliance and remain budgetarily self-financing. Applying the CO-STIRPAT dynamic system—estimated on Korean data (1980–2024) and integrated with the OECD EDISON six-component fiscal accounting framework—to the Republic of Korea over 2025–2050, we find that a +10 trillion KRW annual investment shock generates a benefit-to-cost ratio of 1.37, confirming fiscal self-financing. However, the probability of NDC implementation rises only slightly, from approximately 10 to 11 percent by the 2030 review date, and remains well below 50 percent. This demonstrates that the 2030 NDC is a highly ambitious target, while also suggesting that the effectiveness of green investment could be largely offset by increased emissions arising from the economic activity that the fiscal multiplier sets in motion: faster GDP growth raises energy demand and emissions, counteracting the carbon-intensity gains from the green transition. The result implies that, to raise the probability of achieving the NDC while promoting accelerated GDP growth, green transition spending must be focused on carbon-neutral technology innovation that maximizes energy-efficiency improvements and carbon-intensity reductions—effects that must outweigh the increases in energy demand and emissions induced by green investment itself.

title: Spatio-Temporal Analysis of Drought and Land Use/Land Cover Change in Guli Locality, White Nile state Sudan

detail.title: Spatio-Temporal Analysis of Drought and Land Use/Land Cover Change in Guli Locality, White Nile state Sudan
detail.abstract: This study investigates drought severity, vegetation dynamics, and land use/land cover (LULC) changes in Guli locality, Sudan, using multi-temporal Landsat imagery (1985, 1995, 2015, and 2022). Remote sensing indices-Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), and Normalized Difference Drought Index (NDDI)-were applied to assess vegetation health, water stress, and drought intensity. Supervised classification with Support Vector Machine (SVM) was used to generate LULC maps. Results show a marked shift in drought severity. Very low severity declined from 21% in 1985 to 1.7% in 2022, while moderate severity expanded from 18% to 47.6%, becoming the dominant category. High severity peaked at 59% in 2015 before declining to 30% in 2022, while very high severity dropped from 18% to 4.5%. NDVI analysis revealed localized vegetation recovery in northern and central areas, but persistent degradation in southern and eastern zones. LULC results highlight dramatic transformations: agriculture expanded from 8% to 26%, settlements grew from 6.4% to 38.8%, while rangelands declined from 61% to 22% and forests shrank by over 84%. These findings underscore the dual dynamics of drought intensification and land use change, with agricultural and urban expansion occurring alongside severe ecosystem degradation.

title: Social Origins and Access to Formal Employment: The Case of Peru
affiliations: Universidad Complutense Madrid, Instituto Complutense de Análisis Económico | ICAE and Department of Fundamentals of Economic Analysis I (Economic Analysis)

detail.title: Social Origins and Access to Formal Employment: The Case of Peru
detail.abstract: In highly informal economies, access to formal employment is not only a labor market outcome but also a powerful mechanism through which inequality of opportunity is reproduced across generations. We study this process in Peru by linking the 2017 Population Census to administrative payroll records for 2022 and, for the 1997 cohort, to school administrative records on parental education. We estimate cohort-specific probit models for individuals born between 1965 and 1997. Results show persistent circumstance-based stratification across generations. The urban-rural gap is the largest and most persistent source of inequality, accounting for gaps of 13 to 18 percentage points in formal employment across cohorts. Men retain an advantage in formal employment in every cohort, although the gender gap narrows among younger generations. Having Spanish as a mother tongue is associated with a 6-11 percentage-point premium, even after controlling for place of residence, while disability-especially cognitive and speech limitations-remains linked to substantially lower access, with little convergence over time. For the 1997 cohort, maternal education shows a stronger association with formal employment than paternal education. These findings suggest that in segmented labor markets, formal employment continues to reflect inherited disadvantage, and that expanding formalization alone will not level the playing field.

title: Conciliation as a Method of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR): Relationship and Distinction between Arbitration, Mediation and Negotiation

detail.title: Conciliation as a Method of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR): Relationship and Distinction between Arbitration, Mediation and Negotiation
detail.abstract: Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) has emerged as one of the most effective mechanisms for resolving disputes outside traditional courts. Among the various ADR methods, conciliation occupies a unique place because of its cooperative and relationship-oriented nature. The increasing burden on courts, high litigation expenses, and the need for speedy justice have encouraged legal systems worldwide to adopt ADR frameworks. This article critically examines conciliation as a dispute resolution mechanism and analyses its relationship with arbitration, mediation, and negotiation.

title: Collateral Policy Surprises

detail.title: Collateral Policy Surprises
detail.abstract: Central bank collateral policy specifies which assets banks can pledge as collateral to obtain central bank funding and is an important determinant of liquidity in the banking system. We propose a high-frequency identification approach to study the systematic effects of central bank collateral policy on banks, financial markets, and asset prices. We identify collateral policy surprises using intraday bank stock price changes around Eurosystem collateral policy announcements. Expansionary collateral policy surprises lead to excess returns of bank stocks, a decline in common volatility measures, and a reduction in bank default risk, in particular for riskier banks. They also compress core-periphery government bond spreads, even for policy changes that are unrelated to the collateral treatment of government bonds. The uneven transmission of collateral policy through banks to sovereign bond markets is distinct from both central bank asset purchases and conventional monetary policy.

detail.title: Integrating NDVI, NDWI, and NDDI for Drought Monitoring and Land Use Change Detection in Semi-Arid Sudan
detail.abstract: This study investigates drought severity, vegetation dynamics, and land use/land cover (LULC) changes in Tudulti locality, Sudan, using multi-temporal Landsat imagery (1985, 1995, 2015, and 2022). Remote sensing indices-Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), and Normalized Difference Drought Index (NDDI)-were applied to evaluate vegetation health, water stress, and drought intensity. detail.abstract: Parents play a critical role in shaping children's skills during the first years of life. Yet, identifying the contributors to richer learning environments remains difficult due to various unobservable factors. In this paper, we combine field experiments with AI to explore new acoustic features of parental speech. Specifically, we develop a signal processing model that uses more than 600 hours of recorded parent-child interactions combined with assessment data from two home-visiting experiments conducted in the Chicagoland area to identify features of parental speech that map into children's skills. Our two experiments consist of the same intervention helping parents provide nurturing interactions to their child. We exploit the experimental and natural variation in our data to explore two causal channels and one potential moderator. First, our intervention improves parental speech consistently across the two studies, as measured by acoustic features that are predictive of higher socioemotional skills and adult-child conversational turns. Further, we find that it also increases children's language skills in both experiments, as well as socioemotional skills in the second experiment. Interestingly, our heterogeneity analyses reveal that some of the interventions' impacts vary by socioeconomic groups, with patterns across the two experiments suggesting that the mechanisms are context-dependent.

detail.abstract: This paper examines intergenerational mobility across social classes during the late Qing dynasty employing a remarkable data set from Liaoning province in Northeast China. We identify two distinct epochs with markedly different mobility dynamics. Before 1850, mobility patterns exhibited stability and convergence toward a steady state. The second epoch, beginning around 1850, was characterized by unstable intergenerational class dynamics that persisted until the dynasty's collapse. The transition between epochs coincides with the Opium Wars and Taiping Rebellion, demonstrating how the footprints of major crises in the late Qing era can be traced in mobility dynamics. Employing Markov-chain measures and two alternative mobility conceptsthe persistence of class origin across generations and intergenerational class movement-we document that intergenerational mobility increased over the period. However, this aggregate increase masked a decline in upward mobility alongside a rise in downward mobility-disparate patterns that resonate with broader theories of political instability.

detail.abstract: Modern theories of the business cycle do not allow for the simultaneous rational choice of both prices and quantities, instead assuming that an "invisible hand" determines one of these variables to clear markets. In this paper, we develop a macroeconomic framework in which both prices and quantities are chosen directly by firms, and exchange is both voluntary and efficient. Because of uncertainty about demand and productivity, individual product markets can be in excess supply or rationed. The absence of market-clearing changes pricing and production in qualitatively important ways: markups are no longer determined solely by the elasticity of demand, and higher uncertainty reduces production and increases markups. In equilibrium, production in rationed markets has a negative aggregate demand externality on demand in slack markets. Differently from New Keynesian economies, monetary shocks propagate by reducing economic slack, raising aggregate labor productivity and consumption, while uncertainty shocks act as stagflationary cost-push shocks. We integrate our theory of disequilibrium in a dynamic, rational-expectations "New Old Keynesian Model" and demonstrate its implications for the business cycle.

detail.abstract: In plausibly calibrated heterogeneous-agent models, marginal propensities to consume (MPCs) are highly non-linear in wealth, falling sharply away from borrowing constraints. As a result, the aggregate consumption response to a fiscal transfer is strongly concave in its size: larger transfers shift households out of high-MPC regions and thereby dampen the consumption response. Across partial-and general-equilibrium settings, linear methods substantially overstate the effects of fiscal stimulus at empirically relevant sizes. Local methods are not reliable for studying shocks and policies where a failure of Ricardian equivalence is important.

detail.abstract: The article reconnects debates on Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and the EU budget, challenging their traditional separation. By revisiting early discussions on EMU, it highlights the often-overlooked “budgetary dimension” of European integration. Examining financial instruments from the 1970s to NextGenerationEU (NGEU), the article shows how the EU has repeatedly activated a “dormant” borrowing capacity during crises by building on existing financial models. It argues that the EU budget has acted as a silent guarantor for joint debt issuance and financial stability, making it a crucial yet underappreciated pillar of European economic integration and fiscal governance.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes how patterns of change in global value chains (GVCs) have evolved among seven major Asian countries as the structural transformation of GVCs has deepened after the U.S.–China trade war. In particular, we closely examine whether India, Vietnam, and other key ASEAN countries are likely to play roles as indirect export and production hubs in response to GVC change. To this end, we use the ADB Multiregional Input–Output (MRIO) data for the 2015–2023 period and conduct an analysis that includes the latest information. To identify the flow of GVC change before and after the U.S.–China trade war, we divide the analysis period into three stages: the pre-trade-war period, Trump’s first term, and the Biden administration period. Through this analysis, the study aims to present policy proposals that enable Korea to respond effectively to the rapidly changing GVC environment by cooperating with India and major ASEAN countries such as Vietnam and Indonesia, thereby coping effectively with the evolving global economic order.

detail.title: Operational Flexibility in Gas-Fired Power Plants Under Climate Policy Uncertainty
detail.abstract: We study the valuation of a flexible gas-fired turbine for electricity production under uncertainty in clean spark spread components and under varying degrees of environmental policy stringency. Within a real options framework, we develop a fast and computationally efficient lattice-based valuation methodology that incorporates jump dynamics in electricity and natural gas prices together with regime-switching behaviour in carbon allowance markets, consistently with the empirical evidence of fat tails, skewness, and structural breaks in energy market data. Numerical results show that tighter environmental policies reduce expected cash flows while increasing the value of operational flexibility, particularly under persistent high carbon-cost regimes. When climate policy uncertainty is explicitly modelled, faster resolution further enhances flexibility value by enabling earlier adaptation to changing market conditions, while also affecting downside risk exposure.

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The Act on the Conclusion Procedure and Implementation of Commercial Treaties (hereinafter, the “Commerce Treaty Act”) was enacted in 2012 to address the lack of procedural transparency and insufficient public participation revealed during major trade negotiations, notably the Korea–U.S. Free Trade Agreement (FTA). The Act aimed to institutionalize transparency, predictability, and stakeholder participation across all stages—from negotiation to post-entry implementation—while ensuring systematic and democratic oversight of Korea’s trade policy.

Despite its initial promise, several institutional limitations have emerged. Certain procedures risked becoming mere formalities, undermining the Act’s purpose, while rapid shifts in the trade environment, including digital trade, supply chain realignment, and climate-related regulation, exposed gaps in its scope and adaptability. In particular, new forms of economic agreements that diverge from traditional tariff-based liberalization often fall outside the statutory definition of a “trade agreement,” weakening both democratic control and policy responsiveness.

This study therefore seeks to identify reform directions that can strengthen the Commerce Treaty Act’s legal coherence, democratic legitimacy, and practical effectiveness. The research focuses on four main objectives: enhancing institutional coherence, improving democratic transparency and oversight, ensuring effective domestic implementation, and reinforcing the legal framework to address structural changes in global trade governance.

title:
The Black-scholes Formula as a Hidden Optimization Problem: 
A Reverse-engineering Exercise Connecting the Envelope Theorem to Option Pricing

detail.title:
The Black-scholes Formula as a Hidden Optimization Problem: 
A Reverse-engineering Exercise Connecting the Envelope Theorem to Option Pricing
detail.abstract: Students trained in microeconomic theory are accustomed to the Envelope Theorem: when differentiating a value function with respect to a parameter, the indirect effects operating through optimal choices vanish by the first-order conditions. Upon encountering the Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) formula, these students face a puzzle. Computing the option's sensitivity to time (Theta) requires the chain rule through the auxiliary variables d1 and d2, yet the final expression simplifies dramatically as if some hidden optimization were at work. This note proposes a pedagogical reverse engineering exercise: I construct an artificial constrained optimization problem in which d1 and d2 are elevated from mere statistical definitions to genuine choice variables. The first-order conditions of the associated Lagrangian recover the well-known BSM identity S N ′ (d1) = Ke-r(T-t) N ′ (d2), and the Envelope Theorem then delivers Theta in a single step, bypassing all chain-rule algebra. The exercise bridges a gap between the microeconomic and quantitative-finance curricula, offering students an economic interpretation of a formula that is typically presented as purely statistical.

title: The Effect of Height on Adolescents' Body Image Perceptions and Behaviors

detail.title: The Effect of Height on Adolescents' Body Image Perceptions and Behaviors

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper estimates the causal effect of height on adolescents’ body image, encompassing self-perceptions of weight, the accuracy of those perceptions, and weight-management aspirations. Using data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997 (NLSY97), we leverage within-individual variation in height during adolescence and condition on body mass index (BMI) to isolate the effects of height on body image outcomes. We find that taller adolescents are more likely to perceive themselves as overweight, even holding BMI constant, and are less likely to underestimate their weight category. However, the direction of misclassification diverges by gender: taller boys are more likely to correctly assess their weight category, while taller girls are more likely to overestimate it. These perception shifts translate into behavioral responses for girls but not for boys. A one-inch increase in height raises the probability that a girl reports wanting to lose weight by 3.0 percentage points (6.2 percent), with effects concentrated among girls in the normal weight range. Taken together, these findings establish height as a salient determinant of body image in adolescence, operating independently of body mass.

title: Asymmetric Information, Bank Screening, and Green Credit Allocation

detail.title: Asymmetric Information, Bank Screening, and Green Credit Allocation
detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of firm-type heterogeneity and dual information asymmetry, this study develops a finite-horizon continuous-time dynamic game model between banks and firms, incorporating signal screening, audit verification, and differentiated contracts into a unified analytical framework. The model embeds both adverse selection and moral hazard within a coupled state–costate system, thereby characterizing the dynamic interactions between banks and firms under asymmetric information and examining how dynamic interest rates, audit probabilities, and signaling costs affect firm behavior and resource allocation. Using the Hamiltonian approach and Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle, the study derives the corresponding optimality conditions and conducts numerical simulations to compare dynamic trajectories under three alternative mechanisms: no-screening, signaling-only, and signaling combined with auditing. The results show that reliance on signaling alone is insufficient to sustain effective screening over time, whereas the introduction of auditing helps reduce the discrepancy between firms’ reported and actual investment, improves the precision of green credit allocation, and enhances green capital accumulation. The study provides a theoretical reference for the design and policy optimization of green credit mechanisms, and further indicates that the coordinated use of screening, verification, and differentiated contracts can effectively mitigate adverse selection and moral hazard under asymmetric information.

title: GLP-1 Therapy and the Reshaping of Socioeconomic Gradients in Health
affiliations: University of Southern California, University of Southern California - Schaeffer Center for Health Policy  and Economics, National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) and University of Southern California - Schaeffer Center for Health Policy  and Economics

detail.title: GLP-1 Therapy and the Reshaping of Socioeconomic Gradients in Health

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
GLP-1 therapies for obesity promise substantial health improvements, but little is known about how their benefits vary across socioeconomic and demographic groups. Using a nationally representative microsimulation model of US adults and Shapely-value decomposition, we estimate the lifetime health and economic benefits of GLP-1 treatment and examine how those gains vary across individuals. The largest differences emerge across education. Individuals with less than a high school education experience experience roughly 14% higher gains in lifetime net social value, 16-17% larger improvements in discounted generalized risk- and severity-adjusted life-years (GRASA-QALYs), and 20% greater increases in life expectancy relative to the cohort mean, whereas individuals with college degrees experience gains 15-27% below the mean across these outcomes. Black and Hispanic individuals also tend to experience larger improvements in health outcomes and social value than White individuals, including larger gains in GRASA-QALYs and life expectancy and larger reductions in diabetes risk and duration. Females likewise experience larger predicted treatment gains than men. These patterns are consistent with the idea that the largest gains arise among populations facing greater socioeconomic constraints in sustaining behavioral weight control. GLP-1 innovation may therefore mitigate inequality in obesity-related disease and survival, advancing equity in population health.

title: Does Regional Variation in Wage Levels Identify the Effects of a National Minimum Wage?

detail.title: Does Regional Variation in Wage Levels Identify the Effects of a National Minimum Wage?

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper asks whether regional wage differences can identify the effects of a national minimum wage. I study two common exposure-based approaches: effective-minimum-wage designs, which compare the minimum wage to contemporaneous local wages, and fraction-affected/gap designs, which measure pre-reform exposure to the new minimum. Using theory, simulations, and evidence from Brazil, I show when these approaches can mislead and how their performance depends on specification choices. The results lead to practical recommendations for applied researchers, including when to avoid these designs, how to test their assumptions, which specifications are more reliable, and how similar concerns may apply to other settings.

title: Macroeconomic and Fiscal Consequences of Quantitative Easing

detail.title: Macroeconomic and Fiscal Consequences of Quantitative Easing

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Quantitative easing (QE) has been criticized for helping fuel the post-COVID inflation boom and causing large central bank losses. In this paper, we argue that QE should be evaluated mainly on its ability to achieve core macro-objectives as well for its effects on the consolidated fiscal position of the government and central bank, although central bank losses can matter to the extent that they may weaken central bank credibility. Using a DSGE model with segmented asset markets, we show how QE can provide a sizeable boost to output and inflation in a deep liquidity trap and can reduce public debt substantially. This contrasts to the rise in public debt that occurs under fiscal expansion and makes QE an attractive tool in a high debt environment. There is more reason for caution in using QE in a "shallow" liquidity trap in which the notional interest rate is only slightly negative: QE runs more risk of causing the economy to overheat, especially if forward guidance has a strong element of commitment, and is more likely to generate sizeable central bank losses. Some refinements in strategy, including the use of escape clauses, can help mitigate overheating risks.

title: Explaining the Historical Rise and Recent Decline in Social Security Disability Insurance Enrollment

detail.title: Explaining the Historical Rise and Recent Decline in Social Security Disability Insurance Enrollment

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
After substantial growth in the 1990s and 2000s, enrollment in the U.S. Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) program has been declining since 2013. We use detailed administrative data to quantify the contributions of various factors to trends in SSDI enrollment, focusing especially on the decline in the 2010s. A statistical decomposition suggests that the vast majority of the decline in SSDI enrollment since 2013 is attributable to declines in application rates—and, to a lesser extent, award rates—within demographic groups. There is very little contribution from changes over time in demographic characteristics, eligibility, or exit from SSDI. The decline in SSDI enrollment rates is disproportionately driven by low-to-middle-skilled men who, over time, have become less likely to apply for SSDI and more likely to work. Consistent with this descriptive evidence, we present results from a causal analysis suggesting that improved labor market opportunity for less-skilled men is a key explanation for the decline in SSDI enrollment. We also investigate several other popular hypotheses for the decline in SSDI applications, including lower award rates at the appeals level, and find evidence at odds with them.

title: Do Voters Punish Inflation or Pay Cuts? Inflation and Real Wages in U.S. Elections

detail.title: Do Voters Punish Inflation or Pay Cuts? Inflation and Real Wages in U.S. Elections
