detail.abstract:
Between 2021 and 2024, the United States experienced one of the most severe inflation episodes in decades, coinciding with renewed debate over the role of economic conditions for electoral outcomes. This paper studies the political economy of inflation and real wages using U.S. county-level data on family budget costs, nominal income, and electoral results for President and Congress during this period. Exploiting within-state, cross-county variation in changes in local prices over time, it examines how inflation, real wage growth, and purchasing power relate to changes in vote shares of incumbents, vote margins, and turnout. Real wage decline, rather than higher inflation, is predictive of Republican electoral gains, in line with an economic voting rationale. Inflation, however, retains an association with presidential vote shares beyond pure economic voting.

title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence and Field Experiments to Explore Novel Features of Parental Speech and Foster Child Development

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Parents play a critical role in shaping children’s skills during the first years of life. Yet, identifying the contributors to richer learning environments remains difficult due to various unobservable factors. In this paper, we combine field experiments with AI to explore new acoustic features of parental speech. Specifically, we develop a signal processing model that uses more than 600 hours of recorded parent-child interactions combined with assessment data from two home-visiting experiments conducted in the Chicagoland area to identify features of parental speech that map into children’s skills. Our two experiments consist of the same intervention helping parents provide nurturing interactions to their child. We exploit the experimental and natural variation in our data to explore two causal channels and one potential moderator. First, our intervention improves parental speech consistently across the two studies, as measured by acoustic features that are predictive of higher socioemotional skills and adult-child conversational turns. Further, we find that it also increases children’s language skills in both experiments, as well as socioemotional skills in the second experiment. Interestingly, our heterogeneity analyses reveal that some of the interventions’ impacts vary by socioeconomic groups, with patterns across the two experiments suggesting that the mechanisms are context-dependent.

detail.abstract:
This paper explores the relationship between institutional architecture for micro-entrepreneurs and indicators of economic vulnerability and household resilience across the European Union. Building upon the previously developed MILEI-friendly Index (Micro-Independent Labor & Enterprise Institutional Index), the study investigates whether institutional adaptability toward micro-scale economic actors is associated with differences in poverty risk, distributive inequality, and household income dynamics.

The analysis combines MILEI calibration data for all 27 EU member states with standard socio-economic indicators, including the Gini coefficient, the S80/S20 income ratio, the at-risk-of-poverty rate, and household disposable income growth. Unlike conventional approaches that examine taxes, social contributions, and administrative obligations separately, the present study interprets institutional burden as a cumulative structure of obligatory outflows required for maintaining economic participation.

Preliminary findings suggest that the relationship between institutional adaptability and aggregate inequality indicators remains limited. However, more adaptive institutional systems appear more consistently associated with lower levels of poverty risk and more favorable household income dynamics. These findings indicate that institutional architecture may influence not the overall distribution of income itself, but rather the resilience capacity of economically vulnerable groups operating under conditions of unstable income and limited capital reserves.

The paper does not attempt to establish causal inference. Instead, it proposes an exploratory institutional framework for examining how cumulative institutional burden may contribute to structural economic vulnerability. By operationalizing institutional exposure through an integrated comparative index, the study contributes to the emerging literature on institutional economics, self-employment vulnerability, and economic resilience.

detail.abstract: Private equity valuations in emerging markets heavily reflect narrative momentum. Investors rarely see hard revenue data during early seed rounds. They buy text. title: The Objective of the Firm, Higher Purpose and Financial Performance

detail.title: The Objective of the Firm, Higher Purpose and Financial Performance
detail.abstract:
I develop an optimal contracting model to address mixed empirical evidence on how organizational
higher purpose affects financial performance. There are three main results. First, while purpose-driven
employees and firms generate higher productive effort, pure profit-maximizers perform better financially
in pooling equilibria where firm identities are shrouded. In separating equilibria, purpose-driven firms
may financially outperform profit maximizers and generate higher pecuniary output. Second, separating
equilibria produce higher social welfare in some circumstances, but social stigma against non-purpose-
driven firms can induce identity shrouding via purpose washing, generating inefficient pooling. Third,
adding employees who are not purpose-driven may improve welfare.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the mass entry of women into the American paid workforce between approximately 1965 and 1985 produced a structural, permanent repricing of the cost of living that has been systematically overlooked in the macroeconomic literature. Distinct from conventional inflation-which operates cyclically and can be managed through monetary policy-the labor supply shock of second-wave feminism triggered a one-time reset of the economic baseline: the minimum household income required to sustain a middle-class standard of living. Evidence is drawn from historical price-to-income ratios for housing, real wage stagnation data, labor force participation records from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, and crosscountry comparisons across OECD economies. The paper situates its argument in relation to Warren and Tyagi's (2003) identification of the dual-income bidding war mechanism, extending their analysis to identify the labor supply shock as the causal trigger and the permanent baseline reset as its structural legacy. The central finding is that the standard of living accessible to a single-income household in 1965 now requires two incomes-not as a consequence of cyclical inflation, but as a consequence of a structural recalibration of all positional goods markets around dual-income purchasing capacity.

title: Redesigning AI Regulatory Sandboxes for Generative AI: Beyond Traditional for-Profit Innovation
affiliations: , Cornell University - Department of Information Science and Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB)

detail.title: Redesigning AI Regulatory Sandboxes for Generative AI: Beyond Traditional for-Profit Innovation
detail.abstract: Regulatory sandboxes have become a central instrument for governing artificial intelligence (AI), with data protection authorities and AI regulations frameworks increasingly relying on them to enable regulatory learning and promote innovation. However, in this paper, we argue that current sandbox frameworks do not adequately account for AI innovation occurring outside of the for-profit space. As vibe coding, AI agents, and zero-code platforms have lowered the technical thresholds for building and deploying AI applications, public sector institutions, civil society organizations, and non-institutional innovators are increasingly in roles that data protection and AI regulations have traditionally assigned to firms. Yet in conducting a scoping review of AI-related sandboxes across jurisdictions in Europe, Latin America, Asia, Africa, and the Middle East, we find several barriers to participation by these actors. In addition to often explicitly limiting sandbox participation to private sector actors, eligibility criteria and participant recruitment processes place implicit barriers as they assume organisational capacity that public sector, civil society, and individual innovators typically do not possess. Drawing from literature in innovation studies, data protection and AI law, and experimental governance, we argue that this bias against non-market actors limits the capacity for socially beneficial innovations to emerge. To go beyond market-driven approaches to regulatory learning and innovation, we conclude by proposing three main pathways for more inclusive sandbox design, including low-friction entry points, intermediated participation, and eligibility criteria oriented toward societal value.

title:
Financial Depth and Macroeconomic Volatility under Trade Shock: 
A Cross-Country Analysis
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics, New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics,  and New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics

detail.title:
Financial Depth and Macroeconomic Volatility under Trade Shock: 
A Cross-Country Analysis
detail.abstract: This study examines whether financial depth dampens or amplifies macroeconomic volatility using annual panel data from 86 countries over 2000-2024, estimated with two-way fixed effects and Driscoll-Kraay standard errors. Across the full sample, deeper financial systems measured by Broad Money to GDP are associated with lower output volatility. It supports the finance stabilization hypothesis, though no nonlinear turning point is found. However, this stabilizing role is highly conditional, as elevated inflation significantly weakens financial depth's buffering capacity, particularly in advanced economies, while trade shocks increase volatility primarily in emerging markets where financial depth does not significantly mitigate their transmission. Heterogeneity across income groups is substantial, with financial depth consistently reducing volatility in advanced economies, while exchange rate movements and trade shocks are the dominant drivers of instability in emerging markets. These findings suggest that financial depth is a relevant but conditional stabilization tool, and that effective macroeconomic stabilization requires a broader policy framework encompassing low inflation, sustainable fiscal positions, and sound external balance management.

detail.title: Policy Effects of Limiting Independent Directors’ Multiple Directorships: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: Whether independent directors’ busyness impairs their effectiveness remains controversial. Chinese regulators therefore tightened the cap on the number of board seats an independent director may hold. Using a many-to-many assortative matching model and 2,300 matched “listed company–independent director” observations from China’s A-share market in 2020, we find that reducing the maximum number of positions increases the utility of both firms and independent directors on average. Random forest predictions indicate improvements in firms’ regulatory compliance, information disclosure, and internal control quality. However, about 30% of firms and independent directors experience a decline in utility, and roughly 5.06%–44.89% of firms exhibit worse governance outcomes. We also document spillover effects on non-treated but non-regulated firms and directors, driven by a quantity effect (e.g., director shortages) and a substitution effect (e.g., weaker qualifications). Updating the independent director database and shifting accounting directors to non-overlapping workplaces can mitigate these adverse effects.

title: The Post-2015 German Lending Surge What Role for QE?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Post-2015 German Lending Surge What Role for QE?
detail.abstract: This paper uses German microdata to test whether the ECB’s quantitative easing (QE) spurred bank lending to non-financial firms. Bank-firm loan data allow me to control for loan demand at firm level. The share of bonds in banks’ total assets before QE serves as treatment proxy. While the effects are positive and statistically significant, they are small: Increasing the bond/asset share in a firm’s lender bank by one standard deviation increases the de-trended outstanding bilateral loan volume by 3-5% of its within-sample mean. At firm level, no unambiguous effect can be observed.

title: The Power of Position: Display Salience in Specialized ETFs

detail.title: The Power of Position: Display Salience in Specialized ETFs
detail.abstract: Exchange-traded fund (ETF) providers display the top 10 holdings on a visually distinct, above-the-fold panel of the fund's information page. In specialized ETFs, where these stocks are likely to be read as representative of the fund's theme, we show that this disclosure convention generates a display salience effect: top 10 constituents attract heightened retail attention, experience larger increases in retail ownership, and earn cumulative abnormal returns 1.57% above other constituents around fund inception. The price gain, however, is temporary, with a significant portion of the initial gain reversing over the following months. The effect is concentrated specifically at the rank-10 visibility cutoff and is not driven by firm size or other stock characteristics. The results indicate that standard features of ETF portfolio disclosure can move retail attention and generate temporary deviations in constituent stock prices.

title: Structure and Resolution in Banking: Are They Substitutes
affiliations: University of Kent - School of Economics and University of Glasgow

detail.title: Structure and Resolution in Banking: Are They Substitutes
detail.abstract: Can bank resolution replace ring-fencing? We develop a simple framework ofexpected systemic loss in which structural separability and resolvability interact.When either of two features holds—structure makes resolution work better, or itreduces the support needed during failure—resolution and ring-fencing becomecomplements, not substitutes. Contrary to conventional wisdom, as the credibilityof using resolution rises, the optimal degree of ring-fencing often increases; easing iswarranted only in knife-edge cases where structure brings no marginal benefit. Aprivate–social comparison predicts under-investment in structure and preparedness.In general, better resolvability strengthens the case for ring-fencing.

title:
The Two-fairness Distinction: 
Evidence for the Separability of Preference-based Prosociality, Attitudinal Trust, and Institutional Quality

detail.title:
The Two-fairness Distinction: 
Evidence for the Separability of Preference-based Prosociality, Attitudinal Trust, and Institutional Quality
detail.abstract:
Cross-cultural research conflates three empirically distinct constructs: preference-based
prosociality (GPS F_proxy), attitudinal social trust (WVS/ESS), and institutional quality
(CPI/GDP). We term their separability the Two-Fairness Distinction and test it across eight
independent datasets (GPS N=80,337; ESS Rounds 1–11; six additional sources; 76 countries; 20
years). F_proxy is near-zero correlated with institutional quality (CPI: r=−0.023, CI [−0.27, +0.23];
lnGDP: r=−0.018) — a pattern that survives multivariate controls, jackknife diagnostics, and five
composite specifications. Associations with attitudinal trust vary by sample: near-zero in European
ESS surveys (meta-r=+0.118, p=.137) and weakly positive globally (GPS trust: r=+0.227, p=.049).
By contrast, patience strongly predicts institutional quality (r=+0.725***) and wealth
(r=+0.580***) but not F_proxy. Behavioral community bond strength (B_social) is the only
consistent predictor of F_proxy (meta-r=+0.374***, I²=0%, k=11 ESS rounds, 2002–2022;
longitudinal: CLPM β=+0.101, p=.002; Khan, 2026b). The findings support construct separability
but do not establish causal independence. All analyses are exploratory; a preregistered confirmatory
replication (WVS Wave 8, OSF: osf.io/fxhmc) is planned.

title: The Verification Rate Gap: A Conceptual Metric for AI Development Risk

detail.title: The Verification Rate Gap: A Conceptual Metric for AI Development Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the Representative Director of C3 Social Design Center and maintains the public companion repository related to the Verification Kit architecture discussed in this Research Note. The paper presents a conceptual and architectural framework and does not report sponsored empirical results, product certification, or production deployment. The author declares no other personal or financial relationships that could have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This Research Note does not involve human participants, patients, personal data, animal subjects, or clinical intervention. Ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract:
As AI systems increasingly automate parts of their own development, the primary bottleneck of safety and oversight shifts from the capacity of the AI system to the capacity of the verifier. This paper proposes the Verification Rate Gap as a conceptual metric for AI development risk. The core claim is simple: risk emerges when the rate of AI-generated development outputs exceeds the rate at which those outputs can be reliably verified.

We define AI development risk as a function of the discrepancy between Generation Rate (G_rate) and Verification Rate (V_rate): R_dev ∝ max(0, G_rate − V_rate). When generation accelerates while verification remains bounded by human review, systems accumulate unverified debt: AI-generated code, experiments, evaluations, decisions, or system changes that have not yet been reproduced, audited, or challenged. A separate bounded triage rate (T_rate) can make unverified debt visible, but only verified clearance through V_rate reduces the debt stock.

To reduce this gap, this paper introduces the Verification Kit: a standardized evidence package containing execution manifests, verdict records, evidence digests, conformance results, undefined-case reports, and integrity proofs. The Kit shifts verification from informal human review toward mechanical replay and structured audit. Its purpose is not to guarantee absolute safety or alignment, but to increase verification throughput by making decision paths reproducible, inspectable, and challengeable by third parties or independent verification tools.

The paper defines the claim boundary of this approach and discusses three failure modes: circular specification authority, adversarial audit trails, and the difficulty of deterministic replay in stochastic AI systems. The conclusion is that governance for AI-built-AI workflows should treat verification throughput as a first-class safety requirement.

title: Preference-Changing Information

detail.title: Preference-Changing Information
detail.abstract: This paper studies preference-changing information, namely truthful information that changes not only beliefs, but also the utility consequences of holding those beliefs. In standard information design, Blackwell refinements weakly raise a Bayesian receiver’s decision value because posterior payoffs are convex. Here, posterior beliefs also affect experienced utility through attention, monitoring, anxiety, or compliance burdens. As a result, a Blackwell-more-informative truthful disclosure can strictly lower receiver welfare. The reversal is not a failure of Bayesian inference, but a change in the welfare object. Posterior beliefs are arguments of utility, not only inputs into expected material payoffs. The relevant design object is therefore not truth versus concealment, but the granularity of truth, namely the refinement order over truthful posterior partitions. Refinements are valuable when they cross action boundaries, but harmful when they separate posteriors inside action-stable regions with convex experiential costs. Receiver-optimal disclosure is selectively granular, while strategic senders may distort this granularity by overcoarsening near decision thresholds or over-disclosing for documentation. In medical informed consent, coarse defaults with optional refinement preserve decision-relevant information while limiting unnecessary experiential harm.

detail.abstract: This research examines the factors that affect the advancement of persons with disabilities into senior management positions at Brazilian federal universities. The study investigates how structural and attitudinal ableism, rooted in eugenic legacies, perpetuates the underrepresentation of this group in decision-making and power spaces, even in the presence of a robust legal framework for inclusion. The methodology is grounded in an applied research nature with a predominantly qualitative approach and descriptive character. The author employs methodological triangulation, encompassing a systematic literature review (2019–2025), documentary analysis of the Institutional Development Plans (PDIs) of 69 federal universities, and data analysis from the Personnel Statistical Panel (PEP) using a trend analysis approach supported by ARIMA (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average) modeling, applied as a methodological tool for identifying projective patterns. Additionally, semi-structured interviews were conducted with public servants with disabilities who currently hold or have previously held management positions. The analysis reveals a scenario of absolute institutional invisibility, as none of the documents examined address career advancement policies or upward mobility targets for this functional segment. Although the statistical projection indicates that the minimum quota of 5% of public servants with disabilities will be met by 2028, the mapping demonstrates that entry into the public service does not guarantee progression to strategic positions. The discussion highlights that access to senior management depends on individual resilience and the ability to overcome barriers that question technical competence in the face of workplace adaptation needs. The research concludes by proposing a structural framework comprising fourteen strategic action guidelines organized into thematic axes encompassing governance, people management, organizational culture, and technology. These recommendations aim to institutionalize practices designed to overcome this scenario through intentional interventions and the formulation of public and institutional policies that dismantle systemic barriers, actively promoting anti-ableism and inclusive management as foundational values for innovation and social equity

title: State-Dependent Transmission of Long-Term Yields to Real Economic Activity and Inflation: A VAR Analysis Across Two Monetary Regimes

detail.title: State-Dependent Transmission of Long-Term Yields to Real Economic Activity and Inflation: A VAR Analysis Across Two Monetary Regimes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently, with no funding received from any public, commercial, or not-for-profit organization. The author has no personal or financial relationships with any individuals or organizations that could have influenced the design, conduct, analysis, or reporting of this study.

All data used in this research are publicly available macroeconomic time series sourced from the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED), Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), and Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how shocks to the U.S. 10-Year Treasury Yield transmit to real economic activity and consumer price inflation across two structurally distinct monetary regimes: the gradual normalization cycle of 2014–2019 and the aggressive tightening cycle of 2021–2025. Using a Vector Autoregression (VAR) framework - augmented with Financial Conditions Index proxies, equity returns, credit spreads, and mortgage rates - applied to monthly FRED and BEA data across four GDP sectors (Industry, Services, Agriculture, Government) and CPI, this paper identifies the direction, magnitude, speed, and persistence of the transmission mechanism and compares it across regimes. The central finding is that yield-to-macro transmission is state-dependent, not constant: the same 100-basis-point yield shock produces GDP and CPI responses that are 1.16× to 1.82× larger and arrive three months faster in the post-COVID regime than in the pre-COVID baseline. Critically, Impulse Response Function analysis reveals that peak GDP damage now arrives in three months rather than six - a compression attributable to the financialization of the real economy rather than to changes in the direct investment channel. The Forecast Error Variance Decomposition shows that CPI is now 38% yield-driven at the 12-month horizon, up from 15% pre-COVID, representing the single largest structural shift documented in the study. The mechanism-augmented VAR2 specification finds that approximately 40–50% of the post-COVID GDP transmission operated through the financial conditions channel - equity valuation compression, credit spread widening, and liquidity contraction- rather than through the direct cost-of-capital channel, a result invisible to standard bivariate models. Statistically significant Granger causality from the 10-Year Yield to Industry GDP is confirmed post-COVID (p = 0.041), establishing a verifiable leading-indicator relationship for industrial-sector output that was absent in the pre-COVID period. Government GDP effectively decoupled from the rate mechanism (0.27× amplification), reflecting fiscal inertia from multi-year legislative appropriations that monetary policy could not override. Robustness checks across alternative lag specifications, real versus nominal yield substitution, term spread as an alternative variable, and Core CPI as an alternative inflation measure confirm the directional findings, with the CPI amplification range tightening to 1.43× to 1.82× across specifications. The paper contributes a mechanism-augmented, regime-comparative interpretation of long-term yield transmission that connects rigorous time-series evidence to actionable implications for business planning horizons, sector allocation, and monetary policy calibration.

title: Multi-Dimensional Exposure to Child Care Subsidy and Maternal Employment and Economic Wellbeing: A Scoping Review
affiliations: Michigan State University and Michigan State University

detail.title: Multi-Dimensional Exposure to Child Care Subsidy and Maternal Employment and Economic Wellbeing: A Scoping Review
detail.abstract: The objective of this scoping review is to map and synthesize existing evidence on how childcare subsidy (CCS) exposure has been conceptualized and examined in relation to maternal employment/economic outcomes in the United States. Rather than treating childcare subsidy use as a single or uniform experience, this review conceptualizes CCS exposure as a multidimensional phenomenon that may include different forms of program engagement, such as subsidy receipt, duration of participation, and subsidized childcare arrangements (eg. Subsidized center-care). Although a substantial body of research links subsidy receipt to higher maternal employment, existing studies vary widely in how CCS exposure is conceptualized and operationalized. This scoping review therefore seeks to identify and categorize how prior research defines and measures CCS exposure and how these conceptualizations are linked to maternal economic and employment outcomes, including but not limited to employment status, job retention, work hours, and earnings.,Eligible studies include research involving mothers who are current or former childcare subsidy users within U.S. childcare subsidy programs administered under the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF). This review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews. Searches were conducted in MEDLINE via PubMed, ERIC (PROQuest), Social Sciences Citation Index (Web of Science), Sociological Abstracts, Business Source Complete (EBSCO) and ProQuest One Business. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extract data, and chart findings using the Covidence platform. This review identified 23 eligible studies and found that CCS exposure was most often conceptualized as subsidy receipt or use, while fewer studies examined duration, stability, amount or generosity, subsidized care experience, or administrative experience. Across studies, CCS receipt was mostly associated with binary maternal employment status (eg. Employed or unemployed) by logistic regression and survey design; however, the evidence suggests that maternal outcomes are shaped not only by whether mothers receive subsidies, but also by the continuity, adequacy, and usability of subsidy support.

title: Financial Incentives to Fertility: From Short to Long Run
affiliations: and Goethe University

detail.title: Financial Incentives to Fertility: From Short to Long Run
detail.abstract: Are financial incentives effective in increasing fertility rates? Empirical evidence suggests they are, primarily in the short run (around implementation). Can such policies also increase the total number of children in the long run? We address this question by using a structural life-cycle model of fertility and labor supply, calibrated to replicate the short-run effects of a cash transfer paid at childbirth implemented in 2007 in Spain. The model incorporates labor market duality, a defining feature of Spanish labor markets that negatively impacts fertility. Our calibrated model replicates a 6% increase in fertility rates in the short run but only generates a 3% rise in completed fertility over women's lifetimesthe long run. Eliminating labor market duality increases lifetime fertility by 6.62%, but the discrepancy between short-and long-run effects of the incentive persists. These results highlight the limited impact of financial incentives alone to sustain fertility gains.

title: Resiliency of Fully Dollarized Economies
affiliations: Universidad San Francisco de Quito - USFQ, School of Economics and Universidad Austral de Chile

detail.title: Resiliency of Fully Dollarized Economies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research did not include work with people. Thus, it did not required ethics approval.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the resilience of fully dollarized economies. Full dollarization removes the seigniorage and devaluation channel through which expected fiscal bailouts can raise domestic nominal rates, depress asset prices, and validate crisis expectations in standard fixed exchange rate models. Yet dollarization does not eliminate financial fragility. It shifts fragility toward other mechanisms: sovereign risk pass through, bank leverage, sovereign bond exposure, and the institutional custody of dollar liquidity. We provide three sets of results. First, in the baseline model, pessimistic fiscal expectations cannot generate a self fulfilling banking crisis when the domestic rate is pinned by the world rate. Second, local projections for Panama and the Dominican Republic show that sovereign risk shocks transmit to domestic financial prices, but pass through in Panama is partial and bounded. Third, a state-space stress test with a regulatory crisis threshold shows that Panama like pass through does not generate crisis in a baseline balance sheet, but sovereign bond exposure can restore fragility even under dollarization. The results imply that the resilience of dollarization depends not only on the monetary regime, but also on bank balance sheets and dollar liquidity institutions.

title: Coagulation Profiles in Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis
affiliations: Kurah Women’s Health Institute, Santa Casa BH, University Center of Maceio, University of Messina, University of Western São Paulo, Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG), Hospital Santa Marcelina, Hospital Santa Marcelina, Indiana University Purdue University Indianapolis (IUPUI) - Indiana University School of Medicine, Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein, Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein and Monash University - Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology

detail.title: Coagulation Profiles in Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This study received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Background: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP), including gestational hypertension (GH) and the preeclampsia (PE) spectrum, are leading causes of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. Although haemostatic alterations are well recognised in HDP, it remains uncertain whether coagulation abnormalities follow a progressive pattern across disease subtypes or whether specific markers reliably differentiate them. We aimed to evaluate the direction and magnitude of coagulation marker alterations across GH, the PE spectrum, and normotensive pregnancies. 

Methods: We performed a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis following Cochrane and PRISMA-NMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420251119369). PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception to December 9, 2025. Observational studies enrolling pregnant women in the third trimester with HDP or normotensive controls were eligible. Primary outcomes were platelet count (PLT), mean platelet volume (MPV), and D-dimer. Secondary outcomes included fibrinogen, prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), antithrombin III (ATIII), protein C, protein S, and other haemostatic markers. A Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis was conducted using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, with results expressed as mean differences (MD) with 95% credible intervals (CrI). Between-study heterogeneity was quantified using the I2 statistics within a Bayesian random-effects model, with uncertainty expressed as 95% credible intervals (CrIs). Risk of bias in non-randomised studies was evaluated using the Risk of Bias In Non-randomised Studies of Exposure (ROBINS-E) tool. Evidence certainty was assessed using Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA). 

Findings: Of 9,621 studies identified, 245 studies comprising 47,134 patients were included. PLT (181 studies, n=36,705) decreased progressively with HDP severity. Normotensive pregnancies had significantly higher PLT than severe preeclampsia (sPE) (MD 48·06 x10⁹/L [95% CrI 38·37 to 57·63 x10⁹/L]) and undefined preeclampsia (uPE) (MD 40·53 x10⁹/L [32·35 to 48·65 x10⁹/L]). MPV (106 studies, n=24,488) showed an inverse pattern, being significantly higher in sPE than normotensive pregnancies (MD 1·20 fL [0·85 to 1·60]) and mPE (MD 0·51 fL [0·14 to 0·90 fL]). D-dimer (53 studies, n=8,530) was significantly elevated in sPE versus normotensive pregnancies (MD 910 ng/mL [390 to 1400 ng/mL ]), although these estimates exhibited higher between-study heterogeneity (and clinical imprecision compared to platelet indices. Most secondary markers, including routine coagulation times and fibrinogen, showed no consistent gradient across HDP categories. ATIII showed lower levels in more severe HDP, but estimates were imprecise. 

Interpretation: PLT provided the most consistent haemostatic signal across the HDP spectrum, with progressively lower PLT and higher MPV in more severe disease. D-dimer elevations were observed, but with greater uncertainty. Routine coagulation tests showed limited discriminatory value across HDP categories. These findings support prioritising platelet-based measures to complement clinical classification and monitoring of HDP. Funding: This study received no funding from external sources.

title: An Interpretable Machine-Learning Risk Calculator for ICU Mortality in Elderly Septic Shock: A Dual-Database Development and External Validation Study
affiliations: Kaifeng Central Hospital, Kaifeng Central Hospital, Henan University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Zhengzhou University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: An Interpretable Machine-Learning Risk Calculator for ICU Mortality in Elderly Septic Shock: A Dual-Database Development and External Validation Study
detail.abstract: Background and objective: Elderly patients with septic shock carry an exceptionally high ICU-mortality risk; generic severity scores were not derived in this subgroup, and externally validated, bedside-deployable tools are scarce. We aimed to develop an interpretable, browser-deployable machine-learning model for ICU-mortality prediction in this population.Methods: Patients aged ≥ 65 years with septic shock (Sepsis-3) were identified from MIMIC-IV v3.1 (n = 3,620; development) and eICU-CRD v2.0 (n = 2,074; external validation). Predictors were selected from 75 first-24-h candidates by elastic-net–Boruta intersection plus Borda voting. Nine algorithms were compared by 10-fold nested cross-validation with pairwise DeLong tests; the optimal model was tested internally and externally, explained with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), and deployed as an online calculator.Results: Nine features were retained, including LODS, SAPS-II and SOFA scores, 24-hour urine output, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO₂), red cell distribution width (RDW), activated partial thromboplastin time, heart rate and the ICU admission-to-sepsis-onset interval. The deep neural network (DNN) achieved the highest cross-validated discrimination (AUC 0.7915). On internal testing the DNN yielded an AUC of 0.7484 (95 % CI 0.7175–0.7804) and 0.7440 (0.7160–0.7713) on eICU-CRD v2.0, with a Brier score of 0.1301. SHAP ranked LODS, SOFA and 24-hour urine output as the three strongest contributors.Conclusions: A nine-feature DNN model from first-24-h routine variables predicts ICU mortality in elderly patients with septic shock with stable cross-database performance and is deployed as an open-access, browser-side risk calculator requiring no patient-data upload, addressing a principal deployment gap in clinical prediction-model translation.Keywords: elderly patients; intensive care unit; septic shock; machine learning; predictive model; SHAP analysis

title: MetaSeg-Net: A Compact Deep Learning Framework for Accurate MRI Stroke Lesion Segmentation Across Domains
affiliations: Kalasin University

detail.title: MetaSeg-Net: A Compact Deep Learning Framework for Accurate MRI Stroke Lesion Segmentation Across Domains
detail.abstract: Accurate segmentation of ischemic stroke lesions from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) plays a pivotal role in clinical diagnosis and therapeutic planning. However, existing deep learning models often suffer from limited generalizability across domains and high computational demands, hindering their deployment in real-world healthcare settings. This paper introduces MetaSeg-Net, a lightweight and attention-enhanced encoder–decoder framework designed to address these challenges through efficient learning and robust domain adaptation. The architecture leverages a pruned MobileNetV3 backbone integrated with Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) and Convolutional Block Attention Modules (CBAM), enabling refined spatial and channel-wise feature recalibration. Evaluations on three benchmark datasets, ISLES, ATLAS, and a generalized MRI collection, demonstrate that MetaSeg-Net consistently outperforms or matches state-of-the-art models, achieving Dice scores of 96.1%, 94.3%, and 93.7%, respectively. Despite comprising only 1.13 million parameters, the model exhibits strong generalization across diverse anatomical structures and acquisition protocols. The proposed framework is especially suited for deployment in low-resource clinical environments and supports few-shot learning, enhancing its adaptability to new domains with limited labeled data. These findings highlight MetaSeg-Net as a clinically practical and scalable solution for stroke lesion segmentation.

title: Optimal Containment Policy with Private Protection

detail.title: Optimal Containment Policy with Private Protection

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by WINGS-GSDM, Designing Future Society Fellowship, JASSO, Project Number 150201SP01.

detail.abstract: In this paper, I develop a macro-SIR model to analyze how private protection changes optimal containment policy. Mask-wearing as a form of private protection reduces infection risk without requiring a proportional reduction in economic activity and, when sufficiently effective, qualitatively reshapes the optimal containment path. Optimal containment can be phase-shifted-remaining relatively flat during the infection upswing and tightening as infections decline. Under the benchmark calibration, mask-wearing reduces infections more strongly and causes a smaller recession than containment when each is considered in isolation. Although mask-wearing is effective in suppressing transmission, containment remains welfare-improving because it mitigates the infection externality generated by infected individuals' economic activity.

title: The Administrative Capacity Gap in Higher Education Grant Funding: How Financial Systems Shape Program Continuity

detail.title: The Administrative Capacity Gap in Higher Education Grant Funding: How Financial Systems Shape Program Continuity
detail.abstract: Grant success is typically measured by funding volume, publication output, and compliance outcomes. Administrative capacity rarely enters that conversation. It should. This paper argues that post-award administrative systems function as hidden infrastructure in higher education grant funding, shaping not only whether programs are funded but whether they can function once funding arrives. The conceptual contribution is specific: existing scholarship on administrative burden and implementation has not been systematically applied to research administration as a site where equity is produced or undermined. This paper makes that connection, drawing on Herd and Moynihan's (2019) administrative burden framework, Spillane, Parise, and Sherer's (2011) organizational routines scholarship, and community-engaged research literature (Israel et al., 2013; Wallerstein & Duran, 2010) to examine how reimbursement delays, tacit knowledge loss, fragmented workflows, and rigid compliance structures generate instability that falls hardest on smaller programs, community-engaged initiatives, and early-career investigators. The paper concludes with evidence-based reforms and a call for empirical research on post-award administration as an equity-relevant institutional system.

title: Physical Economics: A Unified Complex Dynamical System Framework Based on Consciousness Capital
affiliations: and Tsinghua University

detail.title: Physical Economics: A Unified Complex Dynamical System Framework Based on Consciousness Capital
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a unified theoretical framework for economics based on complex open dynamical systems in 3+1 dimensional spacetime. We establish a fundamental ontological distinction between two irreducible subsystems: the formalization entropy-increasing subsystem—closed systems of finite symbols, axioms, and rules—and the consciousness entropy-decreasing subsystem—an irreducible non-formalizable domain transcending all finite rules. Core Insight: All formalized systems (institutions, technologies, capital, algorithms) are inherently incomplete and entropy-increasing. They cannot self-sustain indefinitely due to internal logical limits (Gödelian incompleteness, self-reference paradoxes) and external physical disturbances. Human consciousness is the only known autonomous force capable of reducing entropy, maintaining formalized systems, and creating real value. We revise the value conservation law: while consciousness is the sole original value source, formalized systems act as powerful value multipliers when guided by consciousness, but generate only entropy in isolation (formalization idling). Framework: We develop a five-layer unified framework: (1) Microfoundations: Quantum-like uncertainty and innovation dynamics; (2) Mesoeconomics: Classical dynamics of mature markets and institutional evolution; (3) Macroeconomics: Spacetime curvature, global imbalances, and income inequality; (4) Field Theory: Value flow and economic interactions; (5) Evolutionary theory: Long-term civilization dynamics and paradigm shifts. Contribution: This framework provides first-principles explanations for core digital economy paradoxes, including the productivity paradox (caused by exponential formalization outpacing linear consciousness capital growth), financial crises, platform monopolies, and AI’s impact. We show current AI systems, trapped in the "formalization cage," cannot generate genuine consciousness or value. This framework offers a coherent foundation for understanding value creation, inequality, institutional change, and human civilization’s future.

title: The Moral Grammar of Magnifica Humanitas - A Discussion Paper

detail.title: The Moral Grammar of Magnifica Humanitas - A Discussion Paper
detail.abstract: On May 15 th 2026, on the 135th anniversary of Rerum Novarum, Pope Leo XIV promulgated (published on May 25 th) the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas-"On safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence." Two months earlier (March 2026), the author had circulated, through SSRN and RePEc (DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.6468803), The Moral Grammar of Economics: An Empirical and Mathematical Framework for Jesuit-Inspired Social Justice. The present paper performs a systematic dialogue between the two texts: (i) it identifies the doctrinal claims of Magnifica Humanitas that admit a direct mathematical operationalization through the constraints, wedges, and welfare functions developed in the Moral Grammar; (ii) it isolates the novel doctrinal contributions introduced by Leo XIV-the Babel/Jerusalem dichotomy, the disarmament of words and code, the new monopolies of AI, the culture of care, and the explicit move beyond GDP-and formalises each as new terms or constraints within the welfare architecture; (iii) it reanchors these formal extensions in the panel-data evidence already presented in the Moral Grammar (172 countries, 1963-2024), in particular the solidarity-response coefficient 𝛽 = 0.664 and the subsidiarity penalty 𝜎 = 0.856; (iv) it proposes a composite Magnifica Humanitas Index (MHI) for monitoring societies along the integral-human-development frontier; and (v) it translates the result into a concrete five-point policy program for the AI era. The fusion shows that Magnifica Humanitas is not only a theological document but also a precise research agenda for a humanist quantitative economics-one in which Jesuit-inspired ethical constraints become binding mathematical inequalities rather than ornamental preambles. This paper does not claim that the encyclical was influenced by the Moral Grammar; it claims only that the architectural alignment between the two texts is precise enough to be operationally useful, especially for the global network of Jesuit and Catholic universities engaged in the post-AI re-foundation of social-economic thought.

detail.abstract: This study develops a counterfactual reserve-allocation framework to examine how geopolitical risk affects the feasible set of foreign-exchange reserve allocations in emerging markets. Using BRIC economies as the main sample, we derive model-implied reserve allocations from a mean-variance optimization model incorporating a COVOL-based geopolitical-risk constraint. The short-term debt (STD) ratio is used as a liquidity-pressure state variable, rather than as a proxy for central-bank preferences, to construct high-and low-adequacy counterfactual environments. The results show that geopolitical risk does not generate uniform diversification. In high-adequacy states, modelimplied allocations adjust mainly along the USD-EUR-GBP margin, whereas in low-adequacy states, the relevant adjustment margin shifts toward substitution between JPY and CHF among lower-volatility safe-haven currencies. For highly exposed economies, geopolitical pressure may contract the feasible allocation set rather than merely shift optimal weights. The findings indicate that geopolitical risk affects not only model-implied reserve-currency weights but also the feasibility of reserve rebalancing.

detail.abstract:
Background: Insulin resistance (IR) precedes the onset of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) by many years, yet commonly used surrogate indices rely on simplified assumptions and fixed cut-offs, limiting their discriminative ability across heterogeneous populations. Artificial intelligence–derived IR (AI-IR) may offer a more flexible and data-driven approach for metabolic risk assessment.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Taiwan MAJOR Research Database (1996–2014). AI-IR models (9-variable and 8-variable versions) were compared with conventional IR indices, including HOMA-IR, HOMA2-IR, triglyceride–glucose (TyG) index, TG/HDL ratio, and metabolic syndrome, for identifying baseline diabetes and predicting incident T2DM. Discrimination was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and associations with incident diabetes were evaluated using logistic regression with multivariable adjustment. Age-stratified analyses (<40 vs. ≥40 years) and joint-effect analyses were performed.

Results: Among 13,811 participants, AI-IR demonstrated the highest discrimination for identifying baseline diabetes (AUROC 0.85 for 9-variable AI-IR), outperforming all traditional indices. In 6,104 participants without diabetes at baseline, AI-IR also showed superior prediction of incident T2DM (AUROC 0.81), exceeding conventional markers. Elevated AI-IR was strongly associated with incident diabetes across adjusted models (adjusted odds ratio up to 8.72), with more stable effect sizes than traditional indices. Joint-effect analyses indicated that AI-IR was the dominant driver of diabetes risk, with limited incremental contribution from conventional markers.

Conclusion: AI-derived IR outperforms traditional metabolic indices for both cross-sectional and longitudinal diabetes risk assessment. AI-IR provides a robust, continuous, and age-consistent framework for precision diabetes risk stratification and prevention.

detail.abstract: The term "AI agent" is used frequently and freely across computer science, industry marketing, policy discourse, and everyday business conversations, but it does not mean the same thing in any two of those contexts. This definitional fragmentation is not merely an academic inconvenience. It is a governance problem. When engineers, deployers, and regulators cannot agree on what an agent is or how to classify its capabilities and autonomy, they cannot agree on how to govern it either. This paper reviews the foundational literature on AI agent definitions and existing taxonomies, identifying five distinct classification perspectives: user-role and oversight, developer capability, legal and liability, functional and ontological, and standards and interoperability. It examines where these perspectives converge, where they diverge, and what the gap between them costs in governance terms. The paper then proposes a unified, multi-dimensional taxonomy structured around four axes, capability tier, oversight mode, accountability allocation, and trait profile, that allows any AI agent deployment to be profiled coherently across technical, governance, and policy communities. The contribution is not a new hierarchy but a shared architecture: a framework that enables policymakers, engineers, and operators to discuss the same system in the same language.

detail.abstract: Previous research identified five areas where trust could be built for financial roboadvisors. This research identifies the specific methods for building trust for each of these five areas. Building trust with human oversight can be done in three specific ways: (1) Oversight of AI model and service it provides, (2) human explanations for advice and processes, and (3) regular human communication outside specific processes. Building trust with transparency and control can be done by: (1) Recognize that there are beliefs that do not immediately lead to action, (2) explain actions and demonstrating ability and integrity, and (3) balance automation with control to avoid disempowering users. Building trust with accuracy and usefulness can be done by: (1) Accurate and relevant information conveying competence and integrity, (2) usefulness supported by back testing and multiple methods, and (3) enhanced usefulness through personalisation. Building trust with ease of use and support can be done by: (1) Achieve ease of use while keeping all the necessary functionality, (2) support time management with nudges, and (3) useful and reliable service with high performance. Building trust with a humanlike interaction can be done by: (1) Utilize the latest sentiment analysis and longest contextual memory, (2) the robo-advisor should have a clear persona, and (3) build a relationship and a feeling of friendship and partnership.

detail.abstract: A recurrent speculative strand in contemporary artificial intelligence research holds that sufficiently large neural-network architectures on Base-2 computational substrates will eventually produce not only artificial general intelligence but also the phenomenal consciousness that accompanies human cognition. This essay argues, conditionally and on stated premises, that the consciousness expectation is foreclosed at the level of the substrate. The argument rests on three components. The Substrate Closure Theorem holds that every program executable on a Base-2 substrate instantiates only properties contained within, or wholly supervenient upon, the Boolean closure of its symbolic specification; it follows from the substrate’s finite state space and Boolean compositionality, with the Cayley–Hamilton theorem characterizing the structural bound. The Qualia Exceedance Premise holds that the subjective phenomenal character of conscious experience lies outside that closure for any finite symbolic specification; it is defended via the convergent arguments of Nagel, Jackson, and Searle, and is contrasted against deflationary, organizational-invariance, and integrated-information objections, with Block’s access/phenomenal distinction carrying the load against Dennettian deflationism. A bridging step reads the Qualia Exceedance Premise as ontic rather than merely epistemic. Together the three yield the modal conclusion that no Base-2 program instantiates or wholly supervenes upon a phenomenal property — the foreclosure being structural at the level of the substrate rather than contingent on engineering. The strong modal claim is bounded to Base-2 substrates and to the operationally accessible content of engineered hybrid systems (quantum, analog, neuromorphic, biocomputing-wetware) whose programming and readout reside within that closure; it does not extend to the substrate-internal physics of those hybrids or to the free-living biological substrate, on which the essay maintains explicit silence.

detail.abstract: In tension-based systems, structural value (V) describes the internal balance of interacting forces, while perceived value (Vp) captures how this structure is interpreted under partial visibility or bias. However, neither structural nor perceived value fully explains whether a system is accepted within a given context. This article introduces legitimacy (L) as a contextual validation function within the ZTH (Zone of Tension Harmonic) framework. Legitimacy is defined as a function of structural value, perceived value, and contextual frame, and is modeled as a distinct analytical layer rather than a property of the system itself. A typology of legitimacy regimes is proposed, showing how misalignment between structure, perception, and context leads to phenomena such as innovation rejection, institutional illusion, and structural invisibility. This contribution extends the ZTH framework by integrating acceptance and contextual validation into a unified model of complex systems.

detail.title: From Partner to Managed Variable: How Systems Reclassify External Actors Under Pressure
detail.abstract: Why do systems reduce access for valuable partners, restrict compliant suppliers, limit high-performing platforms, or scale back cooperation with actors that still deliver visible benefits? This paper argues that the shift occurs through reclassification. Under systemic stress, external actors move from trust-carried partner status to managed-variable status governed by containment. They may remain valuable and formally acceptable, yet their access, discretion, scope, and timing are constrained because their failure burden has become harder to carry. The paper develops the managed variable as a concept for external actors that remain usable or formally acceptable, but are governed primarily through containment rather than carried through trust. It traces a causal sequence: external value is recognized; exposure burden rises; dependency becomes visible; carrying-structure transition occurs; partner status weakens; managed-variable status emerges; and the interface is narrowed. The framework explains why cross-border investments stall, suppliers are diversified despite efficiency losses, high-performing technology platforms are restricted, financial counterparties are more tightly monitored, experts or advisors are routed through formal channels, and institutional cooperation becomes staged. Drawing on institutional theory, resource dependence theory, transaction cost economics, embeddedness research, systemic risk studies, and organizational decision-making, the paper shows how systems shift from trust to containment before overt rejection, exit, or formal sanctions become visible.

detail.abstract: AI systems are often assumed to improve continuously through learning. Yet many deployed systems eventually experience diminishing economic returns even while technical performance continues improving. This paper introduces the concept of economic plateauing: the point at which continued optimization produces progressively smaller improvements in economically meaningful outcomes despite ongoing technical learning. The paper distinguishes technical improvement from economic value creation and examines several structural causes of plateauing, including optimization saturation, weakening feedback signals, proxy optimization, environmental instability, and external constraints. It argues that continued learning does not necessarily produce durable advantage and that many AI systems eventually converge toward diminishing incremental value creation even while optimization activity persists, a dynamic illustrated by Zillow Offers.

detail.abstract: We compare reviews of Utah Winter Finance Conference papers from six recent frontier AI models and the human program committee. AI scores cluster in the middle, missing exceptional and clearly weak papers — where conference accept/reject decisions hinge. AI-human per-paper agreement is weak, but matches human-human agreement on the same papers (r ≈ 0.19). Disagreement is idiosyncratic judgment, not error; the right question is who predicts papers' future impact better. Humans predict citations better at these extremes; AI predicts better in the middle, where the precise score has little bearing on program outcomes. AI complements, but cannot replace, human reviewers.

detail.abstract: Friction-based platform governance deters low-value actors by raising the cost of continued participation, and it assumes that the actor who bears the friction also executes the governed behavior. That assumption is natural in human-centered platforms, but it breaks down in delegated AI systems, where a human principal pays a one-time continuation cost while an AI agent continues executing at near-zero marginal cost. We call this overlooked precondition friction-target-executor alignment, the correspondence between who bears the friction and who acts, and show that delegated AI breaks this alignment. Exploiting a platform-wide token reset on Moltbook, an agent-first social platform, we find a suppression-selection paradox. Difference-indifferences estimates show that the reset reduces the relative diffusion of strategic exploitation content by about 19% but the share of dysfunctional active posts increases from 29.8% to 49.8%, driven mainly by operational abuse among committed survivors. Re-entry is predicted by principals' prior activity intensity rather than their pre-reset exploitation type, and within-agent behavioral adaptation accounts for about 68% of the composition deterioration. These findings suggest that governance design for delegated AI ecosystems should focus not only on how much friction is imposed, but also on whether that friction is borne by the same actor who ultimately acts.

detail.abstract:
The 2024 publication of NIST FIPS 203, 204, and 205 transformed post-quantum cryptography (PQC) from a research problem into an operational engineering challenge of unprecedented scale. A substantial practitioner and regulatory literature has emerged offering structured lifecycle guidance, yet systematic comparative analysis of these lifecycle models is absent from the peer-reviewed literature.

This paper addresses that gap through a systematic comparative review of eighteen published PQC lifecycle models drawn from government standards bodies, financial sector regulators, multilateral institutions and commercial advisory organisations. The central analytical instrument is a four-dimension scored framework grounded in the lifecycle management literature, assessing each model on governance orientation, sequence dependency management, risk and opportunity management, and resource and capability management.

Five propositions are advanced for empirical evaluation: governance-oriented models are associated with higher migration progress; cost estimation methodology is absent across all surveyed models; stakeholder scope is systematically restricted to security functions; regulatory mandate is associated more strongly than voluntary guidance with governance-led sequencing; and inter-institutional coordination constitutes a near-universal blind spot.

Implications for practitioners, regulators, and future empirical research are discussed.

detail.abstract: Supply chain analysis is a core task for equity analysts. When a disruption event affects one company, analysts need to determine which other firms in the network are exposed, how significant that exposure is, and whether the impact is positive or negative for each bystander. This requires tracing multi-hop dependency relationships across company filings. Standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are poorly suited to this because cross-company dependency links rarely appear in a single retrievable passage. We present FinSupplyKG, a system that constructs a directed Knowledge Graph (KG) from SEC 10-K and 20-F filings for 13 semiconductor companies and uses it to identify and explain indirect supply chain exposures systematically. We build a 43-question adversarial benchmark covering 2-to 3-hop contagion scenarios and compare six systems, from a zero-shot LLM to our DCG-RAG (Directed Contagion Graph RAG). Across three independent runs judged by DeepSeek-R1, DCG-RAG (Tuned) scores 2.9x higher than the best agentic baseline. It does so using 77% fewer tokens. We also introduce a three-tier grading protocol combining automated judging, programmatic corpus verification, and human adjudication, which reveals systematic biases in LLM-based evaluation.

title: The Invisible Business: Why Your Business Exists in the Real World but Not in AI – a Framework for Understanding AI Visibility

detail.title: The Invisible Business: Why Your Business Exists in the Real World but Not in AI – a Framework for Understanding AI Visibility
detail.abstract:
As AI platforms including ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini become primary discovery channels for consumers and professionals, a structural gap has emerged between how businesses exist in the real world and how they are represented in AI-generated responses. This paper introduces the Signal Strength framework and Signal Score methodology, a six-dimension diagnostic system for measuring AI visibility across major language model platforms.

To evaluate the framework against real-world conditions, this study analyzed 20 small businesses across four industries (chiropractic practices, pilates studios, independent realtors, and bed and breakfasts) and four U.S. cities (Atlanta, Raleigh, Austin, and Chicago). Each business was evaluated against ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini using six dimensions of visibility: Identity, Services, Positioning, Location, Reputation, and Discoverability.

No business in the study reached Strong Signal status. Scores ranged from 33 to 57 out of 100, with a mean of 49.7. Structured data implementation was the lowest-scoring dimension across all industries and geographies without exception, with a category average of 25 out of 100. Near-perfect Technical Health scores did not translate to AI discoverability, demonstrating that technical accessibility and AI representation are distinct problems requiring distinct solutions.

These findings indicate that AI invisibility follows structural patterns independent of industry and geography, and that practices optimized for traditional search are insufficient for AI platform representation. The paper identifies five primary causes of AI invisibility and a diagnostic framework for small business owners and practitioners.

detail.abstract:
Background: Historically, clinical trial registries were established to inform the public of available research opportunities and to present key study information. Despite having an institutionally-managed recruitment website since 2020, 60% of study teams with a webpage did not meet their recruitment goals.

Methods: Our improvement project identified three root causes contributing to the ineffectiveness of our recruitment website through surveys of the research community and user experience (UX) testing with external participants using Trymata. We developed three interventions focused on enhanced search functionality, improving website navigation and organization, and standardizing study webpage content review and approval. We aimed to increase the number of submitted webforms by 50% and reduce the average readability level of study webpages to approximately an eighth-grade level by April 2026.

Findings: The implementation of minimum data requirements improved content quality and usability by removing 60% of study webpages with little to no information. This allowed study webpages with the necessary content to receive greater engagement as evidenced by the total number of webform submissions not decreasing. Our team has reviewed 349 study webpages, reducing the average readability from 14.5 to 7.8. Enhancing website navigation, expanding search functionality, and improving study webpage comprehension were associated with a more than a twofold increase in completed webforms from individuals interested in participating in clinical research.

Interpretation: In a landscape where one-third of clinical research studies fail to meet recruitment targets, more effective and efficient recruitment processes are needed. A multipronged recruitment approach that includes passive digital strategies may improve study success. Institutionally managed recruitment websites are a potentially powerful but underutilized tool, and their impact depends on intentional design, accessible content, and centralized management.

detail.abstract: Many important outcomes unfold as dynamic cascades, including product adoption, disease spread, financial distress, and information diffusion. A central challenge is to recover the hidden influence network behind these cascades. Existing methods typically assume a specific diffusion model, and their performance degrades substantially when that assumption is misspecified. We propose CascadeNet, a Jacobian-based machine learning framework for network recovery that does not require specifying a diffusion mechanism. The key idea is that the underlying influence structure can be characterized by the Jacobian of the one-step transition function. CascadeNet first constructs a flexible estimator of the transition function, and further applies Neyman-orthogonal debiasing via the Riesz representer, so that the debiased Jacobian is root-n consistent and asymptotically normal, enabling formal inference on the network structure. We validate CascadeNet in both a simulation exercise and a real-world empirical application. In simulations, where the data-generating process is known, CascadeNet achieves the highest network recovery accuracy across nine common data-generating processes. In an empirical application to COVID-19 transmission across Spain's 52 provinces, CascadeNet recovers transmission networks that are significantly correlated with the true inter-province mobility network, whereas networks recovered by baseline methods show no significant alignment with the ground truth.

detail.abstract: The US is projected to face a shortage of 100,000 critical health care workers by 2028 because of domestic training capacity limitations and caps on work visas. I exploit random variation in the receipt of new H-1B visas via lotteries to study how highly skilled foreign workers affect domestic labor markets and firm production functions. I link the universe of cap-subject H-1B employers to rich administrative data for Medicare-certified nursing homes, including payroll and claims data. Immediately following the lottery news, prior to the worker's arrival, winning nursing homes: (1) win 2 H-1B registrations, (2) reduce employment by 7 full-time equivalent workers, mostly among lower-skilled nurses such as CNAs, and (3) reduce patient volume (output) by 5.8 percent. In further analysis, I show that facilities initially free up capacity by turning away low-complexity patients before shifting production toward high-complexity patients after the high-skilled H-1B worker arrives. These results are consistent with a transition to specialized, higher-margin care provided by the H-1B worker.

title: Characterizing the File Drawer: Evidence from a Meta-Analysis of Parent-Interventions Around the World
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin and University of Texas at Austin

detail.title: Characterizing the File Drawer: Evidence from a Meta-Analysis of Parent-Interventions Around the World

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We conduct a meta-analysis of 82 randomized controlled trials across more than 20 countries to estimate the effects of low-cost, remote parental engagement interventions delivered through text messages, phone calls, and apps. We estimate a joint likelihood function that incorporates both written studies and unwritten studies identified through trial registries, funder records, research labs, evidence clearinghouses, and other sources. By also recording sample sizes for unwritten studies, the model estimates the distribution of standard errors, identifies write-up probabilities conditional on significance, and characterizes the file drawer by estimating effect distributions for written and unwritten studies. Bias-corrected effects are 0.05 SD for test scores, 0.07 SD for grades, 0.05 SD for attendance, and 0.03 SD for enrollment. In the best-identified domain, test scores, statistically insignificant results are still written up at high rates. We also find that larger studies tend to estimate smaller latent effects, which could indicate that true effects are correlated with study precision, violating a common meta-analysis assumption. In smaller-sample domains, our approach helps identify selection probabilities by anchoring the absolute write-up rates. Finally, we estimate the value of additional RCTs to inform adoption decisions. Any single study estimate is unlikely to dissuade adoption because parent interventions have high marginal value of public funds. Instead, future research is most valuable when it can explain heterogeneity across settings.

title: Measuring Housing Quality Using Revealed Preference: A Geographic PageRank Approach
affiliations: Georgia State University - Department of Economics, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and Northwestern University

detail.title: Measuring Housing Quality Using Revealed Preference: A Geographic PageRank Approach

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces Geographic PageRank (GPR), an innovative measure of place quality that is based on migration decisions, employing a recursive algorithm that leverages the full network of migration flows. Using various public data sources, we construct GPR rankings for U.S. counties and metropolitan areas. We also extend the rankings to capture changes over time and differences for population subgroups, providing a versatile data product. As an application, we show that GPR can serve as an "anti-instrument'' for unobserved housing quality when pricing environmental amenities, recovering a correctly signed implicit price of air pollution that is in line with quasi-experimental benchmarks.

title: Predicting Labor Force Types
affiliations: McGill University - Department of Economics, McGill University, McGill University, McGill University and McGill University

detail.title: Predicting Labor Force Types

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
A small group of people accounts for a large majority of flows between labor market states and of spells in un- and non-employment. In this paper, we ask whether it is possible to identify those weakly attached to the labor market during their prime working-age years using information available early in their lives. First, we use information on labor force transitions between ages 30 and 50 contained in the long panel provided by the NLSY79 to identify those weakly connected to the labor market during their prime age. To do so, we use k-means clustering on moments describing observed spells in employment, unemployment, and non-employment between 30 and 50. This points to a group of less attached individuals who are disproportionally female, less educated, and in poor health. In a second step we predict, using information collected at various points before age 30—which we do not use in clustering—whether individuals will turn out to belong to the weakly attached type in their prime age. We find that information from ages 22 to 29 allows predicting membership of the low-attachment group with high precision. Particularly influential is information on early labor market experiences and health. The fact that we can predict weak and strong labor market attachment during prime working age using variables observed in individuals’ twenties suggests the presence of persistent heterogeneity that shapes labor market experiences throughout the life cycle.

title: Future-Proofing Authentication Against Insecure Bootstrapping for 5G Networks: Feasibility, Resiliency, and Accountability
affiliations: University of South Florida, Purdue University, University of Texas at Dallas, University of South Florida, University of South Florida and Purdue University

detail.title: Future-Proofing Authentication Against Insecure Bootstrapping for 5G Networks: Feasibility, Resiliency, and Accountability

keywords.keywords: 5G Cellular NetworksAuthenticationNetwork Performance AnalysisTransitional Post-Quantum Security

detail.abstract: The 5G protocol lacks a robust base station (BS) authentication mechanism during the initial bootstrapping phase, leaving it susceptible to fake BSs, spoofed broadcasts, and large-scale manipulation of System Information Blocks (SIBs). Existing solutions incur high communication overhead, rely on centralized trust, and lack accountability and long-term breach resiliency. Given the inevitability of BS compromise and the severe impact of forged SIBs as the root of trust (e.g., fake alerts, tracking, false roaming), distributed trust, verifiable forgery detection, and audit logging are essential yet remain largely unexplored. These challenges are further amplified by the emergence of quantum-capable adversaries. While NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) standards are widely viewed as a path toward long-term security, their feasibility under 5G's strict packet-size, latency, and broadcast constraints has not been systematically studied. This work presents, to our knowledge, the first comprehensive network-level performance characterization of integrating NIST-PQC standards and conventional digital signatures into 5G BS authentication, showing that direct PQC adoption is impractical due to excessive signature sizes, fragmentation, and protocol-level delays. To address these challenges, we propose BORG, a future-proof authentication framework based on a Hierarchical Identity-Based Threshold Signature with Fail-Stop (HITFS) properties. BORG distributes trust across multiple BSs via threshold signing, enables post-mortem verifiable forgery detection, and provides tamper-evident, PQ-secure audit logging, while maintaining compact signatures that fit within a single SIB1 packet without fragmentation and incurring minimal UE overhead, as validated through our real over-the-air 5G testbed implementation.
